chunks.text: Bisphosphonates: contraindicated with severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30–35 mL/min) — some are avoided in significant renal impairment.
Oral bisphosphonates: avoid in esophageal stricture, achalasia, or inability to sit upright.
Unlike bisphosphonates, denosumab can be used in advanced renal disease (not renally cleared) — watch calcium.
Food, calcium, coffee, and antacids reduce oral bisphosphonate absorption further.
Bisphosphonates have a long skeletal half-life — the effect persists after stopping.
Poor oral absorption (under 1%) → take fasting with plain water.
**Dosing:** alendronate, risedronate — oral, typically weekly; ibandronate — oral, monthly; zoledronic acid — IV, as infrequently as once yearly.
Teriparatide is limited to 2 years lifetime, then follow with an antiresorptive.

Bisphosphonates: less than 10% of an oral dose is absorbed; about half goes to bone, the rest is excreted unchanged in urine. Drug bound in bone is retained for months to years — unlike denosumab, whose effect fades when stopped.
Denosumab 60 mg SC every 6 months; teriparatide 20 mcg SC daily; romosozumab 210 mg SC monthly for one year, then an antiresorptive.

**Oral counseling:** take with a **full glass of water**, first thing in the morning, on an empty stomach well before food, and **remain upright** (sitting or standing) for the specified period after dosing (30 minutes).
Ensure calcium and vitamin D repletion before starting; correct hypocalcemia first.
Consider a **drug holiday after 3–5 years** of oral therapy (osteonecrosis of the jaw, atypical femur fracture with long-term use).
Reassess after 5 years of bisphosphonate (3 for zoledronate); a drug holiday if fracture risk allows.
The “remain upright” point is extremely high-yield: esophageal injury is largely preventable with correct administration.
**Can’t swallow pills?** Yearly IV zoledronic acid or a subcutaneous injectable (e.g., denosumab) avoids the oral route.
Dosing frequency is a major real-world driver of which bisphosphonate a patient actually takes consistently.
Teriparatide, abaloparatide, and romosozumab are the **anabolic exception** — they actively build new bone; most other osteoporosis drugs just slow resorption.
Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis is especially high-yield — it connects to the corticosteroid use for OA/RA in Session 1.

**Choosing therapy:** fracture risk, renal function, previous fracture history, glucocorticoid exposure, adherence (weekly oral vs. yearly IV vs. injectable), and route preference. This checklist is a direct echo of Lecture 1’s clinical decision-making framework.

Applying the whole musculoskeletal pharmacology toolkit: for each patient, name a first-line drug class AND the single biggest safety concern to check before prescribing it.
**1.** Pain and inflammation are related but distinct — treat them accordingly.
**2.** NSAIDs are effective for pain and inflammation, but carry real GI, renal, and cardiovascular risk.
**3.** DMARDs modify the underlying disease process in RA — they do more than mask symptoms.
**4.** Acute gout treatment and chronic urate-lowering therapy are different goals, started at different times.
**5.** Bone pharmacology is fundamentally about the balance between osteoblast and osteoclast activity.
Every mechanism here — COX inhibition, CYP interactions, renal dosing, pharmacogenomics — is Lecture 1’s toolkit applied to one organ system.
**Patient A — acute gout flare, first presentation:** colchicine, NSAID, or corticosteroid; check renal/hepatic function and CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors (colchicine). No ULT yet.
**Patient B — chronic RA, inadequately controlled:** escalate DMARD therapy (biologic); check infection risk — TB and hepatitis screening first.
**Patient C — osteoarthritis + chronic kidney disease:** acetaminophen or a topical NSAID; avoid oral NSAIDs (renal risk).
**Patient D — postmenopausal osteoporosis, high fracture risk:** consider an anabolic agent first; check its limits (teriparatide 2 years; romosozumab CV boxed warning).

**Recall Q1:** acetaminophen is not a reliable first-line choice for an inflammatory joint flare — it has minimal peripheral anti-inflammatory effect; it treats pain and fever, not inflammation itself.

chunks.text: Every case, two answers: **the class** and **the one thing to check before you write it**.
Acid-peptic disease is **a balance between mucosal defense and acid-driven aggression**.
**Aggressive factors:** gastric acid (HCl), pepsin, H. pylori infection, NSAID use (suppresses protective prostaglandins).
**Protective (mucosal defense) factors:** mucus–bicarbonate layer; prostaglandins (stimulate mucus/bicarbonate, maintain mucosal blood flow); epithelial cell turnover.
**GERD:** reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus, causing heartburn/regurgitation and, over time, esophageal mucosal injury.
**Peptic ulcer disease (PUD):** a break in the mucosa of the stomach or duodenum; most commonly caused by H. pylori infection or NSAID use.
**Gastritis:** inflammation of the gastric mucosa — acute (e.g., NSAID- or alcohol-related) or chronic (e.g., H. pylori-driven).
Over 90% of peptic ulcers are caused by H. pylori infection or NSAIDs; bile also counts as an aggressive factor.

Disease appears when aggressive factors win or defenses fall: aggressive factors (acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs) overwhelm mucus, bicarbonate and prostaglandin-driven blood flow → mucosal injury → GERD, ulcer or gastritis.
**NSAIDs block COX-1 prostaglandins**, removing mucosal protection — the clearest example of tipping the balance.
**H. pylori urease makes ammonia**, which injures the mucosa.
**Stress and critical illness raise the risk of stress ulceration.**
**Gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison) causes severe acid hypersecretion.**
**Gastrin, histamine, and acetylcholine all converge on the parietal cell proton pump.** H2 blockers cut one input (histamine); PPIs block the last step itself.

**Physiology of acid secretion:** gastrin acts mainly by releasing histamine from ECL cells; acetylcholine (M3) stimulates the parietal cell directly; somatostatin from antral D cells turns gastrin off.
GERD, PUD and gastritis share the same drug toolkit: reduce acid, protect the mucosa, and/or eradicate H. pylori.
H. pylori and NSAIDs cause most PUD.

**Antacids** neutralize acid already made; **H2 blockers** block the histamine input; **PPIs** block the final common pathway — the most potent acid suppression.

chunks.text: **Antacids — mechanism: directly neutralize existing gastric acid (do not reduce acid production).** **Acid in stomach** → **antacid base (Al/Mg hydroxide, calcium carbonate) neutralizes H+** → **higher gastric pH** → rapid but short relief.

**H2RAs — mechanism: competitively block histamine at the H2 receptor on parietal cells.** Histamine from ECL cells → H2 receptor → cAMP rises → stimulates the proton pump; famotidine occupies the receptor competitively, so less acid.
**PPIs — mechanism: irreversibly inhibit the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase proton pump — the final common pathway of acid secretion.**
**PPI prodrug activated by acid** → **binds H⁺/K⁺ ATPase irreversibly** → **final step of acid secretion blocked**.

Pathway: enteric-coated prodrug absorbed in the small intestine → reaches the parietal cell canaliculus → activated by acid → binds a cysteine on H⁺/K⁺-ATPase covalently → **pump irreversibly blocked until new pumps are made**.
PPIs achieve substantially greater acid-suppression potency and longer duration of effect than H2RAs (Figure 4: potency 95 vs. 45; duration 90 vs. 50, illustrative).
H2 blockers inhibit 60–70% of 24-hour acid secretion; PPIs inhibit 90–98% because they block the final common pathway.
**Antacids:** onset is rapid, but duration is short — best for intermittent, mild symptom relief.
**H2RAs:** mild-to-moderate GERD, maintenance therapy, adjunct for peptic ulcer healing; best at controlling **nocturnal** acid.
**PPIs:** first-line for GERD, PUD healing, and H. pylori regimens.
Infrequent heartburn (fewer than three times per week): antacids or as-needed H2 blockers; antacids act faster but last 1–2 hours vs. 6–10 hours.
PPIs heal over 90% of duodenal ulcers within 4 weeks; GERD recurs in over 80% within 6 months of stopping.
Stress-related bleeding prophylaxis in high-risk ICU patients: an oral PPI if enteral meds are possible, otherwise IV H2 blocker or PPI.

**PPI long-term adverse effects: vitamin B12 deficiency, hypomagnesemia, increased fracture risk, and increased risk of Clostridioides difficile infection** — also pneumonia and acute interstitial nephritis.

Magnesium and aluminum antacids are renally excreted: avoid long-term use in renal insufficiency.
**Antacids can impair absorption of many other oral drugs — separate dosing by at least 2 hours.** They bind levothyroxine, quinolones, tetracyclines, and iron.
**Omeprazole (a CYP2C19 inhibitor) can reduce clopidogrel activation, blunting its antiplatelet effect.** Omeprazole and esomeprazole both inhibit CYP2C19.
**Cimetidine is a potent CYP450 inhibitor (1A2, 2C19, 3A4)** — a callback to Lecture 1: it raises warfarin, phenytoin, and theophylline levels.
Famotidine has minimal CYP450 interaction.
Antacids should not be given within 2 hours of tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, itraconazole, and iron.
With clopidogrel, prefer pantoprazole or rabeprazole (minimal CYP2C19 inhibition).
Less acid lowers absorption of ketoconazole, itraconazole, digoxin, and atazanavir.
**PPIs are best absorbed/effective when taken 30–60 minutes before a meal** (timed to peak pump activity) — they work best on actively secreting pumps.
CYP2C19 genotype alters PPI exposure; ultrarapid metabolizers may need higher doses.
Famotidine needs renal dose adjustment.
PPIs: food cuts bioavailability by about 50%; half-life about 1.5 hours yet acid inhibition lasts up to 24 hours; full effect takes 3–4 days.
PPIs need no renal dose reduction; consider reduction in severe liver impairment.
Many patients stay on PPIs far longer than necessary — the long-term adverse-effect list drives deprescribing conversations.
Ask: what happens to warfarin or phenytoin levels if cimetidine is added? They rise (CYP inhibition).
Name stems: **-prazole** PPIs (irreversibly block H+/K+ ATPase); **-tidine** H2 receptor antagonists (famotidine, ranitidine, cimetidine; competitively block the H2 receptor).

chunks.text: Why before breakfast? PPIs only hit pumps that are actively secreting; a meal switches pumps on, so the drug should be peaking when they turn on.
Why does PPI use cause B12 deficiency? Acid frees B12 from food protein; less acid, less B12 released.
Antacid bowel effects: **Al**uminum **al**ways constipates; **Mg** = **m**ore **g**oing (diarrhea).
Shielding the mucosa (sucralfate, misoprostol, bismuth) and treating the cause (H. pylori eradication).
**H. pylori is the leading identifiable cause of peptic ulcer disease — eradication, not just acid suppression, is the goal.**
Sucralfate — barrier over the ulcer base.

chunks.text: **Sucralfate:** in acid (pH below 4) it polymerizes, binds the ulcer base and **forms a protective barrier**; requires an acidic environment to activate; minimal systemic absorption.
**Misoprostol:** **a prostaglandin E1 analog** — acts on EP receptors to reduce acid and increase mucus and bicarbonate, **restoring the protective prostaglandin tone that NSAIDs suppress**.
**Why H. pylori needs multiple drugs:** it lives in gastric mucus and buffers acid with urease-made ammonia.

A PPI raises gastric pH so bacteria enter a replicating state and antibiotics are more stable; amoxicillin blocks cell wall synthesis; clarithromycin (50S ribosome) or metronidazole adds a second antibiotic.
Sucralfate is sucrose complexed to sulfated aluminum hydroxide; less than 3% is absorbed.
Bismuth coats ulcers, has direct antimicrobial effects and binds enterotoxins (traveler’s diarrhea).
**Triple therapy:** PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin for 10–14 days (usual duration 14 days).

**Bismuth quadruple therapy:** PPI (or H2RA) + bismuth subsalicylate + metronidazole + tetracycline — preferred where clarithromycin resistance is a concern, with recent macrolide exposure, or with penicillin allergy.
**Penicillin allergy:** substitute metronidazole for amoxicillin in triple therapy.
Misoprostol is used specifically to prevent NSAID-induced ulcers.
Misoprostol cuts NSAID-induced ulcers to less than 3% and ulcer complications by 50%, but dosing 3–4 times daily and diarrhea limit use.
**Misoprostol: contraindicated in pregnancy — potent uterotonic/abortifacient effect** (boxed warning). Common adverse effects: diarrhea and cramping.

chunks.text: Avoid tetracycline in pregnancy and in children.
Penicillin allergy rules out amoxicillin in H. pylori regimens.
**Separate sucralfate from other drugs by 2 hours** (give on an empty stomach, separated from antacids/PPIs).
**Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4** — must not be combined with simvastatin, lovastatin, or ergotamine.
**Metronidazole plus alcohol causes a disulfiram-like reaction.**
Sucralfate has minimal systemic absorption.
**Confirm eradication with testing (urea breath test or stool antigen) after completing therapy** — at least 4 weeks after, with the PPI held for 2 weeks (PPIs cause false negatives).
Counsel on completing a 10–14 day, 3–4 drug regimen — multi-drug regimens are a classic adherence problem.
After antibiotics, continue the PPI once daily for a total of 4–6 weeks to complete ulcer healing.
Case: confirmed H. pylori, penicillin allergy, and a macrolide two months ago. **Which eradication regimen is more appropriate for this patient, and why?**
Answer: bismuth quadruple therapy — recent macrolide exposure raises clarithromycin-resistance concern and the allergy rules out standard triple therapy.
Misoprostol’s pregnancy contraindication links to its other use (labor induction/medical abortion) — mechanism explains the contraindication.

Name stems: **-prostol** prostaglandin analogs (misoprostol); **-cillin** penicillins (amoxicillin; blocks cell wall synthesis); **-thromycin** macrolides (clarithromycin; -mycin alone is not reliable, e.g., gentamicin); sucralfate and bismuth subsalicylate share no stem.

Regimen: Triple, penicillin-allergic · Drugs: PPI + metronidazole + clarithromycin · Use when: Penicillin allergy (substitute metronidazole for amoxicillin)
Regimen: Bismuth quadruple · Drugs: PPI (or H2RA) + bismuth subsalicylate + metronidazole + tetracycline · Use when: Clarithromycin resistance, recent macrolide, penicillin allergy
Regimen: Test of cure · Drugs: Urea breath test or stool antigen · Use when: ≥ 4 weeks after therapy, PPI held 2 weeks

Why is misoprostol forbidden in pregnancy? It is a prostaglandin — the same uterotonic effect that makes it a labor-induction drug.
Allergic to penicillin or recently on a macrolide? **Go Bismuth (quadruple)**.
**Four receptor systems feed one final common reflex.**

Four inputs converge on the **vomiting center in the medulla**: **gut and vagal (5-HT3)**, the **chemoreceptor trigger zone (D2, 5-HT3, NK1)**, the **vestibular (H1, M1)** system, and **higher cortical (anxiety, anticipatory)** input — benzodiazepines and cannabinoids.
**Motion sickness is vestibular** — H1/M1 blockers (meclizine, scopolamine) fit it.
Matching each drug to its input pathway (Figure 9) is the single most testable concept in this section.
Ondansetron — 5-HT3 antagonist.

chunks.text: **5-HT3 antagonists** block serotonin at gut vagal afferents/CTZ.

Chemotherapy or gut irritation damages enterochromaffin cells → serotonin binds 5-HT3 on vagal afferents and the CTZ → signal to the vomiting center; **ondansetron blocks 5-HT3, so no signal reaches the vomiting center**.
**D2 antagonists** block dopamine at the CTZ (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine).
**NK1 antagonists** block substance P/neurokinin at the CTZ (aprepitant).
**H1/M1 antagonists** block histamine/acetylcholine from the vestibular system (meclizine, scopolamine).

**Metoclopramide — mechanism: D2 antagonism (antiemetic effect) plus enhancement of upper-GI motility (prokinetic effect).** D2 blockade in the CTZ → less nausea; D2 blockade plus **5-HT4 agonism** in the gut → more acetylcholine → faster gastric emptying.
Dronabinol (CB1 agonist) crosses the blood-brain barrier and activates CB1 receptors in the vomiting center, CTZ and hypothalamus, reducing neurotransmitter release → less nausea, more appetite.
Mechanism is distinct from the four pathways (5-HT3, D2, NK1, H1/M1).
**Pathophysiology of vomiting:** the vomiting center sits in the lateral medullary reticular formation; the CTZ (area postrema) lies outside the blood-brain barrier.
Ondansetron: give before chemotherapy; oral ODT and IV forms are available.
**Metoclopramide clinical uses: nausea/vomiting and diabetic gastroparesis.**

**Dronabinol — a synthetic cannabinoid (CB1 receptor agonist) used for refractory chemotherapy-induced nausea/vomiting and appetite stimulation.** Typically reserved for patients who do not respond adequately to standard antiemetics.
**Chemotherapy:** combine classes with different targets — a 5-HT3 antagonist, an NK1 antagonist, and dexamethasone; avoid duplicating the same mechanism.
**Match drug to cause:** gut/vagal triggers respond to 5-HT3 antagonists; the CTZ to D2 or NK1 antagonists.
5-HT3 antagonists control vagal and chemotherapy emesis but poorly control motion sickness; palonosetron also prevents delayed emesis.
**Pharmacokinetics & pharmacodynamics (5-HT3):** first-generation agents have half-lives of 4–9 hours; palonosetron 40 hours; no dose cut in renal insufficiency.
NK1 antagonist + 5-HT3 antagonist + dexamethasone prevents acute emesis in 80–90% of highly emetogenic chemotherapy patients.
Benzodiazepines (lorazepam, diazepam) prevent anticipatory vomiting before chemotherapy.
Metoclopramide — **boxed warning: risk of tardive dyskinesia, particularly with prolonged use or high doses — limit duration of therapy.** Avoid beyond 12 weeks.

Ondansetron: serotonin syndrome risk with other serotonergic drugs; QT risk with other QT-prolonging drugs.
Cannabinoids: **additive CNS depression with sedatives and alcohol**.
Aprepitant is a CYP3A4 substrate/inhibitor: lowers INR with warfarin; dexamethasone dose is often reduced with it.
**CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers may respond less well to ondansetron.**
**Metoclopramide: renal dosing needed; CYP2D6 poor metabolizers need lower doses** (higher exposure).
**Dronabinol is Schedule III; nabilone is Schedule II.** Use with caution in older adults.
Metoclopramide duration matters — many students remember only that it helps nausea.
Case: first-trimester nausea and vomiting not helped by dietary changes. **Which antiemetic class has the most established safety profile for use in this patient?**

Pyridoxine (vitamin B6), often with doxylamine, is typically first-line; ondansetron is commonly used too, though first-trimester data continue to evolve — weigh maternal benefit against fetal risk and consult current guidance.
Pyridoxine is a vitamin — a preview of Session 2’s vitamins and supplements.
Cannabinoid pharmacology is an expanding area in the newest Katzung edition.

chunks.text: Why does ondansetron fail for motion sickness? Motion sickness comes through the vestibular system (H1/M1), not the gut’s serotonin pathway.
Why combine ondansetron, aprepitant and dexamethasone? Each hits a different target; stacking different mechanisms beats doubling one.
**SeT-D-NK-HM:** ondan**set**ron 5-HT3 · metoclopramide **D**2 · apre**pitant** NK1 · meclizine/scopolamine **H**1/**M**1 — plus dronabinol CB1.
**Opposite problems, each with its own family of mechanisms.** Four laxative buckets: bulk-forming, osmotic, stimulant, secretagogue — sort any laxative name into one of them.
**Bulk-forming** (psyllium, methylcellulose): absorb water, increase stool bulk and transit; slowest onset; generally safest for long-term use.
**Osmotic** (polyethylene glycol, lactulose, magnesium hydroxide): draw water into the lumen; fast, reliable onset.
**Stimulant** (senna, bisacodyl): directly stimulate enteric nerves/motility; reserve for short-term or breakthrough use.
**Secretagogues** (lubiprostone, linaclotide): increase intestinal chloride and fluid secretion; used for chronic constipation, IBS-C.
Polyethylene glycol 3350 — osmotic; first-line for chronic constipation.

chunks.text: Laxative mechanisms: bulk-forming holds water and expands stool; osmotic draws water into the lumen; stimulant activates enteric nerves; secretagogue increases chloride and fluid secretion → softer stool, faster transit.
**Loperamide — a peripheral opioid-receptor agonist that slows GI motility without significant CNS (opioid) effects at normal doses.**
Opioid brake on the gut: opioid agonist binds mu receptors on enteric neurons → less acetylcholine release → slower peristalsis, longer transit → more water absorbed, firmer stool.
Diphenoxylate/atropine — a combination opioid-receptor agonist; **atropine is included at a subtherapeutic dose specifically to discourage misuse/overdose**.
Bismuth subsalicylate — antisecretory, mild antimicrobial, and anti-inflammatory effects; also used for dyspepsia.
Opioid receptor antagonists (methylnaltrexone, naloxegol, naldemedine, alvimopan) block gut μ-receptors without entering the CNS, so analgesia is kept.
**PEG is first-line for chronic constipation**; magnesium laxatives need caution in CKD.

Onset (Figure 2, illustrative): osmotic ~2 h and stimulant ~8 h act fastest; secretagogue ~1 day; stool softener ~2 days and bulk-forming ~60 h take longest. **A patient who needs relief tonight is not a bulk-forming candidate.**
Stimulants cause cramping and are for short-term use. Lubiprostone causes nausea; linaclotide causes diarrhea.

chunks.text: **Avoid antimotility agents (loperamide, diphenoxylate/atropine) in suspected infectious/inflammatory diarrhea (e.g., C. difficile, invasive bacterial infection) — can worsen outcomes by delaying toxin/pathogen clearance.** Also avoid in bloody or febrile diarrhea.

Bulk-forming agents need adequate fluids and are avoided in obstruction. Linaclotide: contraindicated in mechanical obstruction and in children under 2; secretagogues avoided in mechanical obstruction.
Diphenoxylate/atropine is **Schedule V**; avoided in young children (the slides give under 2 and under 6; the profile says under 6).
Antidiarrheals should not be used with bloody diarrhea, high fever, or systemic toxicity.
Psyllium: separate from other drugs by 2 hours.
Bisacodyl: do not crush; avoid with antacids or milk.
Loperamide has limited CNS entry because of P-gp efflux.
Senna works in 6–12 hours orally; bisacodyl in 6–10 hours orally and 30–60 minutes rectally.
Slowing transit in an infectious or inflammatory process can worsen the picture (toxic megacolon risk in C. difficile) — “stopping diarrhea” is not always the right first move.

Case: profuse watery diarrhea and fever three days after clindamycin. **Is loperamide an appropriate choice for symptomatic relief in this patient?** No — think C. difficile; avoid antimotility agents and treat the infection (oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin).

**Step therapy, escalating with disease severity:** 5-ASA agents for mild disease → short-term corticosteroids for flares → immunomodulators for maintenance → biologics/small molecules for moderate-to-severe disease.
This escalation ladder is the organizing framework for every IBD drug — ask where each drug “lives” on it.

chunks.text: **Mesalamine, sulfasalazine — anti-inflammatory action local to the GI mucosa.** Sulfasalazine reaches the colon → colonic bacteria cleave the azo bond → 5-ASA (mesalamine) plus sulfapyridine released → 5-ASA acts on mucosa, reducing inflammatory mediators → less mucosal inflammation.
Azathioprine is converted to 6-mercaptopurine → metabolized to thioguanine nucleotides → block purine synthesis in lymphocytes → fewer proliferating T and B cells → slow, sustained remission.

**Targeted therapy:** TNF-α inhibitors block tumor necrosis factor-alpha (infliximab, adalimumab); the integrin inhibitor blocks α4β7 integrin-mediated leukocyte gut-homing (vedolizumab); the IL-12/23 inhibitor blocks interleukin-12 and -23 signaling (ustekinumab); the JAK inhibitor blocks intracellular JAK signaling (tofacitinib).
Vedolizumab is the most **gut-selective** agent — less systemic immunosuppression than TNF inhibitors, JAK inhibitors, or thiopurines.
**Chemistry & formulations:** azo compounds (sulfasalazine, balsalazide, olsalazine) are cleaved by colonic bacteria; mesalamine formulations release 5-ASA at set pH or times.
5-ASA: first-line for mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis; more limited role in Crohn disease.
Corticosteroids: short-term induction of remission during an acute flare; not appropriate for long-term maintenance given cumulative toxicity.
Immunomodulators: long-term maintenance of remission; onset is slow (weeks to months) — not useful for acute flares.

Why is vedolizumab gut-selective? α4β7 integrin is the gut-homing address tag; block it and leukocytes can’t enter the bowel, while immunity elsewhere is spared.
Why give folic acid with sulfasalazine? Sulfapyridine causes folate deficiency.
**What patients take on their own can change how their medications work.** Ask one question about any vitamin: can it build up to toxic levels?

**Fat-soluble (A, D, E, K):** stored in adipose tissue and the liver; accumulate with excess intake — real toxicity risk; absorption depends on dietary fat and bile, impaired by fat-malabsorption conditions.
**Water-soluble (B-complex, C):** not significantly stored — excreted renally; toxicity is rare except at very high supplemental doses; deficiency develops more quickly without ongoing intake.

Figure 8 (illustrative storage/toxicity-risk index): vitamin A 85 and D 90 (fat-soluble) vs. C 10 and B-complex 8 (water-soluble). Vitamin D and A toxicity from OTC overuse are the clearest real examples.
Cyanocobalamin (B12), folic acid, vitamin D, phytonadione (K1), ferrous sulfate.

chunks.text: **B12 absorption:** dietary B12 is bound to food protein → stomach acid and pepsin release it → free B12 binds intrinsic factor from parietal cells → the complex is absorbed in the terminal ileum.
Reduced vitamin K is recycled by VKORC1; **warfarin blocks VKORC1, so fewer active factors** — active vitamin K carboxylates clotting factors II, VII, IX, X — so fewer active factors.

**Two ways to lower warfarin’s effect:** dietary vitamin K opposes it pharmacodynamically (supports clotting factor synthesis); St. John’s wort induces CYP enzymes and speeds clearance — a pharmacokinetic interaction. **Result: lower INR and less anticoagulation.**
**Enteral nutrition** (oral or tube feeding) is preferred whenever the gut is functional — **“if the gut works, use it”**; lower infection/complication risk.

**Parenteral nutrition** is delivered intravenously, bypassing the GI tract entirely; reserved for a non-functional or inaccessible GI tract; requires close monitoring — electrolyte shifts, refeeding syndrome, catheter-related infection (the main parenteral risk).
Treat B12 deficiency with intramuscular or high-dose oral B12.
**Vitamin B12 deficiency:** megaloblastic anemia and neurologic symptoms/neuropathy that can become irreversible if treatment is delayed.

chunks.text: St. John’s wort: avoid with SSRIs, transplant drugs, HIV protease inhibitors, oral contraceptives, warfarin.
**St. John’s Wort — CYP3A4 induction; reduces effectiveness of many drugs (warfarin, oral contraceptives, some antiretrovirals).**
**Ginkgo biloba and fish oil — can increase bleeding risk, especially combined with anticoagulants/antiplatelets.**
**At risk for B12 deficiency:** long-term PPI or H2 blocker use, metformin (impairs ileal uptake), bariatric surgery, older age, vegan diets.
St. John’s wort activates PXR, inducing CYP 3A4, 2C9, 1A2 and P-glycoprotein: lowers digoxin, birth control, cyclosporine, HIV drugs, warfarin; serotonin syndrome with antidepressants.
Garlic, ginkgo and ginseng have antiplatelet effects — avoid or monitor with anticoagulants and around surgery.
Coenzyme Q10 and melatonin may decrease warfarin’s effect; glucosamine may increase the INR.
Fat-soluble vitamin absorption depends on dietary fat and bile.
Monitor B12 in long-term PPI or metformin users.
**Keep vitamin K intake consistent rather than avoiding it.** Check INR when starting or stopping any supplement; stopping St. John’s wort can raise INR.
**Refeeding:** start feeding slowly in malnourished patients; check phosphate, potassium and magnesium daily at the start; give thiamine before feeding begins.
**Supplements are not held to the same FDA premarket efficacy/safety standards as prescription drugs — potency and purity can vary by product.**
Always ask patients specifically about supplement use — many don’t mention it unless asked; counsel them to disclose all supplement use to every prescriber and pharmacist.

chunks.text: Why tell warfarin patients to keep vitamin K steady rather than avoid it? INR is dosed against their usual intake; swings, not the vitamin itself, cause trouble.
Fat-soluble **ADEK** stay; water-soluble **B and C** wash away.
Applying the whole GI & Nutrition toolkit: for each patient, name a first-line approach AND the single biggest safety concern to check before prescribing/counseling.
**1.** Acid-peptic disease and antiemetics are managed by targeting specific points along well-defined pathways (parietal cell secretion; the vomiting reflex).
**2.** PPIs are the most potent antisecretory agents, but long-term use carries real risks that warrant periodic reassessment.

**3.** IBD therapy follows a step-wise escalation matched to disease severity. **4.** Biologic agents share mechanisms and immunosuppression risk across organ systems. **5.** Nutrition and supplements are not inert.
Pharmacology is cumulative, not siloed by unit: biologic mechanisms (Lecture 2) and drug-metabolism/interaction concepts (Lecture 1) reappear here in a new organ system.
**Patient A — GERD symptoms, needs rapid occasional relief:** an antacid for occasional relief; an H2 blocker or PPI if frequent.
**Patient B — confirmed H. pylori, penicillin allergy:** bismuth quadruple therapy.
**Patient C — moderate-to-severe Crohn disease, inadequately controlled on azathioprine:** a biologic or small molecule such as an anti-TNF agent.
**Patient D — warfarin patient starting an herbal mood supplement:** counsel on St. John’s wort and check INR.
**Recall Q1:** PPIs block the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase proton pump itself — the final common pathway for gastrin, histamine, and acetylcholine — unlike H2RAs, which block only the histamine input.

chunks.text: Every case, two answers: **the approach** and **the one thing to check**.
**One regulatory template governs thyroid, adrenal, and gonadal control alike.**

**Figure 1. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): the hypothalamus drives the anterior pituitary, which drives a target endocrine gland, whose peripheral hormone produces end-organ effects and negatively feeds back to suppress the levels above it.**
This is the conceptual spine for the unit — thyroid, adrenal and gonadal pharmacology all map onto this three-level axis; return to it every time a new gland appears.
The peripheral hormone negatively feeds back on the hypothalamus/pituitary above it — which explains why every exogenous hormone therapy in the unit suppresses the levels above it.
Somatropin (GH deficiency); octreotide, lanreotide, pegvisomant (GH excess); cabergoline, bromocriptine (prolactin); desmopressin (DI); tolvaptan, demeclocycline (SIADH).

chunks.text: GH axis (Figure 2): pituitary somatotroph releases GH → GH drives liver IGF-1 production → octreotide and lanreotide bind somatostatin receptors and lower GH release.
Pegvisomant blocks the GH receptor so IGF-1 falls → acromegaly symptoms improve (monitor IGF-1). GH rises on pegvisomant, so GH is not used to monitor it.

Dopamine normally inhibits prolactin release — dopamine agonists restore that inhibitory tone. Hypothalamic dopamine is the brake on lactotrophs; prolactinoma or drugs (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) lift the brake.
Cabergoline or bromocriptine activate D2 receptors → prolactin release falls and the tumor often shrinks → cycles and fertility return; galactorrhea resolves.
ADH (Figure 4): ADH binds the V2 receptor in the collecting duct → aquaporin-2 channels insert → water is reabsorbed and urine concentrates.
Desmopressin boosts this (diabetes insipidus); tolvaptan or demeclocycline blunt it (SIADH) → free water retained in DI therapy, excreted in SIADH therapy.
Anterior pituitary hormones & their hypothalamic regulators: continuous (not pulsatile) GnRH analogs down-regulate GnRH receptors and suppress LH and FSH.
**●  GH deficiency:** treated with recombinant human growth hormone (somatropin); monitor growth velocity in children and IGF-1 levels in adults.

**●  GH excess (acromegaly):** treated with somatostatin analogs (octreotide, lanreotide — suppress GH release), the GH-receptor antagonist pegvisomant, or dopamine agonists (cabergoline) in select cases.
**●  Clinical pearl:** octreotide also has major uses outside the pituitary axis — variceal bleeding and carcinoid syndrome — worth flagging as a cross-system agent.
**●  Indication:** octreotide and lanreotide treat acromegaly; octreotide also treats carcinoid syndrome and variceal bleeding.
Hyperprolactinemia: dopamine agonists are first-line — cabergoline, bromocriptine — used for prolactinomas and drug-induced hyperprolactinemia.

Diabetes insipidus (ADH deficiency/resistance): desmopressin (DDAVP) for central DI. SIADH (ADH excess): fluid restriction first-line; vasopressin-receptor antagonists (tolvaptan) or demeclocycline for refractory cases.
**●  Somatropin (GH deficiency):** monitor growth velocity or IGF-1.
**●  Adverse effects:** GI upset, gallstones and bradycardia with octreotide and lanreotide (also glucose changes).

Octreotide is 45 times more potent than somatostatin at inhibiting GH; somatostatin analogs come as long-acting monthly depots. Cabergoline’s half-life is about 65 hours.
**●  Monitoring:** pregnancy testing and prolactin monitoring (dopamine agonists). Monitor IGF-1 for acromegaly therapy.
Pegvisomant does not lower GH secretion and may let the adenoma grow — monitor IGF-I and yearly pituitary MRI.
DI vs. SIADH is a classic exam pairing — opposite problems; anchor it to "which way does free water move" rather than drug names in isolation.
Octreotide reappears in GI/variceal contexts — drug classes are not siloed by organ system.
Hyperprolactinemia causes hypogonadism — infertility, amenorrhea, galactorrhea in women; low libido and ED in men; macroadenomas can compress the optic nerves.
Oxytocin (posterior pituitary) is given IV to start or augment labor; it also triggers milk letdown. Its half-life is about 5 minutes.

**Figure 6. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): iodide trapping, organification, and coupling produce T3/T4, which undergo peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion; methimazole and PTU block organification and coupling, while PTU additionally blocks peripheral conversion.**
Figure 6 is the key to the next slides: PTU, not methimazole, is preferred in thyroid storm because it blocks an extra step.

chunks.text: **Mechanism: synthetic T4, converted peripherally to active T3.**
Levothyroxine path (Figure 5): tablet taken on an empty stomach → absorbed in the small intestine; calcium, iron and antacid binders block it.
T4 converted to active T3 in tissues → T3 binds nuclear receptors and restores metabolism → TSH falls to the target range (recheck at 6–8 weeks).
Methimazole and PTU block organification and coupling; PTU also blocks peripheral T4→T3 conversion — a faster symptomatic effect in crisis.
Storm targets (Figure 7): Graves thyroid makes excess hormone — PTU blocks synthesis; hormone is released — iodine (after PTU) blocks release.

T4 converts to T3 in tissues — PTU, propranolol and steroids block conversion; T3 stimulates beta receptors — propranolol blunts tachycardia and tremor; crisis settles with fluids, cooling and support.
Thyroid physiology: large doses of iodine inhibit organification (Wolff-Chaikoff block); amiodarone, contrast, β blockers and corticosteroids inhibit T4-to-T3 conversion.
Levothyroxine: first-line for hypothyroidism; narrow therapeutic index — dose titrated using TSH (primary hypothyroidism) with repeat labs every 6–8 weeks after a dose change.
About 1.6 mcg/kg/day is full replacement; estrogen raises needs. **●  Pregnancy:** often raises dose needs; monitor TSH closely.
Methimazole: first-line for most non-pregnant patients — once-daily dosing, more convenient; avoid in the first trimester of pregnancy (teratogenic risk).
PTU: preferred in the first trimester of pregnancy and in thyroid storm. PTU first trimester (lower teratogenic risk) and thyroid storm (also blocks peripheral T4→T3 conversion).
**A life-threatening hyperthyroid crisis requiring rapid, multi-pronged therapy.** Thyroid storm is treated with four drugs that hit four targets.

Beta-blockers (propranolol) — control adrenergic symptoms (tachycardia, tremor) and blunt peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion. PTU (preferred over methimazole) — blocks new hormone synthesis and peripheral conversion.

Iodine solution (given after PTU/methimazole) — acutely blocks hormone release; must follow the antithyroid drug to avoid providing substrate for new synthesis. Corticosteroids — blunt peripheral conversion and treat relative adrenal insufficiency.

Laboratory diagnosis of Graves disease: suppressed TSH with high free thyroid hormone. Management of Graves disease: antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine, or thyroidectomy; methimazole preferred except in pregnancy and storm.
Pregnant hypothyroid patients often need about 25–30% more levothyroxine; add two extra doses a week as soon as pregnancy is confirmed.
Methimazole boxed warning: agranulocytosis, hepatotoxicity. PTU boxed warning: severe hepatotoxicity (more than methimazole) — reserve for specific indications.

**Glucocorticoid power and mineralocorticoid balance — and what happens when therapy stops.**

**Figure 9. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): chronic exogenous glucocorticoid use suppresses CRH and ACTH via negative feedback, reducing endogenous cortisol production — abrupt withdrawal can precipitate adrenal insufficiency.**
This is the single most clinically important concept in the glucocorticoid section — it explains why tapering (not stopping) is the standard of care.

chunks.text: Glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisone, dexamethasone): anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects, with a spectrum of relative potency and mineralocorticoid activity across agents.

Signaling (Figure 8): prednisone or cortisol crosses the cell membrane → binds the cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptor → the complex moves into the nucleus → switches on anti-inflammatory genes and represses NF-kB cytokines → fewer inflammatory cells and mediators.
Mineralocorticoids (fludrocortisone): promote renal sodium retention and potassium excretion.

Synthesis chain (Figure 10): cholesterol enters the adrenal cortex → CYP enzymes convert it to cortisol and aldosterone → ketoconazole blocks several enzymes; metyrapone blocks the last cortisol step (11-beta-hydroxylase).
Then cortisol or aldosterone binds its receptor → mifepristone blocks the glucocorticoid receptor; spironolactone blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor. Receptor blockers leave hormone levels high.
Glucocorticoids are used across nearly every organ system for inflammatory/autoimmune disease.

Fludrocortisone: replacement therapy in primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), alongside a glucocorticoid — primary adrenal insufficiency needs BOTH hormone classes replaced, not just cortisol.
**●  Ketoconazole:** inhibits multiple steps in steroidogenesis (CYP enzymes); used for Cushing syndrome; significant drug-interaction and hepatotoxicity concerns.
**●  Metyrapone:** blocks the final step of cortisol synthesis (11-β-hydroxylase); used diagnostically and for Cushing syndrome.

**●  Mifepristone:** a glucocorticoid-receptor antagonist; used for hyperglycemia associated with Cushing syndrome when surgery is not an option (distinct from its progesterone-receptor antagonist use in pregnancy termination).

**●  Spironolactone:** a mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonist; used for hyperaldosteronism and as a potassium-sparing diuretic — ties back to the diuretic pharmacology concepts from earlier coursework.
Addison disease: hydrocortisone 20–30 mg daily (more during stress) plus fludrocortisone 0.05–0.2 mg/d.
Dexamethasone suppression test diagnoses Cushing syndrome; antenatal glucocorticoids reduce neonatal respiratory distress.
**●  Adverse effects:** hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, infection, mood change, cataracts, adrenal suppression.

Chronic steroids suppress CRH and ACTH — abrupt withdrawal risks adrenal crisis; taper. Chronic suppression leaves the axis unable to resume adequate cortisol quickly — taper, don’t stop abruptly.

Case: chronic high-dose prednisone for a rheumatologic condition, stopped abruptly after running out of refills; now hypotension, weakness, nausea, confusion. **What is the most likely cause of this presentation, and how should it be managed?**
**This presentation is consistent with acute adrenal insufficiency (adrenal crisis) from abrupt glucocorticoid withdrawal after HPA-axis suppression.**
**Management requires immediate IV hydrocortisone (which has both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity) and IV fluids — this is a medical emergency, not a routine medication-refill issue.**
The fix for a missed refill here is not "just restart the pill" — it is emergent IV steroid replacement; tapering protects against it.

Mifepristone’s dual identity (glucocorticoid-receptor antagonist here vs. progesterone-receptor antagonist elsewhere) is worth flagging explicitly — don’t conflate the two uses or assume a single mechanism.

Drug names reveal the class: **-tide** somatostatin analog (octreotide, lanreotide; lowers GH release); **-pressin** vasopressin analog (desmopressin; central diabetes insipidus); **-vaptan** V2 antagonist (tolvaptan; SIADH).

**-ergoline** dopamine agonist, ergot-derived (cabergoline; lowers prolactin); **-thyroxine** thyroid hormone (levothyroxine; replacement, titrate to TSH); **-imazole / -thiouracil** thionamide antithyroid (methimazole, propylthiouracil; blocks hormone synthesis).

**-sone / -solone** corticosteroid (prednisone, dexamethasone; anti-inflammatory, taper); **-conazole** azole steroidogenesis inhibitor (ketoconazole; Cushing syndrome); **-pristone** receptor antagonist (mifepristone; glucocorticoid-receptor block); **-lactone** mineralocorticoid antagonist (spironolactone; hyperkalemia risk).
**A stem is a memory aid, not a rule: where no shared stem exists, learn the class name instead.**
Recap: **1.** The hypothalamic-pituitary-target gland axis (Figure 1) is a shared regulatory template across thyroid, adrenal, and gonadal systems — drug therapy can intervene at any level.

**2.** Thyroid hormone synthesis has distinct, drug-targetable steps (Figure 6); PTU uniquely blocks peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion, making it preferred in thyroid storm and first-trimester pregnancy.
**3.** Chronic exogenous glucocorticoid use suppresses the HPA axis (Figure 9) — abrupt withdrawal risks adrenal crisis, so chronic therapy is tapered, not stopped.

**4.** Adrenocortical antagonists (ketoconazole, metyrapone, mifepristone, spironolactone) block cortisol or aldosterone synthesis/action at different points for Cushing syndrome and hyperaldosteronism. **5.** Session 2 (Thursday, November 12) continues with gonadal hormones, diabetes, and parathyroid disorders.
Older synthesis inhibitors — aminoglutethimide and trilostane — and the adrenolytic mitotane are rarely used; mifepristone (RU-486) is the receptor antagonist.
Synthesis inhibitors & glucocorticoid antagonists: metyrapone is the only adrenal inhibitor usable in pregnancy; abiraterone treats refractory prostate cancer; mifepristone half-life about 20 hours.

**Suppressing, replacing, or selectively modulating the reproductive axis.** Today the same negative-feedback logic explains contraception.

**Figure 11. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): exogenous estrogen and progestin suppress GnRH pulsatility and the FSH/LH surge, preventing the dominant-follicle development and LH surge required for ovulation.**
This is the same negative-feedback template from Figure 1 (Session 1), now applied to the HPG axis.

Combined oral contraceptives (ethinyl estradiol plus a progestin); progestin-only: norethindrone "minipill," depot medroxyprogesterone, levonorgestrel IUD; SERMs tamoxifen, raloxifene; testosterone; finasteride; spironolactone.

chunks.text: **Mechanism: estrogen + progestin suppress GnRH/FSH/LH, preventing ovulation (Figure 11); progestin also thickens cervical mucus and thins the endometrium.**

Chain (Figure 12): ethinyl estradiol plus progestin enter the bloodstream → hypothalamus lowers GnRH pulses; pituitary lowers FSH and LH → no follicle maturation and no LH surge, so no ovulation → result: pregnancy prevented (over 99% with perfect use).
SERMs: tamoxifen or raloxifene bind the estrogen receptor → the receptor shape recruits different co-factors in each tissue.
Breast: blocked (antagonist), so cancer growth is slowed. Bone: activated (agonist), so bone density is kept. Endometrium: tamoxifen activates (cancer risk); raloxifene blocks.

Testes make testosterone → 5-alpha-reductase converts it to DHT in prostate and skin → DHT drives prostate growth and hair loss → finasteride blocks 5-alpha-reductase → lower DHT: smaller prostate, less hair loss.
Combined contraception is available as oral pills, transdermal patch, or vaginal ring.
Tamoxifen — antagonist in breast tissue (breast cancer treatment/prevention), agonist in endometrium (raises endometrial cancer risk). Tissue-selective activity is the defining feature of this class.
Raloxifene — antagonist in breast/endometrium, agonist in bone (osteoporosis prevention) — ties back to Unit 2 bone pharmacology; prevents vertebral fracture; not used to treat breast cancer.

**Many mechanisms, one shared goal: glycemic control without excess hypoglycemia.** Today we cover the many ways to lower glucose.
**Figure 15. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): glucose entry raises ATP, closing K-ATP channels and triggering depolarization and calcium-dependent insulin release;**
**sulfonylureas/meglitinides force channel closure directly, while GLP-1 receptor agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors amplify glucose-dependent release via the incretin pathway.**

This is the mechanistic foundation for the insulin secretagogue and incretin-based drug classes that follow — the "glucose-dependent" nature of incretin-based therapy is exactly why these agents carry lower hypoglycemia risk than sulfonylureas.
Diabetes mellitus has four categories: type 1 (beta-cell destruction, absolute insulin deficiency), type 2, other specific types, and gestational diabetes (about 7% of US pregnancies).
Diagnosis: fasting plasma glucose ≥126 mg/dL or HbA1c ≥6.5%, confirmed by repeat testing.

chunks.text: **Mechanism: exogenous insulin activates the insulin receptor, promoting cellular glucose uptake and suppressing hepatic gluconeogenesis.**
Chain (Figure 16): insulin binds the insulin receptor on muscle, fat and liver cells → receptor autophosphorylation starts the signal cascade → GLUT4 moves to the cell surface so glucose enters.
Then the liver stores glycogen and stops making glucose → blood glucose falls (hypoglycemia is the main risk).
Rapid-acting (lispro, aspart) — mealtime dosing; onset ~15 minutes. Short-acting (regular) — onset ~30 minutes.
Intermediate-acting (NPH) — cloudy suspension; more variable absorption. Long-acting (glargine, detemir, degludec) — basal coverage; relatively peakless profile.
Rapid-acting is given with meals; regular 30 minutes before. NPH peaks at about 4–10 hours; glargine, detemir and degludec are basal. Only regular insulin is given IV.
Sort any named insulin into rapid, short, intermediate or long-acting before discussing regimens — the scaffold for every insulin question.
Glucagon (IM, SC, IV, or 3-mg nasal powder) treats severe hypoglycemia when oral glucose is impossible; place the patient on their side (vomiting).

**Figure 19. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): glucose-lowering drug classes act at distinct sites — pancreatic β-cell, liver, muscle/fat, kidney, gut, and the incretin axis — each converging on overall blood glucose control.**

Metformin; glipizide, glyburide (sulfonylureas); repaglinide (meglitinide); pioglitazone (TZD); empagliflozin (SGLT2); exenatide, liraglutide, semaglutide (GLP-1 RA); sitagliptin, linagliptin (DPP-4).

chunks.text: Metformin decreases hepatic gluconeogenesis: enters hepatocytes through OCT1 → inhibits mitochondrial complex I and activates AMPK → gluconeogenesis falls → insulin sensitivity improves in muscle → fasting glucose falls without hypoglycemia.
Sulfonylureas / meglitinides force K-ATP channel closure — insulin secretagogues (glipizide, glyburide, repaglinide). TZDs (pioglitazone) increase peripheral insulin sensitivity.

Match each drug class to its mechanism/site: metformin — ↓ hepatic gluconeogenesis; sulfonylureas — force K-ATP channel closure (insulin secretagogue); TZDs — ↑ peripheral insulin sensitivity; SGLT2 inhibitors — block renal glucose reabsorption.

GLP-1 receptor agonists — glucose-dependent insulin release, slowed gastric emptying; DPP-4 inhibitors — prevent endogenous GLP-1 breakdown (incretin pathway). Sulfonylureas carry the highest hypoglycemia risk (glucose-independent insulin release).
SGLT2 inhibitors block renal glucose reabsorption: glucose is filtered at the glomerulus → SGLT2 in the proximal tubule normally reabsorbs about 90% → empagliflozin blocks SGLT2.
Glucose and water are lost in the urine (glucosuria) → glucose, weight and blood pressure fall; infection risk rises.

GLP-1 receptor agonists: glucose-dependent insulin release, slow gastric emptying, promote satiety/weight loss. DPP-4 inhibitors prevent breakdown of endogenous GLP-1, prolonging its glucose-dependent effect.
Incretin chain (Figure 20): food in the gut releases GLP-1 → GLP-1 acts on the beta cell: glucose-dependent insulin release, less glucagon → DPP-4 normally breaks GLP-1 down quickly.
Sitagliptin blocks DPP-4; semaglutide and liraglutide mimic GLP-1 → lower glucose, slower gastric emptying and less appetite.
Metformin: first-line for type 2 diabetes; no weight gain and low hypoglycemia risk.
SGLT2 inhibitors: cardiorenal benefit — benefits in heart failure and chronic kidney disease, beyond glucose lowering.

**while metformin, DPP-4 inhibitors, and SGLT2 inhibitors show a more favorable efficacy-to-hypoglycemia-risk balance.**
Figure 21 is the quantified summary of the drug-class discussion — it answers "why is metformin still first-line": not because it is the most potent, but because of its favorable risk profile.

SGLT2 inhibitors lower HbA1c 0.5–1%, cause 2–5 kg weight loss, and reduce heart-failure events (dapagliflozin hazard ratio 0.74).

Case: a 72-year-old with type 2 diabetes on metformin monotherapy, HbA1c above goal, lives alone, prior fall. **Which class of add-on therapy best balances efficacy and safety for this patient, and why?**

**Given the fall history and the risks of hypoglycemia-induced falls, a DPP-4 inhibitor or SGLT2 inhibitor (low intrinsic hypoglycemia risk) is generally preferable to a sulfonylurea in an older adult living alone —**
**matching drug choice to patient-specific risk, not just HbA1c-lowering potency.**
This vignette applies Figure 21 directly to a geriatric safety scenario: "most potent" and "most appropriate" are not always the same answer.
Drug names reveal the class: **-gliptin** DPP-4 inhibitor (sitagliptin, linagliptin; low hypoglycemia risk); **-glutide** GLP-1 receptor agonist (liraglutide, semaglutide; weight loss, GI upset).

**-gliflozin** SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin; genital infections, euglycemic DKA); **-glitazone** thiazolidinedione (pioglitazone; fluid retention, heart failure); **-glinide** meglitinide (repaglinide; mealtime insulin secretagogue).

**gli- (prefix)** sulfonylurea (glipizide, glyburide; K-ATP closure, hypoglycemia); **-ifene** SERM (tamoxifen, raloxifene; tissue-selective estrogen action); **-steride** 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor (finasteride; lowers DHT); **-gestrel** progestin (levonorgestrel).
**-calcet** calcimimetic (cinacalcet; activates the CaSR, lowers PTH). A stem is a memory aid, not a rule: where no shared stem exists, learn the class name instead.

**A brief recap of bone pharmacology, then a new angle: PTH itself.** Unit 2 covered osteoporosis drug therapy in depth: bisphosphonates, denosumab, teriparatide, and raloxifene (a SERM, also discussed again this session).

That therapy targets bone remodeling directly, generally in patients with normal parathyroid function. **This section takes a different angle: what happens — and what drugs are used — when parathyroid hormone secretion itself is the primary problem.**
**If you need a refresher on bisphosphonate dosing or denosumab safety, revisit the Unit 2, Session 2 materials — that content is not repeated here.**
This section is intentionally NOT re-teaching osteoporosis pharmacotherapy — it is new content on parathyroid pathology, so don’t expect bisphosphonate-level detail here.
**Figure 22. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): hyperparathyroidism (excess PTH, high calcium) is treated with cinacalcet to lower PTH,**
**while hypoparathyroidism (deficient PTH, low calcium) is treated with calcitriol and oral calcium, sometimes with recombinant PTH 1-84 in severe cases.**
Figure 22 is the organizing concept for the section — two opposite pathologies, two opposite drug strategies, both targeting the same hormone axis.
Cinacalcet (calcimimetic); calcitriol (active vitamin D) plus calcium; recombinant human PTH 1-84.

chunks.text: Cinacalcet — a calcimimetic; activates the calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid cells, reducing PTH secretion.
Chain (Figure 23): parathyroid cells sense calcium through the CaSR → low calcium keeps PTH release high → cinacalcet makes the receptor more sensitive to calcium.
The cell reads calcium as high and lowers PTH → PTH and serum calcium fall.
Calcitriol (active vitamin D) plus oral calcium — mainstay for hypoparathyroidism, since PTH deficiency impairs vitamin D activation; calcitriol bypasses the PTH activation step.
Cinacalcet: used for secondary hyperparathyroidism (e.g., in chronic kidney disease on dialysis) and parathyroid carcinoma.
Recombinant human PTH 1-84 — reserved for patients not adequately controlled on calcium/calcitriol alone.
Cinacalcet adverse effects: nausea, hypocalcemia and QT prolongation, so monitor calcium.

chunks.text: Cinacalcet is a CYP2D6 inhibitor. Thiazides raise calcium, loops lower it. Vitamin D (cholecalciferol) replaces or supports calcitriol in deficiency.
Hyperparathyroidism — cinacalcet (lowers PTH secretion); hypoparathyroidism — calcitriol (bypasses the PTH-dependent vitamin D activation step) plus oral calcium.
Opposite monitoring targets: watch for hypocalcemia with cinacalcet, hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria with calcitriol/PTH replacement — a symmetry worth drawing out.

Case: a patient with chronic kidney disease is found to have an elevated PTH level with low-normal serum calcium. A second, unrelated patient who underwent recent thyroidectomy develops perioral numbness and low serum calcium with a low PTH level.
**How does drug therapy differ between these two patients?**
**The CKD patient has secondary hyperparathyroidism and may benefit from cinacalcet to reduce PTH secretion.**

**The post-thyroidectomy patient has surgical hypoparathyroidism (inadvertent parathyroid gland injury) and needs calcitriol plus calcium replacement — the opposite pharmacologic strategy for the opposite underlying problem.**
Post-thyroidectomy hypoparathyroidism is a classic, testable scenario and a bridge back to thyroid surgery from Session 1 (antithyroid drugs can also precede surgical management).
Drug · Hyperparathyroidism: Cinacalcet (calcimimetic) · Hypoparathyroidism: Calcitriol + oral calcium; PTH 1-84 if refractory

**Applying the whole Endocrine pharmacology toolkit.** The shared principle is negative feedback suppression by exogenous hormone. For each patient, name a first-line approach AND the single biggest safety concern.

**1.** The hypothalamic-pituitary-target gland axis is a shared template across thyroid, adrenal, and gonadal pharmacology — exogenous hormone therapy suppresses the levels above it via negative feedback.
**2.** Antithyroid drug selection (methimazole vs. PTU) and glucocorticoid tapering both hinge on understanding exactly where and how each drug intervenes in its pathway.
**3.** Glucose-lowering drugs act at distinct sites (pancreas, liver, muscle/fat, kidney, gut, incretin axis) — drug selection balances efficacy against hypoglycemia and other class-specific risks.

**4.** Hyperparathyroidism and hypoparathyroidism require opposite drug strategies (lowering vs. raising effective PTH activity) — a new angle distinct from, but related to, the osteoporosis pharmacotherapy of Unit 2.
**5.** Endocrine pharmacology is deeply interconnected — spironolactone, dopamine agonists, and SERMs each reappear across more than one organ system in this unit alone.
Connecting back: osteoporosis pharmacology (Unit 2) and drug-metabolism/interaction concepts (Unit 1) both reappear here — pharmacology is cumulative, not siloed by unit.
**Patient A — Graves disease, in thyroid storm:** PTU (blocks synthesis and peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion); check liver toxicity.
**Patient B — chronic prednisone user, abruptly out of refills:** restart the glucocorticoid and taper; the risk is adrenal insufficiency from HPA suppression.
**Patient C — type 2 diabetes, older adult with fall history, needs add-on therapy:** DPP-4 or SGLT2 inhibitor; avoid sulfonylurea hypoglycemia.
**Patient D — post-thyroidectomy, perioral numbness and low calcium:** calcitriol plus calcium; monitor for hypercalcemia.

chunks.text: Choosing the most potent glucose-lowering drug instead of the safest for an older adult who falls.

Integrated case — diabetes: a DPP-4 or SGLT2 inhibitor is preferable to a sulfonylurea given the fall history — sulfonylureas force glucose-independent insulin release, raising hypoglycemia-driven fall risk.

Integrated case — thyroid storm: beta-blocker + PTU first, then iodine solution only after PTU (never before — iodine first would supply substrate for new hormone synthesis before synthesis is blocked, worsening the crisis).
Corticosteroids also help in thyroid storm by blunting peripheral conversion and covering relative adrenal insufficiency.

**Where diuretics act, and why renal function changes how every drug is dosed.** Renal physiology and pharmacokinetic principles set the dosing logic for everything that follows.
**The kidney is a major route of elimination for many drugs and active metabolites — renal function directly determines how long a drug stays in the body.**
Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and creatinine clearance (CrCl) are the standard measures used to estimate renal drug-elimination capacity.

This is foundational Chapter 3 content applied specifically to the renal unit: renal dosing is not a separate topic but the lens through which every drug in this unit (and this course) should be viewed.

Digoxin, most antibiotics (e.g., vancomycin, many beta-lactams), many direct oral anticoagulants, metformin, and the diuretics covered later in this session are examples of drugs requiring renal dose adjustment.
chunks.where: L09 · Part 1 · Prototype + other drugs named

chunks.text: Flow (Figure 1): GFR falls → renally cleared drug or active metabolite accumulates → toxicity.

**Figure 2. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): filtrate flows through the proximal tubule, thick ascending limb, distal convoluted tubule, and collecting duct — each diuretic class blocks sodium reabsorption at a different, specific segment.**
Share of filtered sodium reabsorbed: proximal tubule about 65%, thick ascending limb about 25%, distal tubule 5-8%, collecting duct 2-3% — this previews the potency ranking in Figure 7.
This nephron map is the conceptual spine of the session — every diuretic class is anchored back to its segment.
Match each diuretic class to the nephron segment where it acts: loop diuretics (furosemide) — thick ascending limb; thiazide diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide) — distal convoluted tubule.

Potassium-sparing — aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone) and ENaC blockers (amiloride) — collecting duct; carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide) — proximal tubule; osmotic diuretics (mannitol) — throughout.
CAI — proximal tubule; osmotic — acts osmotically throughout the filtrate-containing segments, mainly the proximal tubule and descending limb.
Renal tubule transport mechanisms: the proximal tubule reabsorbs about 66% of Na⁺ and 85% of NaHCO₃; organic acid secretion there delivers most diuretics to their luminal site.
Collecting tubule system: only 2–5% of NaCl, but where aldosterone acts and K⁺ is secreted; upstream diuretics deliver more Na⁺ here — the basis of diuretic K⁺ wasting.
Renal autacoids: adenosine (A1) lowers GFR; prostaglandins (PGE2) aid loop action; natriuretic peptides (nesiritide) and urodilatin cause natriuresis but have a limited clinical role.
Three levers: reduce the dose, extend the dosing interval, or both — the specific approach depends on the drug. Reduced GFR makes a renally cleared drug accumulate if unadjusted.
Reduce the maintenance dose when the drug’s effect is concentration-dependent; extend the dosing interval when the drug has a long half-life; monitor for toxicity after each dose change.
Loading doses are often unchanged; maintenance doses are what get adjusted.
As GFR falls, renally cleared drugs accumulate — dosing must be adjusted by reducing the dose, extending the interval, or both.

chunks.text: **Renal impairment also raises drug-interaction risk — drugs that are individually safe can become dangerous in combination when renal clearance is already reduced (a theme that returns explicitly in Session 2's "triple whammy" discussion).**
Pharmacokinetics in two numbers: volume of distribution links amount in the body to concentration; clearance links elimination rate to concentration.
Maintenance dose = clearance × target concentration (steady state depends only on clearance); loading dose = volume of distribution × target concentration, given slowly IV.
Drug accumulation: doses repeated more often than every four half-lives accumulate; steady state takes about four half-lives.
Check creatinine clearance before dosing any renally cleared drug (lower maintenance dose, extend the interval, or check CrCl) — especially in older adults.
Reassess as renal function changes — acute illness, dehydration, or new nephrotoxic drugs can drop GFR quickly.
When in doubt, consult dosing references or clinical pharmacy — this is not a "memorize every number" exercise; the point is the habit of checking renal function before dosing.
Distribution & clearance: adjust a renally cleared drug in proportion to creatinine clearance (Cockcroft-Gault; women 85% of the calculated value).
The target concentration strategy: choose a target, predict V and CL from weight and renal function, dose, measure the response, revise, repeat.
Dosing history: without it a drug level loses its predictive value; draw digoxin at least 6 hours after a dose.
Renal function determines drug dosing broadly, not just for diuretics — GFR/creatinine clearance should be checked before dosing any renally cleared drug (Chapter 3).
Textbook case: 85-year-old, 60 kg, CrCl 22 mL/min — digoxin clearance falls to 3.7 L/h, so about 127 mcg/day: two 62.5-mcg tablets.
What changes: Dose, interval, or both — depends on the drug · Practical consideration: Estimate CrCl or eGFR before dosing, especially in older adults

**The two workhorse classes — one for potent natriuresis, one for everyday hypertension control.** They act on the thick ascending limb and the distal tubule.
Loops are the most potent class; thiazides are first-line for hypertension.
Furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide: loop diuretics. Hydrochlorothiazide: thiazide; chlorthalidone: thiazide-like.
chunks.where: L09 · Part 2 · Prototype + other drugs named

chunks.text: **Mechanism: block the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb — the site responsible for ~25% of filtered sodium reabsorption.**

**Figure 3. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): loop diuretics block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, reducing Na+/Cl-/K+ reabsorption and collapsing the lumen-positive potential that normally drives paracellular calcium and magnesium reabsorption —**

**explaining the increased calcium and magnesium excretion seen with this class.** The lumen-positive potential (from K⁺ recycling) is the link students skip when they memorize “loops cause hypocalcemia” without the why.
**Mechanism: block the Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule — a less potent natriuretic site (~5–8% of filtered sodium) than the loop.**
Follow the thiazide chain step by step (Figure 4): NCC block in the DCT → sodium and water loss → lower intracellular sodium → calcium retained through the NCX exchanger → falling urinary calcium.
Contrast this with loop diuretics, which raise urinary calcium (Figure 3).

In one line: loop diuretics collapse the lumen-positive potential driving paracellular Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ reabsorption (↑ excretion); thiazides increase distal calcium reabsorption through a separate mechanism (↓ excretion).
Loops work from the lumen, so their effect tracks proximal secretion; NSAIDs and probenecid compete and reduce it. NSAIDs also blunt the PGE2 contribution.
Loops: edema (heart failure, cirrhosis, renal disease) and, at times, hypertension when a thiazide alone is insufficient (e.g., significant renal impairment).
Loop diuretics increase calcium excretion — useful in hypercalcemia, and the opposite effect of thiazides.
Hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone — first-line agents for essential hypertension; chlorthalidone has a longer half-life and is often preferred for 24-hour BP control.
Thiazides decrease calcium excretion — can be therapeutically useful in patients with osteoporosis and recurrent calcium-containing kidney stones.
Hypercalcemia: normal saline plus IV furosemide (80–120 mg) — a loop alone causes volume contraction and stops working.
Nephrolithiasis: thiazide plus more fluid and less salt; do not restrict dietary calcium.
Diabetes insipidus (nephrogenic, including lithium-induced): thiazides reduce polyuria; amiloride blocks lithium entry; monitor lithium levels.
Nonedematous states, hypertension: chlorthalidone lowers BP more than HCTZ but has more adverse effects; loops reserved for GFR < 30–40 mL/min or heart failure.
**Adverse effects: hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, ototoxicity (especially with rapid IV administration or high doses), and hyperuricemia.**

Case: hypertension and worsening CKD (eGFR now 25 mL/min), well controlled on chlorthalidone for years, but blood pressure has crept up. **What is the most likely explanation, and what change in therapy would you consider?**

**Thiazide diuretics lose much of their natriuretic efficacy once GFR falls below roughly 30 mL/min, because there is too little filtered sodium reaching the distal tubule for the drug to act on meaningfully.**
**A loop diuretic, which acts upstream at the thick ascending limb, remains effective even in advanced CKD and is the more appropriate choice here.**
The “thiazides lose efficacy in advanced CKD” point bridges directly to Session 2’s hypertension-in-CKD content.
Edematous states, heart failure: loops are standard, but overdiuresis cuts preload and cardiac output; hypokalemia worsens arrhythmias and digitalis toxicity.
Kidney disease and renal failure: little benefit below GFR 5 mL/min; high-dose loops or loop plus metolazone treat overload; avoid acetazolamide.
Textbook case: HCTZ added to chronic furosemide in CKD → 15 kg lost, BP 91/58, creatinine 10.8 — hypovolemic AKI; monitor closely, ideally inpatient.
Site, potency · Loop diuretics: Thick ascending limb — most potent natriuresis (~25%) · Thiazide diuretics: Distal convoluted tubule — modest natriuresis (~5–8%)

**Smaller in potency, but each with a distinct and important clinical niche.** Potassium-sparing, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and osmotic diuretics act on the collecting duct and the proximal tubule.
**Two mechanistically distinct subgroups acting at the collecting duct, both reducing potassium and hydrogen ion secretion.**
Spironolactone, eplerenone: aldosterone receptor antagonists. Amiloride, triamterene: epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) blockers.

chunks.text: Aldosterone binds the mineralocorticoid receptor → increases ENaC and Na/K pump activity → K+ and H+ secreted into the tubule. Blocking either step reduces potassium and hydrogen secretion.
Spironolactone and eplerenone block the receptor (block aldosterone’s effect directly); amiloride and triamterene block ENaC directly, independent of aldosterone.
**Acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor):** blocks Na+/HCO3- reabsorption in the proximal tubule → less HCO3- reabsorbed → bicarbonate diuresis, metabolic acidosis; weak diuretic effect.
**Mannitol (osmotic diuretic):** an inert, filtered but poorly reabsorbed solute that holds water in the tubule lumen osmotically — osmotic diuresis.
Side by side: acetazolamide removes bicarbonate reabsorption; mannitol removes water reabsorption by staying in the lumen. Both act before the loop, so their natriuretic potency is modest.
Figure 6 (**Schematic (illustrative)**): proximal tubule — carbonic anhydrase inhibition and osmotic holding of water (illustrative schematic).

**Figure 7. Original illustrative comparison (illustrative values, not from Katzung): loop diuretics block roughly 25% of filtered sodium reabsorption, substantially more than thiazides, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, or potassium-sparing diuretics —**
**directly reflecting the percentage normally reabsorbed at each nephron segment in Figure 2.** This is why loops are reached for first when potent natriuresis is the goal.
Potassium-sparing agents are often used in combination with a loop or thiazide diuretic specifically to offset potassium loss from the more potent class.
Acetazolamide: valued for non-diuretic uses — glaucoma (reduces aqueous humor production), altitude sickness prophylaxis, and metabolic alkalosis correction; also raised intracranial pressure.
Mannitol: used to reduce elevated intracranial or intraocular pressure and in certain cases of rhabdomyolysis-associated kidney injury prevention.
Know the niche, not an everyday use: acetazolamide = glaucoma/altitude sickness; mannitol = ICP/IOP reduction.
Potassium-sparing diuretics fit mineralocorticoid excess: primary (Conn syndrome) or secondary hyperaldosteronism (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome).
Hepatic cirrhosis: resistant to loops but unusually responsive to spironolactone; aggressive diuresis risks hepatorenal syndrome and encephalopathy.
Renal & cardiac protection: aldosterone antagonists are cardioprotective and lower albuminuria; finerenone slowed CKD in type 2 diabetes.
Idiopathic edema (women 20–30): rule out surreptitious diuretic use; prefer moderate salt restriction.

**Primary adverse effect across the class: hyperkalemia — the risk rises sharply when combined with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or in renal impairment (a direct preview of Session 2's cardiorenal drug-interaction content).**

Case: a patient with stage 3 chronic kidney disease and heart failure is taking an ACE inhibitor and is started on spironolactone for additional heart-failure benefit; two weeks later a routine basic metabolic panel shows potassium 6.1 mEq/L.
**What is the mechanistic explanation for this finding, and what does it suggest about future drug combinations in this unit?**

**Both the ACE inhibitor (by reducing aldosterone) and spironolactone (by directly blocking the aldosterone receptor) independently reduce potassium excretion — combined, and in the setting of CKD (which already impairs potassium excretion), the hyperkalemia risk compounds.**
**This is the same additive-risk logic that will reappear as the "triple whammy" in Session 2.** The ACEi/aldosterone-antagonist pair is one of three “whammies” formalized next session.

Recap: diuretic classes are organized by nephron site (Figure 2): loop diuretics (thick ascending limb) are most potent, followed by thiazides (distal tubule), then potassium-sparing and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors.
Recap: loop and thiazide diuretics have opposite effects on calcium excretion (Figure 3); potassium-sparing diuretics carry a hyperkalemia risk that compounds with ACE inhibitors or ARBs.

**One pathway, four drug classes, and the preferred therapy for hypertension in CKD.** Today we follow the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, the pathway these drugs act on.

**Figure 8. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): angiotensinogen is converted to angiotensin I by renin, then to angiotensin II by ACE; angiotensin II drives both vasoconstriction and aldosterone release.**
**Direct renin inhibitors, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and aldosterone antagonists each block a different point in this cascade.**
This is the conceptual spine for the session: walk the cascade before naming drugs — angiotensinogen, renin, angiotensin I, ACE, angiotensin II, vasoconstriction and aldosterone.
ACE inhibitors: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril — "-pril" suffix across the class. ARBs: losartan, valsartan — "-sartan" suffix. Direct renin inhibitor: aliskiren.

chunks.text: **Mechanism: block the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, reducing both vasoconstriction and aldosterone release (Figure 8).**

ACE also breaks down bradykinin: ACE inhibitor blocks ACE → less angiotensin II (less vasoconstriction and aldosterone) → less bradykinin breakdown, so bradykinin accumulates → cough or angioedema → switch to an ARB for cough.
ARBs block the AT1 receptor directly, rather than preventing angiotensin II formation. Aliskiren blocks the rate-limiting first step of the entire cascade.

Renoprotection: by reducing angiotensin II, these drugs preferentially dilate the efferent (outflow) arteriole of the glomerulus, lowering intraglomerular pressure and reducing proteinuria — a direct, structural renoprotective effect beyond systemic BP control.

Chain (Figure 10): angiotensin II normally constricts the efferent arteriole → ACE inhibitor or ARB removes that signal → efferent arteriole dilates; intraglomerular pressure falls → proteinuria falls; creatinine rises up to ~30%.
**ACE inhibitors and ARBs are first-line antihypertensive therapy in CKD, especially with proteinuria — not simply because they lower blood pressure.**
ARBs: no bradykinin-related cough — preferred alternative when ACE inhibitor cough is intolerable. ARBs do not raise bradykinin, so they are the usual switch.
Aliskiren: limited clinical use; useful mainly as a teaching example of where a drug could act upstream of ACE — included for conceptual completeness on Figure 8.
The drug class students might expect to avoid in kidney disease is actually the preferred therapy, precisely because of how it works at the glomerulus.
**Adverse effects: dry cough (bradykinin accumulation — the single most common reason for switching to an ARB), angioedema (rare but potentially life-threatening), and hyperkalemia.**

chunks.text: **Contraindicated in pregnancy — fetal renal toxicity; avoid in women who are or may become pregnant.** ARBs share the same pregnancy contraindication and hyperkalemia risk as ACE inhibitors.
Aliskiren: generally not combined with an ACE inhibitor or ARB due to additive hyperkalemia/hypotension risk with no added benefit — never in diabetes.

Potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics and trimethoprim: hyperkalemia with ACE inhibitors and ARBs. NSAIDs blunt antihypertensives and raise AKI risk with an ACE inhibitor or ARB plus diuretic.
Hyperkalemia with potassium-sparing diuretics rises with drugs that cut renin or angiotensin II: β blockers, NSAIDs, aliskiren, ACE inhibitors, ARBs.
Enalapril’s ACE-inhibition half-life is about 4 hours, yet once-daily dosing works: concentrations stay far above the C50, so ACE stays inhibited.
**Monitor potassium and renal function within 1–2 weeks of starting or up-titrating therapy, and periodically thereafter.**
**Hold or use with caution during acute illness causing volume depletion ("sick day rules") — combined with reduced renal perfusion, RAAS blockade can precipitate acute kidney injury.**

Sick-day rules: hold the ACE inhibitor or ARB during vomiting, diarrhea or dehydration. An early creatinine rise is expected and hemodynamic, not nephrotoxicity; a larger rise warrants checking for volume depletion or renal artery stenosis.

Case: a patient with hypertension and diabetic nephropathy is started on lisinopril; two weeks later serum creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 1.4 mg/dL. **Is this an indication to stop the ACE inhibitor?**
**A rise of roughly 27% is within the expected range for ACE inhibitor initiation, reflecting reduced intraglomerular pressure from efferent arteriolar dilation — not drug toxicity.**
**Therapy should generally continue with ongoing monitoring; a rise beyond approximately 30%, or a much sharper increase, should prompt evaluation for renal artery stenosis or volume depletion.**
A student who reflexively says "stop the drug" has missed that this creatinine rise is expected and even reflects the mechanism working as intended.

chunks.text: Why does creatinine rise on an ACE inhibitor? The drug lowers glomerular pressure on purpose — that same drop protects the kidney from proteinuria.
Thirty is fine, more is a sign: up to ~30% creatinine rise → continue; more → look for renal artery stenosis or volume depletion.
**RAAS blockers are first-line — but rarely the whole story.** Other major classes: CCBs, beta-blockers, diuretics, central agents and direct vasodilators.
This four-card slide is a brief classification recap — CCBs and beta-blockers get fuller treatment later this session (angina) and in cardiovascular coursework.

Calcium channel blockers: dihydropyridines (amlodipine) and non-dihydropyridines (diltiazem, verapamil). Beta-blockers: metoprolol, atenolol. Central α2 agonists: clonidine, methyldopa. Direct arteriolar vasodilator: hydralazine.
