chunks.text: Dihydropyridines (amlodipine): arteriolar dilation. Non-dihydropyridines (diltiazem, verapamil): also ↓ HR/contractility.
Beta-blockers: ↓ heart rate, ↓ contractility, ↓ renin release.
Chain (Figure 11): dihydropyridine arteriolar dilation → afterload falls; blood pressure lowers. Non-DHP CCB or beta-blocker: heart rate and contractility fall → renin release falls.
Clonidine or methyldopa stimulates central α2 receptors → sympathetic outflow falls, so BP falls. Hydralazine dilates arterioles directly → reflex tachycardia and fluid retention.
Beta-blockers: not generally first-line for uncomplicated HTN, but compelling indications include concurrent CAD/heart failure/arrhythmia.

If all these classes lower blood pressure similarly, why are RAAS blockers preferred in CKD? Similar BP lowering; ACE inhibitors and ARBs add renoprotection — the renoprotective gap in Figure 12, not a difference in BP control.
Thiazide / loop diuretics (covered in depth in Session 1): thiazides first-line with preserved renal function; loops preferred as GFR falls.
Central agents (clonidine, methyldopa) and hydralazine: reserved for resistant hypertension or specific situations (e.g., methyldopa in pregnancy).
Diuretics enhance the efficacy of many agents, particularly ACE inhibitors; hydralazine and minoxidil need a diuretic because they cause salt and water retention.
Spironolactone may be the most effective single agent for drug-resistant hypertension.
Peripheral edema is a CCB class adverse effect.

Verapamil and diltiazem raise digoxin levels. Rifampin and carbamazepine lower CCB levels; grapefruit juice raises dihydropyridine levels.
**Resistant hypertension (BP above goal despite three or more antihypertensive classes, including a diuretic) is common in CKD, often driven by volume overload.**
First step: confirm diuretic therapy is adequate — a thiazide may simply no longer be effective at the patient’s current GFR (Session 1’s loop-vs-thiazide cutoff).
Switching from a thiazide to a loop diuretic, or increasing loop diuretic dosing, is often the most effective single change in advanced CKD.
**Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone) can be added for resistant hypertension, but require close potassium and renal-function monitoring, especially on top of an ACE inhibitor or ARB.**

"Resistant hypertension in CKD" is often really a diuretic-selection problem, not a need for an entirely new drug class — check diuretic adequacy first; thiazide to loop switch; add spironolactone with close monitoring.

Case: CKD (eGFR 28 mL/min), still hypertensive despite lisinopril, amlodipine, and hydrochlorothiazide. **What is the most likely contributor to inadequate control, and what change would you suggest first?**

**At this GFR, hydrochlorothiazide has largely lost its natriuretic efficacy (Session 1). Switching to a loop diuretic such as furosemide or torsemide is usually the most effective next step before adding an entirely new drug class.**

**Where cardiovascular and renal pharmacology converge — and where that convergence can go wrong.** This section covers vasodilators and angina, then the cardiorenal overlap.
**Figure 15. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): angina results when myocardial oxygen demand exceeds supply; nitrates reduce preload, dihydropyridine CCBs reduce afterload,**
**non-dihydropyridine CCBs also reduce heart rate/contractility and increase coronary flow, and beta-blockers reduce heart rate and contractility.**
This figure organizes every antianginal drug class by exactly which side of the supply/demand equation it affects — sort nitrates, each CCB subtype, and beta-blockers onto it from memory.
Nitroglycerin (sublingual for acute angina; IV/patch for sustained use), isosorbide mononitrate/dinitrate (oral, longer-acting).
chunks.where: L10 · Part 3 · Prototype + other drugs named

chunks.text: **Mechanism: release nitric oxide, activating guanylate cyclase and increasing cGMP, producing smooth muscle relaxation — predominantly venodilation at usual doses, reducing preload and myocardial oxygen demand.**
Chain (Figure 14): nitrate donates nitric oxide (NO) → NO activates guanylate cyclase, so cGMP rises → cGMP relaxes smooth muscle: venodilation → preload and oxygen demand fall.
**Dihydropyridines (amlodipine, nifedipine) — predominantly arteriolar dilation, reducing afterload; the same mechanism used for hypertension (Section 5).**

**Non-dihydropyridines (diltiazem, verapamil) — also reduce heart rate and contractility and increase coronary blood flow; avoid combining with beta-blockers due to additive bradycardia/AV block risk.**
CCBs are the clearest example in the unit of the same drug class, same mechanism, treating two different conditions (hypertension and angina).

This is the deliberate cardiovascular-renal "overlap" moment the lecture title promises — calcium channel blockers are not a separate topic from the antihypertensive content in Section 5; they are the same drugs doing double duty.
**Adverse effects: headache (vasodilation), reflex tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension.**

chunks.text: **Adverse effects: peripheral edema and reflex tachycardia (dihydropyridines); bradycardia, AV block, and constipation (non-dihydropyridines, especially verapamil).**

chunks.text: **Absolute contraindication: concurrent use with PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil and similar) — the combination can cause life-threatening hypotension.**
PDE5 inhibitors such as sildenafil block cGMP breakdown, causing severe hypotension with nitrates.
The PDE5-inhibitor interaction is one of the highest-stakes medication-safety points in this whole unit — a real-world, repeatedly tested safety question worth a memorable callout.

**Figure 16. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): an NSAID (afferent arteriolar constriction), an ACE inhibitor or ARB (efferent arteriolar dilation), and a diuretic (volume depletion) each independently reduce glomerular filtration pressure —**
**combined, the effect on kidney perfusion is additive to synergistic, substantially raising acute kidney injury risk.** An extremely common, often missed, entirely preventable cause of AKI.
Three hits (Figure 17): NSAID constricts the afferent arteriole → ACE inhibitor or ARB dilates the efferent arteriole → diuretic causes volume depletion → filtration pressure collapses: AKI.
NSAIDs blunt loop and thiazide action by reducing renal prostaglandins — significant in nephrotic syndrome or cirrhosis.
Tolerance develops with continuous exposure — a nitrate-free interval (typically overnight) is required to maintain efficacy with long-acting formulations.
Prevention: counsel patients about over-the-counter NSAIDs — ask which OTC NSAIDs they commonly take.
The triple whammy is the capstone cardiorenal interaction: Session 1’s diuretics + this session’s RAAS blockers + NSAIDs students will meet constantly in practice.
Hypertension → CKD: uncontrolled blood pressure causes glomerular capillary injury and nephrosclerosis over time — a leading cause of CKD progression, alongside diabetes.
CKD → hypertension: reduced renal function causes volume overload and RAAS activation, which worsens and complicates blood pressure control, often requiring multiple drug classes.

**Figure 18. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): hypertension and chronic kidney disease drive one another in a self-reinforcing cycle — uncontrolled blood pressure causes glomerular injury and CKD progression,**
**while CKD causes volume overload and RAAS activation that worsens hypertension.**
Figure 18 is the conceptual closer for the whole unit — tie it back to Figure 8: RAAS blockade is effective precisely because it intervenes in both directions of this cycle at once.

Case: an older adult on lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide starts a regular OTC NSAID for a knee injury; one week later, lethargy and an acute rise in creatinine. **What is the most likely explanation, and how could this have been prevented?**

**This is a classic "triple whammy" presentation (Figure 16) — the NSAID, ACE inhibitor, and diuretic each independently reduced glomerular filtration pressure, and together precipitated acute kidney injury.**
**Prevention requires counseling patients on RAAS blockers and diuretics to avoid regular NSAID use and to seek guidance before starting one, even an over-the-counter product.**
This case is the direct clinical application of Figure 16 and reinforces IO5.6 (patient counseling): the preventable element is entirely what the patient was or wasn’t told about OTC NSAID use.

Same patient, eGFR now 25: hydrochlorothiazide has likely lost much of its efficacy — switching to a loop diuretic (furosemide, torsemide) is more effective for blood pressure regardless of the NSAID issue.
Counsel the patient to avoid regular OTC NSAID use and to check with a prescriber or pharmacist before starting any new OTC product, given the RAAS blocker + diuretic combination already in place.

**Applying the whole Renal pharmacology toolkit.** Integration: put the drug classes together — for each patient, name a first-line approach AND the single biggest safety concern to check before prescribing or counseling.

**1.** Diuretic classes (Session 1) and RAAS-blocking antihypertensives both map onto specific, drug-targetable points in renal physiology — the nephron (Figure 1) and the RAAS cascade (Figure 8), respectively.
**2.** ACE inhibitors and ARBs are preferred first-line therapy for hypertension in CKD because of their renoprotective efferent-arteriolar mechanism, not just their blood-pressure-lowering effect.
**3.** Calcium channel blockers exemplify the cardiovascular-renal overlap directly — the same drug class, same mechanism, treats both hypertension and angina.
**4.** The "triple whammy" (NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic) is a classic, common, and preventable cause of acute kidney injury that draws on content from both sessions at once.
**5.** Hypertension and chronic kidney disease exist in a bidirectional, self-reinforcing cycle (Figure 18) — which is exactly why managing one well so often means managing the other.
All three threads center on glomerular filtration pressure.

Connecting back to earlier units: drug-metabolism/dosing concepts (Unit 1) and the biologic-mechanism callbacks from Units 2–4 all reinforce that pharmacology is cumulative — the cardiorenal interface is where several organ-system units visibly intersect.
**Patient A — advancing CKD, hypertension no longer controlled on a thiazide:** switch to a loop diuretic; check potassium and volume status.
**Patient B — proteinuric CKD, needs first-line antihypertensive therapy:** ACE inhibitor or ARB; check potassium and creatinine in 1–2 weeks and pregnancy potential.
**Patient C — on an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic, about to start a daily OTC NSAID:** counsel against regular NSAID use — triple whammy AKI risk.

**Patient D — stable angina, already on a beta-blocker, needs additional symptom control:** add a dihydropyridine CCB or a long-acting nitrate; avoid diltiazem/verapamil (AV block) and PDE5 inhibitors with nitrates.
**A cumulative self-test spanning both sessions — use this to review before exams.** The recall quiz is a standalone resource, separate from in-lecture quick checks.

**The two core gonadal steroid classes, and how they are combined for contraception and hormone therapy.**

**Figure 2. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): GnRH drives FSH/LH release, which drives gonadal sex-steroid production, which in turn negatively feeds back on the hypothalamus and pituitary —**

**with four distinct classes of drugs intervening at different points along this axis.** This is the organizing map for the session: GnRH agonists/antagonists, SERMs, aromatase inhibitors and antiandrogens each anchor to a point on it.
Estradiol and ethinyl estradiol (estrogens); norethindrone, medroxyprogesterone, levonorgestrel (progestins); combined oral contraceptives.

chunks.text: **Mechanism: bind intracellular estrogen receptors (ER-alpha, ER-beta), regulating gene transcription in reproductive, bone, cardiovascular, and CNS tissue.**
Estrogen physiologic effects: endometrial proliferation, breast development, bone density maintenance, favorable lipid profile effects (↑ HDL, ↓ LDL).
**Mechanism: bind progesterone receptors, counteracting estrogen-driven endometrial proliferation and thickening cervical mucus.**

Unopposed estrogen chain (Figure 1): estrogen binds ER in the endometrium → proliferation and thickening of the lining → without progestin: hyperplasia and cancer risk → progestin binds PR: limits proliferation, matures the endometrium.
Unopposed estrogen drives unchecked endometrial proliferation; a progestin counteracts this proliferation.
Combined methods (oral pills, transdermal patch, vaginal ring) suppress ovulation via negative feedback on FSH/LH.
Estrogens raise hepatic clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and lower antithrombin III — the basis of the clotting risk; transdermal or vaginal routes avoid first-pass liver exposure.
Estrogen clinical uses: hormonal contraception (combined with a progestin), menopausal hormone therapy for vasomotor symptoms, and hypogonadism.
Progestins: a required component of combined hormonal contraception (protects the endometrium from unopposed estrogen), progestin-only contraception, and management of abnormal uterine bleeding.

Progestin-only methods — the "mini-pill," depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) injection, the subdermal implant, and the levonorgestrel intrauterine system — avoid estrogen-related VTE risk entirely.
Combined methods are often chosen for added benefits: cycle regulation, acne/hirsutism improvement.
When estrogen is contraindicated, a progestin-only method is not a compromise — it is often the correct first choice (safe with VTE history, migraine with aura, or smokers over 35).
Postmenopausal hormonal therapy: vasomotor symptoms, genital atrophy and bone loss; after hysterectomy estrogen alone is fine because no progestin is needed.
An implantable progestin preparation (subdermal implant) provides long-acting progestin-only contraception.
Contraception with progestins alone suits patients with hepatic disease, hypertension, or prior thromboembolism.

**Adverse effects: venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk, increased risk with smoking and age over 35, nausea, breast tenderness, and a possible increase in certain hormone-sensitive cancer risks with long-term use.**

Smoking combined with age over 35 makes a progestin-only method (no estrogen, no added VTE risk) the appropriate choice.
Combined methods carry estrogen-related VTE risk — require screening for contraindications. Hysterectomy patients can take estrogen alone.
Contraindications & cautions: thrombophlebitis or past thromboembolism, cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease, estrogen-dependent cancer, undiagnosed genital bleeding, liver disease.
Enzyme inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John’s wort) lower combined contraceptive efficacy.
Rifampin and phenytoin speed estrogen/progestin metabolism, and antibiotics that disturb gut flora may cut enterohepatic recycling — both can cause contraceptive failure.
Progestin-only methods have more irregular bleeding patterns, especially initially; DMPA specifically: reversible bone density loss with long-term use.
The "unopposed estrogen" point is a classic exam item: any patient with a uterus receiving estrogen needs a progestin too, unless she has had a hysterectomy.
Beneficial effects of oral contraceptives: lower risk of endometrial and ovarian cancer, ovarian cysts and benign breast disease; lifetime breast cancer risk unchanged.
Mifepristone (RU-486) blocks progesterone and glucocorticoid receptors; 600 mg with misoprostol ends early pregnancy in over 95%.

**Tissue-selective and blocking strategies — how drugs can turn hormone signaling on in one tissue and off in another.**
A receptor-blocking strategy and a synthesis/activation-blocking strategy exist on both the estrogen and androgen sides.
Tamoxifen, raloxifene (SERMs); anastrozole, letrozole (aromatase inhibitors); testosterone; spironolactone, flutamide, bicalutamide (antiandrogens); finasteride, dutasteride (5-ARIs).
chunks.where: L11 · Part 2 · Prototype + other drugs named

chunks.text: **Mechanism: bind the estrogen receptor, but act as an agonist in some tissues and an antagonist in others — the defining feature of this class.** Same receptor, different conformation and co-regulators in each tissue.
Tamoxifen: ER antagonist in breast tissue but an ER agonist in bone (preserves density) and, notably, in the endometrium. Tamoxifen antagonizes breast and agonizes bone and endometrium.

Raloxifene: ER antagonist in breast and ER agonist in bone, but — unlike tamoxifen — essentially neutral at the endometrium; tamoxifen is an ER agonist at the endometrium (raising endometrial cancer risk), both being ER antagonists in breast.

Aromatase chain (Figure 5): androgens (androstenedione, testosterone) → aromatase in fat tissue converts them to estrogens → estrogens drive ER-positive tumor growth → anastrozole and letrozole block aromatase.

**Figure 4. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): SERMs block the estrogen receptor directly in breast tissue (while remaining agonists elsewhere), while aromatase inhibitors block the peripheral enzymatic conversion of androgens to estrogen —**
**two distinct strategies converging on the same clinical goal in hormone-sensitive breast cancer.** Receptor blockade versus synthesis blockade.
Androgen pathway (Figure 6): testosterone (circulating androgen) → 5-alpha-reductase converts it to DHT (more potent) → binds the androgen receptor → hair follicle and prostate effects.

Finasteride and dutasteride block 5-alpha-reductase, lowering DHT; spironolactone, flutamide and bicalutamide block the androgen receptor. Blocking the enzyme or the receptor both reduce androgen action — different mechanisms grouped under the same broad "antiandrogen" label.
Tamoxifen: ER-positive breast cancer treatment and prevention. Raloxifene: preferred option for osteoporosis prevention in postmenopausal women without a breast cancer indication.

Aromatase inhibitors block peripheral enzymatic conversion of androgens to estrogen rather than acting at the receptor — postmenopausal use only: before menopause the ovaries are the dominant estrogen source (often combined with ovarian suppression).
**●  Testosterone (androgen):** used for male hypogonadism.

**●  Spironolactone (antiandrogen):** blocks the androgen receptor (in addition to its aldosterone-antagonist diuretic effect from Unit 5) — used off-label for hirsutism and acne in women, especially in PCOS.
**●  Flutamide / bicalutamide (antiandrogens):** pure androgen receptor blockers used primarily in prostate cancer, often combined with a GnRH agonist (leuprolide).

**●  Finasteride / dutasteride (5-alpha-reductase inhibitors):** block conversion of testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone (DHT); used for hirsutism and androgenetic alopecia here, and — in Session 2 — for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).
Estrogen-pathway drugs are used primarily in hormone-sensitive breast cancer; androgen-pathway drugs for hirsutism, prostate cancer, alopecia, and BPH.
Tamoxifen as adjuvant therapy cuts contralateral breast cancer by 35%; benefit does not grow beyond 5 years.
Clomiphene, a partial estrogen agonist, blocks hypothalamic feedback to trigger ovulation (mostly in PCOS); multiple pregnancy about 10%.
Other inhibitors: danazol suppresses the midcycle LH/FSH surge (endometriosis; hepatic caution); exemestane is an irreversible aromatase inhibitor.
**Tamoxifen’s endometrial agonist activity increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial cancer — patients require counseling on abnormal bleeding and routine gynecologic follow-up.**

Case: a 52-year-old postmenopausal woman with ER-positive breast cancer starts tamoxifen; six months later, new-onset irregular vaginal bleeding. **What is the most likely explanation, and what should happen next?**

**Tamoxifen acts as an estrogen receptor agonist in the endometrium even while acting as an antagonist in breast tissue — this tissue-selective agonism increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial cancer.**
**New abnormal bleeding on tamoxifen warrants prompt gynecologic evaluation, not reassurance.** A natural contrast with raloxifene’s neutral endometrial profile.

**Where Chapter 40 and Chapter 41 meet — insulin resistance as a driver of reproductive endocrine disease.**

**Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is defined by a combination of hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovarian morphology — but its pharmacologic management is fundamentally a metabolic problem as much as a reproductive one.**

**This is why PCOS management routinely pulls drugs from Chapter 41 (antidiabetic agents) as well as Chapter 40 (hormonal agents) — the two chapters converge on the same patient.** PCOS pharmacology is not purely "gynecologic."
Metformin; combined hormonal contraception; spironolactone; GLP-1 receptor agonists.

chunks.text: Insulin resistance and compensatory hyperinsulinemia are central to PCOS pathophysiology in most patients, independent of body weight.

Hyperinsulinemia stimulates ovarian theca-cell androgen production directly and lowers hepatic sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) production, raising free (biologically active) testosterone — the mechanistic core of PCOS.

**Figure 7. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): insulin resistance and hyperandrogenism reinforce one another in a self-sustaining cycle — hyperinsulinemia raises free testosterone, and hyperandrogenism worsens insulin resistance,**
**explaining why metabolic therapy improves reproductive symptoms and vice versa.** Walk both arrows of the cycle.

Metformin is not a direct hormonal agent — it improves hyperandrogenism indirectly, by reducing hyperinsulinemia’s stimulatory effect on ovarian androgen production (Figure 7) — by improving insulin sensitivity, not by acting on any hormone receptor.
Chain (Figure 8): insulin resistance → high insulin → ovarian androgens up; liver SHBG down → free testosterone up → metformin lowers insulin → androgens fall; cycles and ovulation can return.

Clinical features follow the mechanism: hirsutism, acne, and anovulation/irregular cycles from hyperandrogenism; an elevated long-term risk of type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome from insulin resistance.

**Metformin: first-line insulin-sensitizing agent in PCOS management; improves insulin sensitivity, can restore ovulatory cycles, and is commonly used alongside or instead of hormonal therapy depending on the patient's goals (cycle regulation vs. fertility).**
GLP-1 receptor agonists are increasingly used off-label in PCOS patients with obesity, given their weight-loss and insulin-sensitizing effects — an emerging extension of the same principle.

Combined hormonal contraception remains first-line specifically for cycle regulation and hirsutism/acne when pregnancy is not desired — metformin and hormonal therapy are frequently used together, not as alternatives.
Polycystic ovary syndrome affects about 7% of women of reproductive age.
**Adverse effects: GI upset (common, often transient), and rare but serious lactic acidosis risk in renal impairment — recall the renal dose-adjustment principles from Unit 5.**

Case: a 24-year-old with PCOS — irregular cycles, hirsutism, BMI 31 — not trying to conceive, no contraindications to estrogen. **What are the two major pharmacologic strategies available, and how do their goals differ?**

**Combined hormonal contraception directly regulates cycles and improves hirsutism/acne through its hormonal effects, while metformin addresses the underlying insulin resistance driving the condition metabolically.**
**The two are frequently combined rather than chosen as alternatives — contraception for immediate symptom control, metformin for the metabolic driver and long-term diabetes risk reduction.**

Drug names reveal the class: **Stem** · **Class** · **Examples** · **Memory aid** — estr-/-estradiol estrogen (estradiol, ethinyl estradiol); -gest-/-gestrel progestin (levonorgestrel, norethindrone, medroxyprogesterone: gest- = pregnancy hormone).

-ifene SERM (tamoxifen, raloxifene: modulates the estrogen receptor); -trozole aromatase inhibitor (anastrozole, letrozole: blocks aromatase); -steride 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor (finasteride, dutasteride: blocks steroid enzyme).

-lutamide antiandrogen (flutamide, bicalutamide: blocks the androgen receptor); -sterone androgen or antagonist (testosterone, spironolactone: steroid; drug sets the effect); -formin biguanide (metformin: lowers insulin).
Recap: **1.** Estrogens and progestins are always paired in a patient with a uterus — unopposed estrogen significantly raises endometrial cancer risk (Chapter 40).

**2.** SERMs and aromatase inhibitors are two distinct strategies for reducing estrogen signaling in hormone-sensitive breast cancer — tissue-selective receptor modulation (Figure 3) vs. blocking peripheral synthesis (Figure 5), compared in Figure 4.

**3.** Finasteride and dutasteride appear here for hirsutism and alopecia — the same drugs return in Session 2 for BPH. **4.** PCOS: insulin resistance and hyperandrogenism reinforce one another (Figure 7), so metformin and hormonal therapy are frequently combined.

**5.** Session 2 (Tuesday, December 1) shifts to autonomic pharmacology of the bladder and lower urinary tract — mechanistically different, but sharing cross-system drug-class connections with Units 5 and 6.

**Three nerve supplies, three receptor families — the physiologic foundation for every drug in this session.**
Parasympathetic M3 contracts the detrusor, sympathetic alpha-1 closes the bladder neck and beta-3 relaxes the reservoir, and somatic nicotinic control holds the external sphincter.

**Figure 9. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): the parasympathetic, sympathetic, and somatic nervous systems each innervate a different structure of the lower urinary tract through a distinct receptor family —**
**the organizing map for every drug class covered this session.** Every class is anchored back to its receptor and anatomic location; Sections 5 and 6 "zoom in" on parts of this map.
Oxybutynin (blocks M3 on the detrusor), tamsulosin (blocks alpha1 at the bladder neck/prostate) and mirabegron (stimulates beta3 on the detrusor body) each target one receptor of this map.

chunks.text: **The parasympathetic pelvic nerve releases acetylcholine, which acts on M3 muscarinic receptors on the detrusor muscle to produce contraction — the primary driver of bladder emptying (voiding).**
M3 is the dominant muscarinic subtype in the bladder, though M2 receptors are also present in high density (smaller functional contribution normally, may increase in disease).
Chain (Figure 10): pelvic nerve releases acetylcholine → ACh binds M3 on the detrusor → Gq activates phospholipase C; calcium rises → detrusor contracts and the bladder empties.
**M3 is the dominant bladder muscarinic subtype.** **M2 is more abundant but contributes less to contraction.** **Blocking M3 underlies antimuscarinic OAB treatment.**

**The sympathetic hypogastric nerve releases norepinephrine, which acts on two different adrenergic receptor subtypes in two different locations, producing two different (and complementary) effects.**
Chain (Figure 11): sympathetic hypogastric nerve releases norepinephrine → alpha-1: outlet closed; beta-3: reservoir relaxed → continence maintained during storage.
Alpha1 receptors at the bladder neck, trigone, and proximal urethra: norepinephrine causes contraction, helping maintain continence during storage.
Beta3 receptors on the detrusor body: norepinephrine causes relaxation, allowing the bladder to fill without a premature urge to void (low pressure).
**Because M3 blockade reduces detrusor contraction, antimuscarinic drugs (Section 5) are a logical treatment for conditions of bladder overactivity.**
**Both of these receptor subtypes become specific drug targets later in this session: alpha1 blockers for BPH (Section 6), and beta3 agonists for overactive bladder (Section 5).**

Net storage effect: sympathetic tone keeps the outlet closed (alpha1) while keeping the reservoir relaxed (beta3) — parasympathetic tone is low; both arms work together for continence. During voiding, this pattern reverses.
This is applied Chapter 6: the same muscarinic family that governs other smooth muscle and glands throughout the body — the bladder is simply one more target organ.
Know which receptor does what where (alpha1 at the outlet vs. beta3 on the detrusor body) before moving on — it makes the rest of the session’s pharmacology make sense.
Dominant tone · Storage phase: Sympathetic · Voiding phase: Parasympathetic

**Two mechanisms, one goal — calming an overactive detrusor to improve storage and reduce urgency.** Antimuscarinics block the detrusor’s muscarinic signal, while beta-3 agonists relax it.
**Figure 13. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): antimuscarinics block the M3-mediated contraction signal, while beta3 agonists enhance the norepinephrine-mediated relaxation signal —**
**two distinct mechanisms converging on the same clinical goal of improved bladder storage.** Complementary, not competing — the basis for combination therapy.
Oxybutynin, tolterodine, solifenacin, darifenacin (antimuscarinics); mirabegron (beta3 agonist).

chunks.text: **Mechanism: block M3 (and, to a lesser extent, M2) muscarinic receptors on the detrusor, reducing involuntary contractions and increasing functional bladder capacity.**
Antimuscarinic agents differ mainly in receptor selectivity and anticholinergic side-effect burden rather than core mechanism.

Chain (Figure 14): drug blocks M3 receptors on the detrusor → fewer involuntary contractions, larger capacity → same blockade in brain, salivary gland and bowel → bladder relaxes, but dry mouth, constipation and confusion follow.
Oxybutynin has the highest CNS anticholinergic burden; mirabegron, a beta-3 agonist, avoids this anticholinergic burden.

**Mechanism: stimulate beta3 adrenergic receptors on the detrusor, enhancing smooth muscle relaxation during the storage/filling phase.** Mirabegron is the primary beta3 agonist in clinical use for overactive bladder.
**Key advantage: lacks the systemic anticholinergic burden of antimuscarinics, making it a preferred option in older adults or patients already on multiple anticholinergic medications.**
Mirabegron can be used alone or combined with an antimuscarinic for refractory symptoms — complementary (not redundant) mechanisms.
**Adverse effects follow directly from systemic antimuscarinic blockade: dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, and — importantly — cognitive impairment and confusion, especially in older adults.**

Case: a 78-year-old with mild cognitive impairment and urge incontinence starts oxybutynin; three weeks later, worsening confusion and new difficulty with daily tasks. **What is the most likely explanation, and what change in therapy would you consider?**
**Oxybutynin carries a relatively high CNS anticholinergic burden, and in an older adult — especially one with pre-existing cognitive impairment — this can precipitate or worsen confusion.**

**Switching to a beta3 agonist (mirabegron), which lacks anticholinergic activity, treats the same overactive bladder symptoms without this risk.** Review other anticholinergics too (medication reconciliation).
The anticholinergic-burden-in-older-adults point is the highest-yield safety point in this section; "no anticholinergic burden" is mirabegron’s single most important advantage.
Mechanism · Antimuscarinics: Block M3 (and M2) on the detrusor · Mirabegron (beta3 agonist): Stimulate beta3 on the detrusor

**Where genitourinary pharmacology meets the cardiovascular system — alpha1 blockade, nitric oxide signaling, and a life-threatening drug interaction.** Alpha1 blockers relax the prostate; nitric oxide and cGMP drive erection.
Tamsulosin, silodosin, doxazosin, terazosin (alpha1 blockers); finasteride, dutasteride (5-ARIs); sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil (PDE5 inhibitors).
chunks.where: L12 · Part 3 · Prototype + other drugs named

chunks.text: **Mechanism: block alpha1 receptors at the bladder neck, prostatic smooth muscle, and proximal urethra, relaxing outflow resistance and improving urinary flow in benign prostatic hyperplasia.**

**Figure 14. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): sympathetic norepinephrine normally contracts bladder neck and prostatic smooth muscle via alpha1 receptors, narrowing the outflow tract;**
**alpha1 blockers relax this same muscle to improve urinary flow — while the same receptor family elsewhere mediates vascular tone.**

**Mechanism: block 5-alpha-reductase, the enzyme that converts testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone (DHT) — the same mechanism introduced in Session 1 for hirsutism and androgenetic alopecia.**
5-ARI chain (Figure 15): testosterone is converted by 5-alpha-reductase → the enzyme makes DHT → DHT drives prostate growth → enzyme blocked, DHT falls, prostate shrinks slowly.
**Figure 16. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): non-adrenergic, noncholinergic (NANC) nerves release nitric oxide, raising cGMP and relaxing corpus cavernosum smooth muscle;**
**PDE5 normally terminates this signal by breaking down cGMP, and nitrates independently raise NO/cGMP systemically — the mechanistic basis for the absolute nitrate/PDE5-inhibitor contraindication.**

**Mechanism: block phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5), the enzyme that normally breaks down cGMP, prolonging smooth muscle relaxation in the corpus cavernosum and sustaining erectile function (Figure 16).**

Chain (Figure 17): sexual stimulation → NANC nerves release nitric oxide → guanylate cyclase makes cGMP → cGMP relaxes corpus cavernosum smooth muscle → erection. PDE5 breaks down cGMP and ends the signal.
Sildenafil, tadalafil and vardenafil block PDE5 and prolong the signal; an erection still needs sexual stimulation to start the pathway.
Tamsulosin, silodosin (more uroselective, less vascular effect) vs. doxazosin, terazosin (less selective, more likely to lower blood pressure systemically).
Finasteride, dutasteride: in BPH, reducing DHT shrinks prostatic tissue over time, improving urinary symptoms.

Onset: 5-ARI benefit typically takes 3–6 months, unlike the rapid onset of alpha1 blockers — the classes are frequently combined (alpha1 blocker for rapid relief, 5-ARI for long-term disease modification). Alpha1 blockers act in days; 5-ARIs take months.
PDE5 agents: sildenafil, tadalafil (longer half-life, allows more flexible dosing), vardenafil.
Finasteride is moderately effective in reducing prostate size in BPH; 1 mg/d is approved for early male pattern baldness.

**Adverse effects: orthostatic hypotension and a "first-dose effect" (pronounced hypotension with the first dose) — because alpha1 receptors also mediate vascular smooth muscle tone, not just bladder neck tone.**

chunks.text: **Absolute contraindication: concurrent use with any nitrate — both raise NO/cGMP signaling, and together they can cause profound, life-threatening hypotension.**

Why absolute rather than relative: nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors independently raise NO/cGMP signaling, and together can produce profound, life-threatening hypotension — pharmacodynamic and severe regardless of dose.
**This mirrors the identical nitrate/PDE5-inhibitor warning from Unit 5's angina content, now from the opposite side of the interaction.** Riociguat is also contraindicated with PDE5 inhibitors.
5-ARI pregnancy caution: finasteride/dutasteride can cause ambiguous genitalia in a male fetus; pregnant partners should avoid handling crushed or broken tablets.
Use caution with alpha1 blockers and PDE5 inhibitors together — additive hypotension, less severe than with nitrates, still warrants spacing doses or careful monitoring.

Nitrate + PDE5 inhibitor (Figure 18): nitrate raises NO and cGMP systemically → PDE5 inhibitor stops cGMP breakdown → together, vasodilation becomes profound → severe hypotension and syncope. Never combine.
Antihypertensives: additive hypotension with alpha-1 blockers. Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, clarithromycin) raise PDE5 inhibitor levels.
Finasteride lowers DHT within 8 hours, lasting about 24 hours; dutasteride has a slow onset and a much longer half-life.
PSA falls about half on long-term 5-ARI therapy; read PSA accordingly.

**This is the exact same receptor family targeted by alpha1-blocking antihypertensives and central agents discussed in Unit 5 — the difference here is clinical intent (urinary flow vs. blood pressure), not a different drug class.**
Finasteride/dutasteride here are a deliberate callback to Session 1: same mechanism, same drugs, different clinical application.

Figure 16 applies the Chapter 6 non-adrenergic, noncholinergic neuron reading; the nitrate warning is the highest-stakes safety point in the unit — students saw it from the nitrate side in Unit 5, today from the PDE5 side.
Case: a 64-year-old with stable angina on isosorbide mononitrate asks for an ED prescription — a friend takes sildenafil "with no problems." Ask yourself: **What should the PA do, and why?**
**PDE5 inhibitors are absolutely contraindicated with any nitrate — both raise NO/cGMP signaling, and the combination can cause severe, life-threatening hypotension.**

**This prescription should not be written while the patient remains on a nitrate; the conversation should include alternative angina management or alternative ED options that do not involve this interaction, in consultation with his cardiologist.**
This case pulls a Unit 5 drug (isosorbide mononitrate) into a Unit 6 decision, making the shared NO-cGMP mechanism unmistakable.

Drug names reveal the class: **-osin** alpha1 blocker (tamsulosin, doxazosin, terazosin, silodosin; opens the outlet); **-terodine** antimuscarinic (tolterodine, fesoterodine; dampens detrusor M3 signal); **-fenacin** antimuscarinic (solifenacin, darifenacin; same class, same target).

**oxybutynin / trospium** antimuscarinic (older, higher CNS burden); **-begron** beta-3 agonist (mirabegron, vibegron; relaxes the reservoir); **-afil** PDE5 inhibitor (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil; keeps cGMP high).
**-steride** 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor (finasteride, dutasteride; lowers DHT, shrinks prostate); **-nitrate / nitro-** nitrate (isosorbide, nitroglycerin; never with a PDE5 inhibitor).
Mechanism · Alpha1 blockers: Relax prostate/bladder-neck smooth muscle · 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors: Block testosterone → DHT; shrink the gland

**Applying the whole genitourinary and reproductive pharmacology toolkit, across both sessions.**

**Figure 19. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): the detrusor, bladder neck/prostate, and corpus cavernosum each rely on receptor families — muscarinic, adrenergic, and NO-cGMP signaling — that recur in the systemic vasculature,**
**explaining why so many genitourinary drug classes have direct cardiovascular counterparts or interactions.** Receptor families are shared with the vasculature — the unifying theme of the session.

Session 1’s gonadal hormone pharmacology (Ch. 40) and PCOS (Ch. 41 overlap) and Session 2’s autonomic bladder pharmacology (Ch. 6) are distinct but connect through shared classes — 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors appear in both sessions.
The lower urinary tract is governed by three nerve supplies and three receptor families (Figure 9): parasympathetic/M3, sympathetic/alpha1 and beta3, and somatic/nicotinic.

Antimuscarinics and beta3 agonists treat overactive bladder through complementary mechanisms — blocking contraction vs. enhancing relaxation — with anticholinergic burden the key safety differentiator in older adults.
Alpha1 blockers and 5-ARIs treat BPH through different timescales and mechanisms and are often combined; alpha1 blockade overlaps directly with Unit 5’s antihypertensive pharmacology.

The NO-cGMP pathway (Figure 16) underlies both erectile function and nitrate angina therapy (Unit 5) — therapeutic in one context, dangerous in combination in another: one of the highest-stakes safety points in the course.
Close by naming the cross-unit integration: genitourinary pharmacology shares receptor families and drug classes with cardiovascular pharmacology covered earlier in the course.
**Patient A — older adult with urge incontinence and mild cognitive impairment, needs therapy that avoids anticholinergic burden:** mirabegron (Section 5).
**Patient B — man with BPH, wants both rapid symptom relief and long-term disease modification:** combine an alpha1 blocker with a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor (Section 6).
**Patient C — woman with PCOS, irregular cycles, and hirsutism, not currently trying to conceive:** combined hormonal contraception ± metformin (Session 1).

**Patient D — man with stable angina on a long-acting nitrate, requesting treatment for erectile dysfunction:** PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated; this requires a cardiology-involved conversation about alternatives.
**A cumulative self-test spanning both sessions — use this to review before exams.**

chunks.text: Integrated case: a PDE5 inhibitor should not be prescribed while this patient remains on isosorbide mononitrate — both drugs independently raise NO/cGMP signaling; the combination can cause profound, life-threatening hypotension.
This is an absolute contraindication, and any ED treatment decision must involve his cardiologist and consideration of whether his anginal nitrate therapy can be modified first.

Even without the nitrate, tamsulosin and a PDE5 inhibitor both lower blood pressure (alpha1 blockade and NO-cGMP potentiation) — additive orthostatic hypotension warrants spacing doses or close monitoring.
His wife’s new vaginal bleeding on tamoxifen should not be dismissed — tamoxifen’s endometrial agonism raises hyperplasia/cancer risk; she needs prompt gynecologic evaluation.

Match each drug or drug class to its mechanism or site of action — tamoxifen: breast antagonist, bone/endometrium agonist; raloxifene — endometrium neutral; finasteride/dutasteride — 5-alpha-reductase inhibition; oxybutynin — M3 (and M2) antagonism on the detrusor.

Match: mirabegron — beta3 agonism on the detrusor; tamsulosin — uroselective alpha1 antagonism; sildenafil/tadalafil — PDE5 inhibition prolonging cGMP; metformin (PCOS) — insulin sensitization, indirectly lowering ovarian androgens.

Chemical used to diagnose, treat, cure, prevent disease, or alter a physiologic process
Any measurable biological change vs. the intended, beneficial effect
Unintended, harmful response at **normal therapeutic doses**
Harm when dose/exposure **exceeds the therapeutic range**
