quiz.stem: A patient says they take no medications, but separately mentions using "Tylenol" for headaches and a combination cold-and-flu product. What does this scenario illustrate?

options.A: Brand names can obscure a shared generic ingredient, risking unintentional double-dosing
options.B: Chemical names are standardized internationally, so this mix-up could not happen
options.C: Generic names vary by manufacturer, which caused the confusion
options.D: Pharmacologic effect and therapeutic effect are simply two words for the same thing

quiz.why: Different brand-name products (Tylenol, many combination cold/flu products) can share the same active generic ingredient. Prescribing and counseling by generic name avoids hiding duplicate therapy — the reason PAs default to generic names.
quiz.label: Lecture check 1 · S8-9

quiz.stem: In which clinical trial phase is a drug first tested in a large patient population specifically to confirm efficacy and monitor for adverse effects at scale, just before approval?

options.B: Phase II
options.C: Phase III

quiz.why: Phase III trials enroll hundreds to thousands of patients, often at multiple sites, to confirm efficacy and monitor safety at scale before approval. Phase I is small-scale safety/dosing, Phase II is preliminary efficacy, and Phase IV is postmarketing surveillance after approval.
quiz.label: Lecture check 2 · S16-17

quiz.stem: In Figure 1 above, the dashed curve (+ Competitive antagonist) is shifted to the right of the agonist-alone curve but reaches the same plateau at the top. What does this pattern show?

options.A: More agonist is needed to reach the same effect, but the same maximal effect is still achievable
options.B: The competitive antagonist lowers the drug’s efficacy (Emax)
options.C: The competitive antagonist increases the drug’s potency
options.D: The competitive antagonist has no measurable effect on the agonist’s curve

quiz.why: A rightward shift with an unchanged plateau is the graphical signature of competitive antagonism: it takes more drug to reach a given effect (potency falls), but because the antagonism is surmountable, enough agonist can still reach the original Emax. Contrast this with the noncompetitive/irreversible curve in the same figure, which plateaus lower instead of shifting right.
quiz.label: Lecture check 3 · S24-25

quiz.stem: A drug binds the same receptor as an endogenous agonist and lowers the tissue’s baseline (constitutive) activity below normal, without any agonist present. This drug is best classified as a(n):

options.B: Partial agonist
options.C: Competitive antagonist

quiz.why: An inverse agonist actively reduces constitutive (baseline) receptor activity below normal — a true antagonist merely blocks the agonist without lowering baseline activity itself.
quiz.label: Lecture check 4 · S27-28

quiz.stem: On the dose-response curve in Figure 2, the point marked EC₅₀ sits exactly halfway up the rising part of the curve. What does this point represent?

options.A: The dose at which the drug becomes toxic
options.B: The concentration producing 50% of the drug’s maximal effect
options.C: The point where the drug has zero effect

quiz.why: EC₅₀ is read directly off the curve at the halfway point between baseline and Emax (the plateau) — it is the standard graphical measure of potency, not a measure of toxicity or bioavailability.
quiz.label: Lecture check 5 · S32-33

quiz.stem: In the left panel of Figure 3, Drug A’s curve sits to the left of Drug B’s curve, but both curves plateau at the same height. What does this tell you?

options.A: Drug A is more potent than Drug B, and both have equal efficacy
options.B: Drug A is more efficacious than Drug B
options.C: Drug A and Drug B have different Emax values
options.D: Drug B is more potent than Drug A

quiz.why: A curve positioned farther left reaches the same effect at a lower dose — that is greater potency. Because both curves reach the same plateau height, their Emax (efficacy) is identical; only potency differs, exactly as the right panel then shows the reverse case (same potency, different efficacy).
quiz.label: Lecture check 6 · S36-37

quiz.stem: Comparing the two number lines in Figure 4, the narrow-TI drug’s ED₅₀ and TD₅₀ markers sit much closer together than the wide-TI drug’s. What is the clinical implication?

options.A: The narrow-TI drug is safer because it requires a lower dose
options.B: The narrow-TI drug has a smaller margin between an effective and a toxic dose, requiring closer monitoring
options.C: The wide-TI drug is more likely to cause toxicity
options.D: Therapeutic index has no bearing on dosing safety

quiz.why: The distance between the ED₅₀ and TD₅₀ markers on the number line is the therapeutic index itself — a narrow gap (as with warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin) means a small dosing error can move a patient from effective to toxic, which is why these drugs require blood-level monitoring.
quiz.label: Lecture check 7 · S40-41

quiz.stem: Drug X requires a much lower dose than Drug Y to achieve the same effect, but both drugs achieve the same maximum effect (Emax). Which statement is correct?

options.A: Drug X is more efficacious than Drug Y
options.B: Drug X is more potent than Drug Y
options.C: Drug X has a narrower therapeutic index than Drug Y
options.D: Drug X and Drug Y have different Emax values

quiz.why: Needing a lower dose for the same effect is the definition of greater potency. Since both drugs reach the same Emax, their efficacy is equal — potency and efficacy are independent properties.
quiz.label: Lecture check 8 · S42-43

quiz.stem: In Figure 5, two separate arrows leave the Central Compartment box: one labeled "M" pointing to Metabolism (Liver), and one labeled "E" pointing to Excretion (Kidney). Together, these two arrows represent which part of ADME?

options.B: Distribution only
options.C: Metabolism and Excretion — how the drug is transformed and cleared

quiz.why: The diagram shows drug leaving the Central Compartment by two separate routes: the "M" arrow to the liver (biotransformation) and the "E" arrow to the kidney (elimination). Together these are the back half of ADME — how the body gets rid of the drug, as opposed to Absorption and Distribution, which govern how the drug arrives and spreads.
quiz.label: Lecture check 9 · S47-48

quiz.stem: Which route of administration bypasses first-pass hepatic metabolism entirely, by entering systemic venous circulation directly?

options.B: Oral, taken on an empty stomach
options.C: All routes undergo first-pass metabolism equally

quiz.why: Sublingual absorption enters systemic venous circulation directly, bypassing the portal vein and the liver’s first-pass metabolism — unlike oral dosing, which is absorbed into the portal circulation and passes through the liver first.
quiz.label: Lecture check 10 · S54-55

quiz.stem: A 45-year-old patient takes a new medication exactly as prescribed. Drug levels are within the therapeutic range, yet the patient develops an unintended, harmful response. Which term best describes this event?

options.A: Toxicity, because any harmful drug response counts as toxicity
options.B: An adverse drug reaction, because it occurred at a normal therapeutic dose
options.C: A therapeutic effect, because the drug was taken exactly as prescribed
options.D: A pharmacologic effect only, because it was a measurable biological change
options.E: Irreversible antagonism, because the receptor was permanently inactivated

quiz.why: An ADR is an unintended and harmful response occurring at normal therapeutic doses (S5).

whys.A: Toxicity is harm that occurs as dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range (S5); here levels were within range.
whys.B: An ADR is an unintended and harmful response occurring at normal therapeutic doses (S5).
whys.C: A therapeutic effect is the intended, beneficial effect (S5); this response was unintended and harmful.
whys.D: Every ADR is a pharmacologic effect, but 'unintended and harmful at normal doses' is the more specific, best answer (S5).
whys.E: Irreversible antagonism describes receptor inactivation until new receptor is synthesized (S22) — not a type of adverse event.

quiz.label: Q1 · Clinical vignette · The Language of Pharmacology

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes pharmacokinetics from pharmacodynamics?

options.A: Pharmacokinetics studies receptor binding; pharmacodynamics studies absorption and excretion
options.B: Pharmacokinetics applies only to IV drugs; pharmacodynamics applies only to oral drugs
options.C: Pharmacokinetics studies genetic variation; pharmacodynamics studies poisoning and overdose
options.D: Pharmacokinetics is what the drug does to the body; pharmacodynamics is what the body does to the drug
options.E: Pharmacokinetics is what the body does to the drug; pharmacodynamics is what the drug does to the body

quiz.why: PK = what the body does to the drug (ADME); PD = what the drug does to the body (receptors & effect) (S6).

whys.A: Receptors & effect belong to PD; absorption and excretion (ADME) belong to PK (S6).
whys.B: Neither branch is defined by route; PK covers ADME for any route (S6, S49).
whys.C: Genetic variation = pharmacogenomics; poisoning = clinical pharmacology/toxicology (S6).
whys.E: PK = what the body does to the drug (ADME); PD = what the drug does to the body (receptors & effect) (S6).

quiz.label: Q2 · Mechanism · The Language of Pharmacology

quiz.stem: A drug relieved symptoms in most participants of a controlled multi-site trial. In your clinic, far fewer patients improve; many miss doses and have several comorbidities. Which concept best explains the gap?

options.A: A narrow therapeutic index that appeared after approval
options.B: Lower potency than was measured during trial dose-finding
options.C: Extensive first-pass metabolism in the clinic's patients
options.D: Competitive antagonism of the drug by the comorbid conditions
options.E: Real-world effectiveness falling below the drug's trial efficacy

quiz.why: Efficacy is performance under ideal trial conditions; effectiveness is performance in everyday practice with real-world adherence and comorbidities (S14).

whys.A: TI describes the gap between effective and toxic doses (S38), not missed doses or comorbidities.
whys.B: Potency is the dose needed for an effect and matters for dosing, not for whether patients improve (S34).
whys.C: First-pass effect lowers oral bioavailability (S50-51); it doesn't explain adherence- and comorbidity-driven differences.
whys.D: Competitive antagonism is a drug competing at the same receptor site (S22), not a disease effect.
whys.E: Efficacy is performance under ideal trial conditions; effectiveness is performance in everyday practice with real-world adherence and comorbidities (S14).

quiz.label: Q3 · Clinical vignette · Drug Development & Regulation

quiz.stem: Two years after approval, reports reveal a serious reaction occurring in about 1 in 10,000 patients — never seen in the clinical trials. Which best explains why it was missed before approval?

options.A: Adverse-event reporting systems accept only voluntary reports
options.B: Approval came before the drug completed any clinical trial phase
options.C: Phase I trials enrolled patients who already had the target condition
options.D: Trial populations were too small and too short to detect so rare an event
options.E: Phase III trials are not designed to monitor adverse effects

quiz.why: Rare adverse effects are often first detected in Phase IV because trial populations are too small and too short in duration to catch 1-in-10,000 events (S12 notes).

whys.A: Reporting systems are both voluntary and mandatory (S14).
whys.B: Approved drugs pass through a structured pipeline with clinical trials before FDA review (S12, S56).
whys.C: Phase I uses a small group of healthy volunteers (S13).
whys.D: Rare adverse effects are often first detected in Phase IV because trial populations are too small and too short in duration to catch 1-in-10,000 events (S12 notes).
whys.E: Phase III confirms efficacy AND monitors adverse effects at scale (S13).

quiz.label: Q4 · Clinical vignette · Drug Development & Regulation

quiz.stem: According to the textbook, which clinical trial phase has the highest rate of drug failures?

options.B: Phase IV
options.C: FDA review

quiz.why: Phase II has the highest failure rate; only about 25% of drugs move on to Phase III (p. 17).

whys.A: Phase II has the highest failure rate; only about 25% of drugs move on to Phase III (p. 17).
whys.B: Phase IV is postmarketing surveillance after approval (p. 17).
whys.C: FDA review is the approval step after Phase III, not a trial phase (p. 17).
whys.D: Phase III confirms efficacy in thousands, after most failures have occurred (p. 17).
whys.E: Phase I sets the safe dose range in 20–100 subjects; it is not the main failure point (p. 17).

quiz.label: Q5 · Mechanism · Drug Development & Regulation

quiz.stem: A 22-year-old patient inhales albuterol, and within minutes the bronchial smooth muscle relaxes. Which sequence best explains this effect?

options.A: β2 receptor blockade → falling intracellular cAMP → smooth muscle relaxation
options.B: Enzyme inhibition → falling intracellular cAMP → bronchial smooth muscle dilation
options.C: β2 receptor activation → rising intracellular cAMP → smooth muscle relaxation
options.D: Ion channel opening → rising intracellular cAMP → smooth muscle contraction
options.E: Inverse agonism at β2 → lowered baseline activity → smooth muscle relaxation

quiz.why: Albuterol is a selective β2 agonist: binding activates β2 → increases cAMP → relaxes bronchial smooth muscle → bronchodilation (S26).

whys.A: Albuterol is an agonist — it activates, not blocks, β2, and cAMP rises (S26).
whys.B: The mechanism is receptor activation with rising cAMP (S26).
whys.C: Albuterol is a selective β2 agonist: binding activates β2 → increases cAMP → relaxes bronchial smooth muscle → bronchodilation (S26).
whys.D: Albuterol acts on the β2 receptor, and the result is relaxation, not contraction (S26).
whys.E: Inverse agonists reduce baseline activity (S22); albuterol is a selective β2 agonist (S26).

quiz.label: Q6 · Clinical vignette · Pharmacodynamics: Targets & Receptors

quiz.stem: A patient receives a drug that blocks a receptor. Raising the dose of the agonist medication eventually restores the full original maximal response. The blocking drug is most likely a(n):

options.B: Inverse agonist
options.C: Irreversible antagonist

quiz.why: A competitive antagonist reversibly competes at the same site and is overcome by more agonist — same Emax, curve shifted right (S22, S22 notes).

whys.A: Noncompetitive antagonists reduce the maximal effect, so full Emax is not restored (S22).
whys.B: An inverse agonist lowers baseline activity; the scenario describes surmountable blockade (S22, S28).
whys.C: Irreversible antagonists permanently inactivate receptors until new ones are synthesized, lowering Emax (S22, S22 notes).
whys.D: A competitive antagonist reversibly competes at the same site and is overcome by more agonist — same Emax, curve shifted right (S22, S22 notes).
whys.E: A partial agonist itself gives submaximal activation (S22); it is not described as a blocker overcome by more agonist.

quiz.label: Q7 · Mechanism · Pharmacodynamics: Targets & Receptors

quiz.stem: A 54-year-old is given phenoxybenzamine before surgery for pheochromocytoma. Blood pressure stays controlled even when the tumor releases large catecholamine surges. What best explains why the blockade persists?

options.A: It activates opposing receptors, producing a physiologic counter-effect instead
options.B: It binds receptors irreversibly; effect lasts until new receptors are made
options.C: It is a partial agonist that caps the maximal catecholamine response
options.D: It neutralizes catecholamines chemically in plasma before they reach receptors
options.E: It competes reversibly, so high catecholamine levels easily displace it

quiz.why: An irreversible antagonist's duration depends on receptor turnover, and high agonist levels cannot overcome it (p. 25).

whys.A: That is physiologic antagonism, like insulin vs glucocorticoids (p. 27).
whys.B: An irreversible antagonist's duration depends on receptor turnover, and high agonist levels cannot overcome it (p. 25).
whys.C: Partial agonists produce a submaximal response; phenoxybenzamine is an irreversible antagonist (p. 25; p. 26).
whys.D: That is chemical antagonism, like protamine–heparin (p. 26).
whys.E: That describes competitive antagonism, which surges CAN overcome (p. 25).

quiz.label: Q8 · Clinical vignette · Pharmacodynamics: Targets & Receptors

quiz.stem: A patient asks why an inhaled bronchodilator works in minutes but an oral corticosteroid takes hours. What best explains the corticosteroid’s delay?

options.A: It acts on an intracellular receptor that changes gene transcription
options.B: It is a partial agonist with low efficacy
options.C: It acts on a ligand-gated ion channel
options.D: It must first be activated by CYP2D6
options.E: It binds a G protein–coupled receptor that raises cAMP

quiz.why: Gene-acting drugs need time to make new proteins, so effects lag 30 minutes to several hours (p. 28).

whys.A: Gene-acting drugs need time to make new proteins, so effects lag 30 minutes to several hours (p. 28).
whys.D: Prodrug activation is not the reason for this lag (p. 28).
whys.E: That is how a β₂ agonist bronchodilator works, quickly (p. 31; p. 32).

quiz.label: Q9 · Mechanism · Pharmacodynamics: Targets & Receptors

quiz.stem: A drug activates a receptor coupled to Gq. Which change follows inside the cell?

options.A: Adenylyl cyclase is stimulated, so cAMP rises
options.B: Phospholipase C makes IP₃ and DAG; calcium rises
options.C: Phosphodiesterase breaks down cGMP in the cell
options.D: A JAK kinase activates STAT transcription proteins
options.E: Adenylyl cyclase is inhibited, so cAMP falls

quiz.why: Gq stimulates phospholipase C, producing IP₃ (calcium release) and DAG (protein kinase C) (p. 32; p. 35).

whys.B: Gq stimulates phospholipase C, producing IP₃ (calcium release) and DAG (protein kinase C) (p. 32; p. 35).
whys.C: That is Gt in the retina (p. 32).
whys.D: That is a cytokine receptor, not a G protein (p. 29).

quiz.label: Q10 · Mechanism · Pharmacodynamics: Targets & Receptors

quiz.stem: A PA is starting a patient on lithium. Compared with a drug that has a wide therapeutic index, what does lithium's narrow therapeutic index mean for this patient's care?

options.A: Lithium is more potent, so it can be dosed without monitoring levels
options.B: Lithium has a higher Emax, so lower doses than usual are always enough
options.C: Lithium is 100% bioavailable, so blood levels never need to be checked
options.D: Effective and toxic doses are close, so dose carefully and monitor blood levels
options.E: Lithium has a large safety margin, so dosing errors are well tolerated

quiz.why: A narrow TI means effective and toxic doses are close together — requiring careful dosing and often blood-level monitoring; lithium is a classic narrow-TI drug (S38).

whys.A: Potency matters for dosing amount, not safety margin; narrow-TI drugs need monitoring (S34, S38).
whys.B: TI is about toxic vs. effective doses, not Emax (S30, S38).
whys.C: Bioavailability is a different concept (S50); narrow-TI drugs need monitoring (S38).
whys.D: A narrow TI means effective and toxic doses are close together — requiring careful dosing and often blood-level monitoring; lithium is a classic narrow-TI drug (S38).

quiz.label: Q11 · Clinical vignette · Dose-Response Relationships

quiz.stem: Two drugs relieve the same symptom. Drug A works at 5 mg and Drug B at 50 mg, but at maximal doses Drug B produces a much greater maximal effect. Which statement best guides drug selection?

options.A: Drug B has greater efficacy, which matters more clinically than Drug A's potency
options.B: Drug A should be chosen because greater potency means it works better
options.C: Both drugs have equal efficacy because both relieve the same symptom
options.D: Drug A has greater efficacy because it needs a much smaller dose
options.E: Drug B has greater potency because its maximal effect is much higher

quiz.why: Efficacy (Emax) clinically matters much more than potency — a highly potent drug with low efficacy may be clinically useless (S34).

whys.A: Efficacy (Emax) clinically matters much more than potency — a highly potent drug with low efficacy may be clinically useless (S34).
whys.B: Potency alone never tells you whether a drug works better (S34 notes).
whys.C: Drug B reaches a higher maximal effect, so its efficacy is greater (S30).
whys.D: A smaller dose means greater POTENCY; efficacy is the maximum effect (S30).
whys.E: Higher Emax = more efficacious, not more potent (S34).

quiz.label: Q12 · Clinical vignette · Dose-Response Relationships

quiz.stem: A patient stable on IV propranolol is switched to the oral form and needs a much higher oral dose to reach the same systemic exposure. Which best explains this?

options.A: Propranolol has a narrow therapeutic index, so oral doses must be higher
options.B: Extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism lowers the drug's oral bioavailability
options.C: Propranolol is highly protein-bound, so the oral form is inactive in plasma
options.D: The IV form was less than 100% bioavailable, so less drug reached the blood
options.E: Oral propranolol cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, so more must be given

quiz.why: Propranolol has a large first-pass effect; oral doses pass GI → portal → liver before systemic circulation, so higher oral doses are needed to match IV exposure (S51, S50).

whys.A: Narrow TI calls for careful dosing and monitoring (S38); propranolol is named for first-pass, not narrow TI (S51).
whys.B: Propranolol has a large first-pass effect; oral doses pass GI → portal → liver before systemic circulation, so higher oral doses are needed to match IV exposure (S51, S50).
whys.C: Protein binding affects free drug in plasma regardless of route (S52); the IV-to-oral gap is the first-pass effect (S51).
whys.E: BBB crossing relates to CNS entry (S53), not systemic exposure after an oral dose.

quiz.label: Q13 · Clinical vignette · Pharmacokinetics: ADME — Absorption & Distribution

quiz.stem: A patient with meningitis receives a highly polar antibiotic. Which statement best describes this drug's ability to reach the CNS?

options.A: Polar drugs never reach the CNS, even when the meninges are inflamed
options.B: Polar drugs cross easily because P-glycoprotein pumps them into the CNS
options.C: Polar drugs usually cross poorly, but inflamed meninges allow better entry
options.D: Polar drugs cross easily because tight junctions favor polar molecules
options.E: Polar drugs cross well because the brain is a poorly perfused tissue

quiz.why: A highly polar antibiotic generally would not cross the BBB well — unless the meninges are inflamed, as in meningitis (S53 notes).

whys.A: Inflamed meninges (meningitis) are the stated exception (S53 notes).
whys.B: Efflux transporters like P-glycoprotein pump some drugs back OUT of the CNS (S53).
whys.C: A highly polar antibiotic generally would not cross the BBB well — unless the meninges are inflamed, as in meningitis (S53 notes).
whys.D: Tight junctions restrict paracellular movement; small lipophilic non-ionized drugs cross more easily (S53).
whys.E: The brain is highly perfused (S52), and perfusion does not overcome the BBB for polar drugs (S53).

quiz.label: Q14 · Clinical vignette · Pharmacokinetics: ADME — Absorption & Distribution

quiz.stem: A patient overdoses on a weak-acid drug. To speed its renal excretion, what should be done to the urine?

options.B: Slow glomerular filtration
options.C: Keep urine pH unchanged and give more fluids only

quiz.why: In alkaline urine a weak acid is mostly ionized, so it cannot diffuse back across the tubule and is trapped in the urine (p. 10).

whys.A: Acidic urine keeps a weak acid nonionized and lipid-soluble, so more is reabsorbed (p. 10).
whys.B: Less filtration would slow excretion, not speed it (p. 10).
whys.C: Fluids alone do not trap the drug; ionization is the lever (p. 10).
whys.D: Protein binding does not trap drug in the urine (p. 8; p. 10).
whys.E: In alkaline urine a weak acid is mostly ionized, so it cannot diffuse back across the tubule and is trapped in the urine (p. 10).

quiz.label: Q15 · Clinical vignette · Pharmacokinetics: ADME — Absorption & Distribution

quiz.stem: In Figure 6, the "+ Enzyme inhibitor" bar rises to 240% of baseline, while the "+ Enzyme inducer" bar falls to 42%. For a patient on a stable dose of the substrate drug, which condition poses the greatest risk of toxicity?

options.B: Enzyme induction
options.C: Neither condition changes risk
options.D: Enzyme inhibition — because it raises the substrate drug’s blood level

quiz.why: The tallest bar in the chart is the enzyme-inhibitor condition at 240% of baseline — the substrate drug accumulates because it can no longer be cleared normally, raising toxicity risk. The inducer bar shows the opposite problem (42%, risking therapeutic failure), not toxicity.
quiz.label: Lecture check 1 · S8-9

quiz.stem: A patient stable on a CYP3A4-substrate medication with a narrow therapeutic index is started on a new drug that is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor. What is the most likely consequence?

options.A: No change, since CYP3A4 only affects Phase II metabolism
options.B: Decreased substrate drug level and reduced effect
options.C: Increased substrate drug level and increased toxicity risk
options.D: Increased renal clearance of the substrate drug

quiz.why: Inhibiting the CYP enzyme responsible for clearing the substrate drug slows its metabolism, raising its blood level — especially dangerous when the substrate has a narrow therapeutic index.
quiz.label: Lecture check 2 · S10-11

quiz.stem: A patient’s eGFR drops significantly due to new chronic kidney disease. For a drug that is primarily renally eliminated, what dosing adjustment is most appropriate?

options.B: Increase the dose
options.C: Switch to IV administration only
options.D: Decrease the dose and/or extend the dosing interval

quiz.why: Reduced renal clearance raises drug exposure for renally-eliminated drugs; the standard response is a lower dose, a longer interval, or both, guided by eGFR/CrCl.
quiz.label: Lecture check 3 · S16-17

quiz.stem: Using Figure 7, approximately what percentage of the original drug concentration remains after 3 half-lives (3 t½)?
quiz.why: Each half-life cuts the remaining concentration in half: 100% → 50% (1 t½) → 25% (2 t½) → 12.5% (3 t½), exactly as marked on the curve. By 5 half-lives the drug is roughly 97% eliminated (about 3% remaining).
quiz.topic: PK Calculations: Half-Life, Steady State & Clearance
quiz.label: Lecture check 4 · S21-22

quiz.stem: In Figure 8, the dashed orange line (loading dose + maintenance) starts at the target concentration immediately, while the solid teal line (maintenance only) climbs gradually over several doses. What is the clinical advantage of adding a loading dose?

options.A: It permanently lowers the maintenance dose needed
options.B: It eliminates the need for monitoring
options.C: It has no advantage over maintenance dosing alone
options.D: It reaches the therapeutic target immediately instead of waiting ~4–5 half-lives

quiz.why: The dashed loading-dose curve starts at the dotted steady-state line from the very first dose, while the solid maintenance-only curve needs several dosing intervals (~4–5 half-lives) to climb to that same level — exactly as defined on the previous slide. A loading dose does not change the maintenance dose itself or remove the need for monitoring.
quiz.topic: PK Calculations: Half-Life, Steady State & Clearance
quiz.label: Lecture check 5 · S25-26

quiz.stem: Approximately how many half-lives are required for a drug to reach steady state with regular, repeated dosing?

options.D: Steady state is reached immediately after the first dose

quiz.why: Steady state — where drug intake equals drug elimination — is reached in roughly 4–5 half-lives, regardless of dose size. This is also why a drug is roughly 97% eliminated about 5 half-lives after stopping it.
quiz.topic: PK Calculations: Half-Life, Steady State & Clearance
quiz.label: Lecture check 6 · S29-30

quiz.stem: A patient is found to carry the HLA-B*5801 allele before starting allopurinol. Why does this matter clinically?

options.A: It identifies a sharply increased risk of a severe hypersensitivity reaction
options.B: It predicts reduced drug absorption
options.C: It only affects how the drug tastes
options.D: It has no bearing on drug selection

quiz.why: HLA-B*5801 is associated with severe hypersensitivity reactions to allopurinol — a textbook pharmacogenomic screening consideration you will see again in Thursday’s gout lecture.
quiz.label: Lecture check 7 · S35-36

quiz.stem: Before prescribing any new medication, which single check is most directly aimed at preventing a toxic, often-predictable drug-drug interaction?

options.B: Checking the drug’s chemical name
options.C: Reviewing the drug’s half-life alone
options.D: Reviewing CYP450 interactions with the patient’s current medications

quiz.why: CYP450 interaction screening is one of the single highest-yield steps for preventing predictable, preventable toxicity before adding any new drug to a regimen.
quiz.topic: Putting It All Together: Clinical Decision-Making
quiz.label: Lecture check 8 · S42-43

quiz.stem: A drug has high potency but low efficacy compared to an alternative. For a patient needing maximum symptom relief, which factor matters more when choosing between the two?

options.B: Potency
options.C: Both matter equally

quiz.why: Efficacy (the maximum achievable effect) matters more than potency for most clinical outcomes.
quiz.topic: PK Calculations: Half-Life, Steady State & Clearance
quiz.label: Lecture check 9 · S46; S48

quiz.stem: A patient with CKD is prescribed a renally-cleared, narrow-TI drug without dose adjustment. Which two consequences would you expect together?

options.B: Increased clearance and decreased Vd
options.C: Increased half-life and increased concentration

quiz.why: Reduced renal clearance raises both drug concentration and half-life.
quiz.topic: PK Calculations: Half-Life, Steady State & Clearance
quiz.label: Lecture check 10 · S46; S48

quiz.stem: Which best differentiates a competitive antagonist from a noncompetitive antagonist?

options.A: Competitive lowers Emax; noncompetitive does not
options.B: Noncompetitive lowers Emax; competitive shifts the curve right without changing Emax
options.C: They are pharmacologically identical
options.D: Only competitive antagonists cause adverse effects

quiz.why: Noncompetitive/irreversible antagonists lower Emax; competitive antagonists shift the curve right without changing Emax.
quiz.topic: PK Calculations: Half-Life, Steady State & Clearance
quiz.label: Lecture check 11 · S46; S48

quiz.stem: Drug A, a CYP enzyme inducer, is started in a patient taking Drug B, a substrate of that same CYP enzyme. What happens to Drug B’s level and effect?

options.B: No change
options.C: Drug B’s route of elimination changes to biliary

quiz.why: Enzyme induction speeds substrate clearance, lowering its level and effect — the opposite of inhibition.
quiz.topic: PK Calculations: Half-Life, Steady State & Clearance
quiz.label: Lecture check 12 · S47; S48

quiz.stem: A narrow-therapeutic-index medication requires monitoring. Which pharmacokinetic parameter most directly determines how long it takes to reach steady-state concentration?

options.B: Bioavailability
options.C: Route of administration

quiz.why: Time to steady state (about 4–5 half-lives) is governed by half-life.
quiz.topic: PK Calculations: Half-Life, Steady State & Clearance
quiz.label: Lecture check 13 · S47; S48

quiz.stem: A PA reviews indication, contraindications, renal/hepatic function, interactions, and a monitoring plan before prescribing. This process best reflects:

options.B: Receptor pharmacology alone
options.C: The clinical decision-making framework

quiz.why: This checklist is the clinical decision-making framework from the "Putting It All Together" section.
quiz.topic: PK Calculations: Half-Life, Steady State & Clearance
quiz.label: Lecture check 14 · S47; S48

quiz.stem: A drug undergoes glucuronidation, which attaches a polar group to the molecule. Which statement best describes this step?

options.A: A Phase I oxidation that unmasks a reactive functional group on the drug
options.B: A CYP450-driven hydrolysis that always precedes any Phase II reaction
options.C: A Phase II reaction that makes the drug more lipophilic and longer-acting
options.D: A Phase II conjugation that makes the drug more water-soluble for excretion
options.E: A reduction reaction that converts a prodrug into its active form

quiz.why: Glucuronidation is a Phase II (conjugation) reaction that attaches a polar group, producing a more water-soluble product for renal/biliary excretion (S5).

whys.A: Oxidation is Phase I; glucuronidation is Phase II conjugation (S5).
whys.B: Hydrolysis is Phase I, and Phase I does not always come first (S5, S5 notes).
whys.C: Phase II produces a more water-soluble (polar) product (S5).
whys.D: Glucuronidation is a Phase II (conjugation) reaction that attaches a polar group, producing a more water-soluble product for renal/biliary excretion (S5).
whys.E: Reduction is a Phase I reaction (S5).

quiz.label: Q1 · Mechanism · Drug Metabolism & CYP450 Interactions

quiz.stem: A 19-year-old arrives 6 hours after a large intentional acetaminophen ingestion. Labs are pending. Which treatment best protects against fulminant liver injury?

options.A: Sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize the urine and speed excretion
options.B: N-acetylcysteine, started within the 8–16 hour window
options.C: Protamine to bind and neutralize the circulating drug
options.D: Rifampin to induce CYP enzymes and clear the drug faster
options.E: Waiting for levels before giving any treatment at all

quiz.why: N-acetylcysteine given within 8–16 hours protects against acetaminophen hepatotoxicity by replacing depleted glutathione (p. 66).

whys.A: Urine alkalinization is used for aspirin overdose, a weak acid (p. 20).
whys.B: N-acetylcysteine given within 8–16 hours protects against acetaminophen hepatotoxicity by replacing depleted glutathione (p. 66).
whys.D: Induction would increase toxic metabolite formation, not protect the liver (p. 66).
whys.E: The protective window is 8–16 hours, so delay risks liver failure (p. 66).

quiz.label: Q2 · Clinical vignette · Drug Metabolism & CYP450 Interactions

quiz.stem: A heavy smoker on a CYP1A2-metabolized drug quits smoking abruptly. What should the PA anticipate?

options.A: No change, since smoking affects only the lungs
options.B: Drug levels will fall because metabolism speeds up
options.C: The drug becomes a prodrug that needs activation
options.D: Drug levels may rise as CYP1A induction fades
options.E: Renal clearance will double right away

quiz.why: Tobacco smoke induces CYP1A; when the inducer stops, metabolism slows and levels can rise (p. 60; p. 72).

whys.A: Smoke chemicals induce liver CYP1A enzymes (p. 60).
whys.B: Quitting removes induction, so metabolism slows (p. 60).
whys.C: Quitting does not change how the drug is activated (p. 60).
whys.D: Tobacco smoke induces CYP1A; when the inducer stops, metabolism slows and levels can rise (p. 60; p. 72).
whys.E: The effect is on hepatic metabolism, not renal clearance (p. 60).

quiz.label: Q3 · Clinical vignette · Drug Metabolism & CYP450 Interactions

quiz.stem: A patient arrives after an aspirin overdose, and the team alkalinizes the urine. How does this increase elimination of the drug?

options.A: It shifts elimination from the kidney to bile and feces
options.B: It makes the drug more lipophilic so it is reabsorbed
options.C: It increases glomerular filtration of protein-bound drug
options.D: It activates tubular transporters that secrete the drug
options.E: It traps ionized drug in the tubule, blocking its reabsorption

quiz.why: Urine pH manipulation works by trapping ionized drug in the tubule, blocking reabsorption (S14 notes); only lipophilic, un-ionized drug is reabsorbed (S14).

whys.A: The mechanism acts in the renal tubule (S14 notes).
whys.B: Lipophilic, un-ionized drug is reabsorbed — the opposite of the goal (S14).
whys.D: Secretion uses active transporters (S14), but urine pH works by blocking reabsorption (S14 notes).
whys.E: Urine pH manipulation works by trapping ionized drug in the tubule, blocking reabsorption (S14 notes); only lipophilic, un-ionized drug is reabsorbed (S14).

quiz.label: Q4 · Clinical vignette · Drug Excretion & Renal Dosing

quiz.stem: Which renal process REDUCES the net elimination of a drug?

options.B: Passive reabsorption of lipophilic, un-ionized drug
options.C: Excretion of volatile agents by the lungs
options.D: Filtration of drug based on molecular size
options.E: Glomerular filtration of free, unbound drug

quiz.why: Tubular reabsorption: lipophilic, un-ionized drug passively diffuses back into the blood, reducing net elimination (S14).

whys.A: Secretion moves additional drug INTO the tubule (S14).
whys.B: Tubular reabsorption: lipophilic, un-ionized drug passively diffuses back into the blood, reducing net elimination (S14).
whys.C: Lung elimination removes volatile agents; it's not a renal process (S13).
whys.D: This is glomerular filtration, which adds drug to the tubule (S14).
whys.E: Filtration moves drug INTO the tubule (S14).

quiz.label: Q5 · Mechanism · Drug Excretion & Renal Dosing

quiz.stem: A patient receives an IV dose that gives a starting plasma concentration of 100 mg/L. The drug's half-life is 6 hours. What is the plasma concentration at 18 hours?

options.A: 6.25 mg/L, with 93.75% of the drug eliminated
options.B: 25 mg/L, with 75% of the drug eliminated
options.C: 12.5 mg/L, with 87.5% of the drug eliminated
options.E: 50 mg/L, with 50% of the drug eliminated

quiz.why: 18 h = 3 half-lives: C(t) = 100 × (1/2)^3 = 12.5 mg/L (87.5% eliminated) (S19).
quiz.topic: PK Calculations: Half-Life, Steady State & Clearance
quiz.label: Q6 · Clinical vignette · PK Calculations: Half-Life, Steady State & Clearance

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly pairs each dose type with the parameter it is based on?

options.A: Loading dose is based on bioavailability; maintenance dose on Vd
options.B: Loading dose is based on Vd; maintenance dose is based on clearance
options.C: Both loading and maintenance doses are based on clearance alone
options.D: Loading dose is based on clearance; maintenance dose is based on Vd
options.E: Both loading and maintenance doses are based on half-life alone

quiz.why: Loading doses are based on Vd; maintenance doses are based on clearance (S23 notes).

whys.B: Loading doses are based on Vd; maintenance doses are based on clearance (S23 notes).
whys.C: Loading doses are based on Vd (S23 notes).
whys.E: The lecture pairs loading with Vd and maintenance with clearance (S23 notes).

quiz.topic: PK Calculations: Half-Life, Steady State & Clearance
quiz.label: Q7 · Mechanism · PK Calculations: Half-Life, Steady State & Clearance

quiz.stem: A drug is given every 8 hours instead of every 24 hours, keeping the same total daily dose. What happens to its average steady-state concentration?

options.A: It depends on Vd, which now changes
options.B: It triples because doses come more often
options.C: It falls because each dose is smaller
options.D: It stays the same; only peaks and troughs change
options.E: It doubles because half-life gets longer

quiz.why: The average steady-state level depends only on dosing rate and clearance; the interval changes only the swings (p. 51).

whys.A: Vd sets the loading dose, not the average level (p. 51; p. 52).
whys.B: Total dose per day is unchanged, so the average is unchanged (p. 51).
whys.C: Smaller, more frequent doses narrow the swings, not the average (p. 51).
whys.D: The average steady-state level depends only on dosing rate and clearance; the interval changes only the swings (p. 51).
whys.E: Dosing interval does not change half-life (p. 51).

quiz.topic: PK Calculations: Half-Life, Steady State & Clearance
quiz.label: Q8 · Clinical vignette · PK Calculations: Half-Life, Steady State & Clearance

quiz.stem: A patient is about to start azathioprine. Testing shows TPMT deficiency. What is the main clinical concern?

options.A: Reduced activation of the drug into its active form
options.B: Faster CYP2D6 metabolism of the drug and lost effect
options.C: Increased risk of toxicity from the thiopurine drug
options.D: Severe HLA-associated hypersensitivity to the drug
options.E: No concern, since genotype never affects therapy

quiz.why: TPMT deficiency raises toxicity risk with thiopurine drugs such as azathioprine (S33).

whys.A: Reduced activation is the CYP2C19–clopidogrel example (S33).
whys.B: CYP2D6 variation affects antidepressants and opioids (S33).
whys.C: TPMT deficiency raises toxicity risk with thiopurine drugs such as azathioprine (S33).
whys.D: That is the HLA allele example (e.g., HLA-B*5801 with allopurinol) (S33, S36).
whys.E: Genotype is one input among several — it still matters (S34).

quiz.label: Q9 · Clinical vignette · Pharmacogenomics

quiz.stem: Which pairing of a genetic variant with the drug it most affects is correct?

options.B: CYP2D6 variation — azathioprine toxicity
options.C: HLA-B*5801 — clopidogrel activation

quiz.why: CYP2C19 variation affects clopidogrel activation and some antidepressant/PPI dosing (S33).

whys.C: HLA-B*5801 is tied to allopurinol hypersensitivity (S36).
whys.D: CYP2C19 variation affects clopidogrel activation and some antidepressant/PPI dosing (S33).

quiz.label: Q10 · Mechanism · Pharmacogenomics

quiz.stem: Which statement about using pharmacogenomic results best matches the lecture's personalized-pharmacotherapy model?

options.A: Genotype affects adverse-reaction risk but never drug metabolism
options.B: Genotype alone should determine both the drug and its dose
options.C: Genotype becomes irrelevant once a drug reaches steady state
options.D: Genotype matters only for drugs that are given by the IV route
options.E: Genotype is one input alongside phenotype, disease, and other drugs

quiz.why: Pharmacogenomics is one input among several — genotype alone never dictates therapy in isolation (S34).

whys.A: Genetic variation can alter metabolism (e.g., CYP activity) (S32).
whys.B: Genotype alone never dictates therapy in isolation (S34).
whys.C: Nothing in the materials limits genotype's relevance this way (S32, S34).
whys.D: Genetic variation alters metabolism, transport, targets, and response (S32).
whys.E: Pharmacogenomics is one input among several — genotype alone never dictates therapy in isolation (S34).

quiz.label: Q11 · Mechanism · Pharmacogenomics

quiz.stem: A 62-year-old has a coronary stent placed. Genotyping shows he is a CYP2C19 poor metabolizer. Which antiplatelet choice does CPIC guidance support?

options.A: Prasugrel or ticagrelor instead of clopidogrel
options.B: Azathioprine at 30–70% of the usual starting dose
options.C: Clopidogrel at the standard dose with routine follow-up
options.D: Clopidogrel plus a CYP2C19 inhibitor to raise its level

quiz.why: Clopidogrel needs CYP2C19 activation; poor metabolizers make little active drug, so prasugrel or ticagrelor is recommended (p. 81; p. 82).

whys.A: Clopidogrel needs CYP2C19 activation; poor metabolizers make little active drug, so prasugrel or ticagrelor is recommended (p. 81; p. 82).
whys.B: That dose rule is for TPMT-intermediate thiopurine use (p. 83).
whys.C: Standard clopidogrel risks stent thrombosis in poor metabolizers (p. 81).
whys.D: Inhibiting CYP2C19 would reduce clopidogrel activation further (p. 81).
whys.E: Codeine relates to CYP2D6, not antiplatelet choice (p. 81).

quiz.label: Q12 · Clinical vignette · Pharmacogenomics

quiz.stem: A patient starts a new drug that binds the same receptor as their home medication, and the home medication's effect becomes weaker. Raising the home medication's dose restores the full effect. What does this support?

options.A: The new drug is a strong CYP3A4 inducer
options.B: The new drug is an irreversible antagonist
options.C: The home medication has become toxic
options.D: The new drug is a competitive antagonist
options.E: The new drug is a full agonist itself

quiz.why: A competitive antagonist can be overcome by increasing the agonist dose — restoring the effect supports competitive rather than irreversible antagonism (S41).

whys.A: Nothing here involves CYP metabolism; it's receptor competition (S41).
whys.B: Irreversible antagonism would NOT be overcome by raising the dose (S41).
whys.C: A weaker effect restored by a higher dose points to competition (S41).
whys.D: A competitive antagonist can be overcome by increasing the agonist dose — restoring the effect supports competitive rather than irreversible antagonism (S41).
whys.E: A drug that weakens the home medication's effect is acting as an antagonist (S41).

quiz.topic: Putting It All Together: Clinical Decision-Making
quiz.label: Q13 · Clinical vignette · Putting It All Together: Clinical Decision-Making

quiz.stem: A 68-year-old woman with stage 4 CKD (eGFR 24 mL/min) is starting a narrow-TI oral antiarrhythmic eliminated mainly unchanged by the kidney. Three weeks ago she began a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor. What is the best step before the prescription is filled?

options.A: Shorten the dosing interval so steady state is reached more quickly
options.B: Prescribe the standard dose, since only hepatic drugs are affected by CKD
options.C: Increase the dose, since the CYP3A4 inhibitor will lower the drug's level
options.D: Start the drug, and check renal function only if symptoms appear later
options.E: Check eGFR/CrCl, lower the dose or extend the interval, and plan close monitoring

quiz.why: Reduced renal clearance will raise the drug's concentration and prolong its half-life; before dispensing, check eGFR/CrCl, consider a lower dose or extended interval, and monitor renal function and toxicity (SG U1-S).

whys.A: Intervals are EXTENDED in renal impairment; shortening raises accumulation (S17, S28).
whys.B: CKD reduces renal clearance, raising concentration and half-life of renally-eliminated drugs (S15, SG U1-S).
whys.C: A CYP3A4 inhibitor RAISES substrate levels (S6); induction lowers them.
whys.D: Check eGFR/CrCl and adjust BEFORE dispensing, then monitor closely (SG U1-S).
whys.E: Reduced renal clearance will raise the drug's concentration and prolong its half-life; before dispensing, check eGFR/CrCl, consider a lower dose or extended interval, and monitor renal function and toxicity (SG U1-S).

quiz.topic: Putting It All Together: Clinical Decision-Making
quiz.label: Q14 · Clinical vignette · Putting It All Together: Clinical Decision-Making

quiz.stem: In Figure 1, corticosteroids are shown blocking the pathway at the "Membrane Phospholipids → Arachidonic Acid" step, while NSAIDs act one step later. What does this positioning explain?

options.A: Corticosteroids act upstream of NSAIDs, which is why they can suppress a broader range of inflammatory mediators, not just prostaglandins
options.B: Corticosteroids and NSAIDs block the exact same enzyme
options.C: NSAIDs act upstream of corticosteroids
options.D: Neither drug class affects the arachidonic acid pathway

quiz.why: By inhibiting phospholipase A₂, corticosteroids block the release of arachidonic acid itself — upstream of COX — which is why they suppress a broader range of inflammatory mediators (not just prostaglandins) than NSAIDs, which act only at the COX step.
quiz.label: Lecture check 1 · S10-11

quiz.stem: Which mediator is the primary target of NSAID therapy within the inflammatory pain pathway?

options.B: Histamine
options.C: Bradykinin
options.D: Cytokines broadly (e.g., all of TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6)

quiz.why: NSAIDs inhibit COX enzymes, directly reducing prostaglandin synthesis. Histamine, bradykinin, and cytokines are important inflammatory mediators too, but they are not the primary target of NSAID mechanism.
quiz.label: Lecture check 2 · S12-13

quiz.stem: In acetaminophen overdose, hepatotoxicity results primarily from which mechanism?

options.A: Direct COX inhibition in the liver
options.B: Excess Phase II glucuronidation
options.C: Accumulation of NAPQI after glutathione stores are depleted

quiz.why: NAPQI, normally detoxified by conjugation with glutathione, accumulates once glutathione stores are exhausted in overdose, causing hepatocyte injury — which is why N-acetylcysteine (a glutathione precursor) is the antidote.
quiz.label: Lecture check 3 · S21-22

quiz.stem: Based on Figure 2, a patient with a history of GI ulcer but no cardiovascular disease is switched from ibuprofen to celecoxib. What is the most likely net effect on this patient’s risk profile?

options.A: Lower GI risk, with some increase in cardiovascular risk
options.B: Both GI and cardiovascular risk decrease
options.C: No change in either risk, since all NSAIDs carry identical risk profiles
options.D: Both GI and cardiovascular risk increase

quiz.why: Figure 2 shows celecoxib’s illustrative GI-risk bar is lower than the nonselective NSAID bar, while its cardiovascular-risk bar is higher — exactly the trade-off described in the celecoxib bullet slide. For this GI-ulcer-history patient without cardiovascular disease, that trade may be favorable, but the increased cardiovascular risk should still be discussed.
quiz.label: Lecture check 4 · S32-33

quiz.stem: A patient with CKD, hypertension, and anticoagulant use needs analgesia for osteoarthritis. Which class carries the highest combined renal and bleeding risk for this patient?

options.B: Oral NSAIDs
options.C: Topical capsaicin

quiz.why: This patient has multiple NSAID red flags at once: CKD (renal risk), anticoagulant use (bleeding risk), and hypertension (cardiovascular risk) — oral NSAIDs carry the highest combined risk here.
quiz.label: Lecture check 5 · S38-39

quiz.stem: In Figure 3, which biologic DMARD acts earliest in the cascade shown, before cytokines like TNF-α and IL-6 are even released?

options.B: Tocilizumab
options.C: Abatacept

quiz.why: Abatacept blocks T-cell costimulation — the step furthest upstream in the diagram, occurring before activated T cells drive cytokine release (blocked downstream by adalimumab/tocilizumab) or B-cell activity (blocked by rituximab).
quiz.label: Lecture check 6 · S54-55

quiz.stem: Which feature distinguishes a DMARD from an NSAID in the management of rheumatoid arthritis?

options.A: DMARDs provide faster pain relief than NSAIDs
options.B: NSAIDs suppress the immune system more potently than DMARDs
options.C: DMARDs modify the underlying disease process rather than only masking symptoms
options.D: DMARDs are only available as biologic agents

quiz.why: An NSAID can make a patient feel better without changing RA’s disease trajectory; a DMARD (conventional or biologic) is intended to slow or halt joint destruction and systemic inflammation itself.
quiz.label: Lecture check 7 · S58-59

quiz.stem: In acetaminophen overdose, why is N-acetylcysteine effective?

options.A: It speeds renal excretion of unchanged acetaminophen
options.B: It is a glutathione precursor that restores NAPQI detoxification
options.C: It blocks COX in the liver and lowers prostaglandin levels
options.D: It inhibits the enzyme that forms NAPQI from the drug
options.E: It binds acetaminophen in the gut and prevents absorption

quiz.why: Overdose depletes glutathione so NAPQI accumulates; N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione to detoxify NAPQI (S19; SG U2-R3).

whys.A: The antidote works by refilling glutathione, not by renal excretion (S19).
whys.B: Overdose depletes glutathione so NAPQI accumulates; N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione to detoxify NAPQI (S19; SG U2-R3).
whys.C: COX blockade is the NSAID mechanism, not the antidote’s (S24).
whys.D: The lecture’s mechanism is glutathione replenishment (SG U2-R3).
whys.E: The lecture explains the antidote through glutathione, not binding (S19).

quiz.label: Q1 · Mechanism · Acetaminophen

quiz.stem: A 40-year-old with an acutely swollen, inflamed knee asks for the drug that best treats the inflammation itself. Why is acetaminophen not the best choice?

options.A: It only works when given intravenously in hospital
options.B: It causes more GI bleeding than the NSAIDs do
options.C: It is contraindicated in anyone with joint swelling
options.D: Its anti-inflammatory effect at the periphery is minimal
options.E: It has no analgesic effect in musculoskeletal pain

quiz.why: Acetaminophen relieves pain and fever centrally, but its peripheral anti-inflammatory effect is minimal — it is not a reliable anti-inflammatory agent (S15).

whys.A: No route restriction is taught; it is used orally first-line for mild OA pain (S43).
whys.B: GI bleeding is the NSAID risk (S34).
whys.C: No such contraindication is taught; the issue is weak anti-inflammatory action (S15).
whys.D: Acetaminophen relieves pain and fever centrally, but its peripheral anti-inflammatory effect is minimal — it is not a reliable anti-inflammatory agent (S15).

quiz.label: Q2 · Clinical vignette · Acetaminophen

quiz.stem: Which statement best explains why nonselective NSAIDs cause GI and renal adverse effects?

options.A: They block TNF-α, which normally protects the stomach lining
options.B: They block phospholipase A₂ and stop all mediator release
options.C: They inhibit COX-1, which protects gastric mucosa and renal blood flow
options.D: They inhibit COX-2, the only source of protective prostaglandins
options.E: They deplete glutathione, which injures the gut and kidney

quiz.why: COX-1 is the housekeeping enzyme that maintains gastric mucosal protection and normal renal blood flow; inhibiting it contributes to GI and renal adverse effects (S26; SG U2-R4).

whys.A: TNF-α blockade is a biologic DMARD mechanism (S51).
whys.C: COX-1 is the housekeeping enzyme that maintains gastric mucosal protection and normal renal blood flow; inhibiting it contributes to GI and renal adverse effects (S26; SG U2-R4).
whys.D: COX-2 is the main source of inflammatory prostaglandins (S26).

quiz.label: Q3 · Mechanism · NSAIDs & COX-2 Selective Inhibition

quiz.stem: A patient on lisinopril (an ACE inhibitor) and hydrochlorothiazide starts daily naproxen for knee pain. Two weeks later, creatinine has risen sharply. What pattern explains this?

options.A: Expected COX-2 renal protection failing under stress
options.B: Bleeding from the NSAID plus the ACE inhibitor together
options.C: The “triple whammy”: NSAID + ACE inhibitor + diuretic causing AKI
options.D: A GI ulcer from NSAID plus diuretic, causing dehydration
options.E: Hepatotoxicity from NAPQI formed by naproxen metabolism

quiz.why: NSAIDs with ACE inhibitors/ARBs raise AKI risk, and adding a diuretic is the high-yield “triple whammy” AKI pattern (S36; S36 notes).

whys.A: COX-2 selectivity does not protect the kidney, and naproxen is nonselective (S28-29).
whys.B: NSAID + anticoagulant raises bleeding; this is a renal pattern (S36).
whys.C: NSAIDs with ACE inhibitors/ARBs raise AKI risk, and adding a diuretic is the high-yield “triple whammy” AKI pattern (S36; S36 notes).
whys.D: NSAID + corticosteroid raises ulcer risk; this is a kidney injury pattern (S36).

quiz.label: Q4 · Clinical vignette · NSAIDs & COX-2 Selective Inhibition

quiz.stem: Which nonselective NSAID does the lecture restrict to short-term use because of significant GI and renal risk?

options.B: Ibuprofen
options.C: Diclofenac

quiz.why: Ketorolac is for short-term use only because of significant GI/renal risk (S28).

whys.A: Ketorolac is for short-term use only because of significant GI/renal risk (S28).
whys.B: Ibuprofen is a common first-line choice for mild-moderate pain (S28).
whys.C: Diclofenac is noted for oral and topical formulations (S28).
whys.D: Celecoxib is COX-2 selective; its trade-off is cardiovascular risk (S29).
whys.E: Naproxen is noted for its longer half-life and twice-daily dosing (S28).

quiz.label: Q5 · Mechanism · NSAIDs & COX-2 Selective Inhibition

quiz.stem: A patient takes low-dose aspirin for cardioprotection and starts regular ibuprofen for back pain. What is the textbook concern?

options.A: Ibuprofen converts aspirin to the toxic metabolite NAPQI
options.B: Ibuprofen speeds aspirin’s renal excretion fivefold
options.C: Ibuprofen blocks aspirin’s irreversible platelet inhibition
options.D: Aspirin makes ibuprofen COX-2 selective, raising CV risk
options.E: Both drugs together protect the kidney from injury

quiz.why: Concomitant ibuprofen antagonizes aspirin’s irreversible platelet inhibition, limiting its cardioprotective effect (p. 680).

whys.C: Concomitant ibuprofen antagonizes aspirin’s irreversible platelet inhibition, limiting its cardioprotective effect (p. 680).
whys.D: Aspirin does not change ibuprofen’s selectivity (p. 680).
whys.E: NSAIDs reduce renal perfusion; they don’t protect the kidney (S34).

quiz.label: Q6 · Clinical vignette · NSAIDs & COX-2 Selective Inhibition

quiz.stem: A 66-year-old has knee pain worse with activity, no systemic symptoms, and mild disease. Which first-line drug does the lecture call reasonable?

options.B: Methotrexate to slow joint destruction
options.C: Hydroxychloroquine for mild disease

quiz.why: Acetaminophen is a reasonable first-line for mild OA pain (S43).

whys.A: Acetaminophen is a reasonable first-line for mild OA pain (S43).
whys.B: Methotrexate is the anchor DMARD for RA, an autoimmune disease (S41; S47).
whys.C: Hydroxychloroquine is a DMARD for milder RA (S47).
whys.D: Biologic DMARDs treat RA, not degenerative OA (S41; S51).

quiz.label: Q7 · Clinical vignette · Osteoarthritis, Rheumatoid Arthritis & DMARDs

quiz.stem: What is the key difference in treatment goals between osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis?

options.A: Both aim only at pain relief with NSAIDs
options.B: OA aims at cartilage regrowth with DMARDs
options.C: OA aims at pain and function; RA aims to suppress disease activity
options.D: OA aims to suppress immunity; RA aims at pain relief only
options.E: RA aims at weight loss; OA aims at infection control

quiz.why: OA treatment targets pain control and function; RA treatment must suppress disease activity, not just pain (S41).

whys.B: OA is managed mainly with analgesics/NSAIDs (S41 notes).
whys.C: OA treatment targets pain control and function; RA treatment must suppress disease activity, not just pain (S41).

quiz.label: Q8 · Mechanism · Osteoarthritis, Rheumatoid Arthritis & DMARDs

quiz.stem: A patient newly started on methotrexate for RA asks whether to take a tablet every morning “to keep levels steady.” What is the correct counseling?

options.A: Take it daily but skip the folate supplement
options.B: Take it only on days when joints are painful
options.C: Take it twice daily, like naproxen, for steady levels
options.D: Take it once weekly, because daily dosing can be fatal
options.E: Take it daily with food to reduce stomach upset

quiz.why: Methotrexate is dosed weekly, not daily — a critical patient-safety point, since daily dosing can be fatal (S49; SG U2-R7).

whys.A: Folate is co-prescribed to reduce toxicity, and dosing is weekly (S49).
whys.B: It is a scheduled weekly DMARD, not an as-needed analgesic (S45; S49).
whys.D: Methotrexate is dosed weekly, not daily — a critical patient-safety point, since daily dosing can be fatal (S49; SG U2-R7).
whys.E: Daily dosing is the dangerous error (S49).

quiz.label: Q9 · Clinical vignette · Osteoarthritis, Rheumatoid Arthritis & DMARDs

quiz.stem: What is methotrexate’s mechanism as taught in the lecture, and what is co-prescribed to reduce its toxicity?

options.A: COX-2 inhibition; a proton pump inhibitor
options.B: Phospholipase A₂ blockade; calcium supplementation
options.C: TNF-α blockade; tuberculosis screening

quiz.why: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, reducing immune cell proliferation at low RA doses; folate is routinely co-prescribed (S49; SG U2-R7; SG U2-M).

whys.B: Phospholipase A₂ is the corticosteroid site (S9).
whys.C: TNF blockade is the biologic DMARD mechanism (S51).
whys.D: That is acetaminophen toxicity and its antidote (S19).
whys.E: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, reducing immune cell proliferation at low RA doses; folate is routinely co-prescribed (S49; SG U2-R7; SG U2-M).

quiz.label: Q10 · Mechanism · Osteoarthritis, Rheumatoid Arthritis & DMARDs

quiz.stem: A 29-year-old with active RA who is planning a pregnancy needs a DMARD. Which drug from the lecture is contraindicated?

options.A: Celecoxib, because it is a disease-modifying drug
options.B: Sulfasalazine, because it is only used alone
options.C: Acetaminophen, because it is a DMARD
options.E: Hydroxychloroquine, because of its poor safety profile

quiz.why: Methotrexate is contraindicated in pregnancy because it is teratogenic (S49).

whys.A: Celecoxib is an NSAID, not a DMARD (S29; S45).
whys.B: Sulfasalazine is often used in combination regimens (S47).
whys.C: Acetaminophen is an analgesic, not a DMARD (S15; S45).
whys.D: Methotrexate is contraindicated in pregnancy because it is teratogenic (S49).
whys.E: Hydroxychloroquine has a relatively favorable safety profile (S47).

quiz.label: Q11 · Clinical vignette · Osteoarthritis, Rheumatoid Arthritis & DMARDs

quiz.stem: Before starting adalimumab for rheumatoid arthritis, which baseline step does the lecture specifically call for?

options.A: Screening for tuberculosis and hepatitis B/C
options.B: Starting folate to prevent bone marrow toxicity
options.C: Adding an ACE inhibitor to protect the kidney
options.D: Checking for all hidden acetaminophen sources
options.E: Avoiding all vaccines until therapy has begun

quiz.why: Biologics cause immunosuppression; baseline tuberculosis and hepatitis B/C screening comes before starting them (S56).

whys.A: Biologics cause immunosuppression; baseline tuberculosis and hepatitis B/C screening comes before starting them (S56).
whys.C: Not a DMARD safety step; NSAID + ACEi raises AKI risk (S36).
whys.E: Vaccines, especially live vaccines, are updated before therapy (S56).

quiz.label: Q12 · Clinical vignette · Osteoarthritis, Rheumatoid Arthritis & DMARDs

quiz.stem: A patient on a biologic DMARD calls with a fever of 38.6 °C and a productive cough. What lecture principle drives the advice to be seen promptly?

options.A: NSAID-like renal toxicity makes fever dangerous
options.B: Fever means the biologic is working as intended
options.C: Immunosuppression raises infection risk across all DMARDs
options.D: Biologics raise cardiovascular risk like celecoxib

quiz.why: The major safety theme across all DMARDs is immunosuppression → increased infection risk; patients should report fevers or infection symptoms promptly (S56; SG U2-R8).

whys.A: Renal toxicity is an NSAID theme, not the DMARD safety theme (S34; S56).
whys.B: Fever signals possible infection in an immunosuppressed patient (S56).
whys.C: The major safety theme across all DMARDs is immunosuppression → increased infection risk; patients should report fevers or infection symptoms promptly (S56; SG U2-R8).
whys.E: Hidden acetaminophen comes from combination cold products (S20).

quiz.label: Q13 · Clinical vignette · Osteoarthritis, Rheumatoid Arthritis & DMARDs

quiz.stem: Match the drug to its target: which pairing is correct?

options.B: Tocilizumab — IL-6 receptor signaling
options.C: Etanercept — IL-6 receptor signaling

quiz.why: Tocilizumab is the lecture’s IL-6 inhibitor (S51; SG U2-R8).

whys.B: Tocilizumab is the lecture’s IL-6 inhibitor (S51; SG U2-R8).
whys.E: Rituximab depletes B cells; TNF is adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab (S51).

quiz.label: Q14 · Mechanism · Osteoarthritis, Rheumatoid Arthritis & DMARDs

quiz.stem: A patient with RA and high cardiovascular risk is being considered for tofacitinib. Which boxed warning applies to all JAK inhibitors?

options.A: Lymphoma only, exactly the same as the TNF inhibitors
options.B: Teratogenicity that requires strict weekly-only dosing
options.C: Retinopathy that requires annual eye examinations
options.D: Venous thromboembolism, major cardiovascular events, and cancer
options.E: Fatal hepatotoxicity from NAPQI accumulating in the liver

quiz.why: All JAK inhibitors carry an FDA boxed warning for VTE (DVT, PE), MACE, and cancer (p. 686).

whys.A: The TNF inhibitor warning is malignancy; JAK inhibitors add VTE and MACE (p. 686; p. 692).
whys.B: Weekly dosing is a methotrexate rule (S49).
whys.D: All JAK inhibitors carry an FDA boxed warning for VTE (DVT, PE), MACE, and cancer (p. 686).

quiz.label: Q15 · Clinical vignette · Osteoarthritis, Rheumatoid Arthritis & DMARDs

quiz.stem: Which conventional DMARD requires a baseline eye exam and annual screening after 5 years because of retinopathy?

options.B: Mycophenolate mofetil
options.C: Sulfasalazine

quiz.why: Antimalarials bind melanin-rich tissue such as the retina; a baseline exam and annual screening after 5 years are recommended (p. 684).

whys.A: Methotrexate monitoring targets liver, marrow, and lung (S49).
whys.B: Mycophenolate’s issues are GI, liver, cytopenias, and infection (p. 689).
whys.C: Sulfasalazine’s issues are GI, rash, and cytopenias (p. 690).
whys.D: Leflunomide’s issues are diarrhea and liver tests (p. 688).
whys.E: Antimalarials bind melanin-rich tissue such as the retina; a baseline exam and annual screening after 5 years are recommended (p. 684).

quiz.label: Q16 · Mechanism · Osteoarthritis, Rheumatoid Arthritis & DMARDs

quiz.stem: In Figure 4, probenecid and allopurinol both lower serum uric acid, but through different mechanisms. What is the key difference?

options.A: Probenecid increases renal excretion of uric acid; allopurinol decreases uric acid production
options.B: Both drugs block xanthine oxidase
options.C: Probenecid decreases uric acid production; allopurinol increases renal excretion
options.D: Neither drug affects serum uric acid levels

quiz.why: Figure 4 shows allopurinol (and febuxostat) acting as xanthine oxidase inhibitors that reduce uric acid production, while probenecid acts at the kidney to increase renal excretion of uric acid that has already been produced — two different strategies for the same goal of lowering serum uric acid.
quiz.label: Lecture check 1 · S7-8

quiz.stem: A patient presents with an acute gout flare. Which action is most appropriate at this visit?

options.A: Treat the acute flare (colchicine, NSAID, or corticosteroid) and defer urate-lowering therapy
options.B: Start allopurinol immediately to lower uric acid
options.C: Start febuxostat and allopurinol together
options.D: No treatment is needed until uric acid is measured

quiz.why: Starting or changing urate-lowering therapy during an acute flare can worsen or prolong it. Treat the flare first; urate-lowering therapy is started or adjusted only once it resolves.
quiz.label: Lecture check 2 · S17-18

quiz.stem: In Figure 5, which agent is the odd one out, acting directly on the skeletal muscle fiber rather than within the central nervous system?

options.B: Tizanidine
options.C: Baclofen

quiz.why: Dantrolene decreases calcium release from the skeletal muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum, acting directly on the muscle fiber — unlike cyclobenzaprine, tizanidine, and baclofen, which all act within the CNS to reduce excitatory output to motor neurons.
quiz.label: Lecture check 3 · S25-26

quiz.stem: Which skeletal muscle relaxant acts directly on skeletal muscle itself (not the CNS), making it the agent of choice in malignant hyperthermia?

options.B: Dantrolene
options.C: Tizanidine

quiz.why: Dantrolene’s peripheral mechanism — decreasing calcium release from the skeletal muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum — is unique among these agents and is exactly why it is the emergency treatment for malignant hyperthermia.
quiz.label: Lecture check 4 · S36-37

quiz.stem: In Figure 6, PTH release raises serum calcium through three parallel actions. Which organ system is NOT one of the three direct targets of PTH shown in the diagram?

options.B: Kidney
options.C: Intestine (directly)

quiz.why: PTH acts directly on bone (↑ osteoclast resorption) and kidney (↑ calcium reabsorption, activates vitamin D); its effect on the intestine is indirect, mediated through activated vitamin D. The lung is not part of this feedback loop at all.
quiz.label: Lecture check 5 · S44-45

quiz.stem: Based on Figure 7, which bisphosphonate requires the fewest doses per year, and by what route is it given?

options.B: Ibandronate, given orally
options.C: All bisphosphonates require the same number of annual doses

quiz.why: Figure 7 shows zoledronic acid dosed as infrequently as once yearly by IV infusion, versus weekly oral dosing for alendronate/risedronate and monthly oral dosing for ibandronate — an important consideration for patients with adherence challenges.
quiz.label: Lecture check 6 · S50-51

quiz.stem: In Figure 8, teriparatide and romosozumab sit on the "bone formation" side of the balance, while alendronate and raloxifene sit on the "bone resorption" side. What does this grouping represent?

options.A: Teriparatide and romosozumab stimulate osteoblast activity, while alendronate and raloxifene inhibit osteoclast activity
options.B: All four drugs work through the identical mechanism
options.C: Teriparatide and romosozumab inhibit osteoclasts, while alendronate and raloxifene stimulate osteoblasts
options.D: This grouping reflects route of administration, not mechanism

quiz.why: The "anabolic" agents (teriparatide, abaloparatide, romosozumab) sit on the bone-formation side because they stimulate osteoblasts, while bisphosphonates (alendronate), denosumab, SERMs (raloxifene), and calcitonin sit on the bone-resorption side because they inhibit osteoclasts — two different strategies for shifting the same remodeling balance.
quiz.label: Lecture check 7 · S57-58

quiz.stem: A patient is counseled to take their oral bisphosphonate with a full glass of water and remain upright for a specified period. What complication is this counseling primarily meant to prevent?

options.B: Atypical femoral fracture
options.C: Esophageal irritation or injury

quiz.why: Taking the tablet with a full glass of water and staying upright reduces the time the pill is in contact with the esophageal mucosa, lowering the risk of esophageal irritation or injury.
quiz.label: Lecture check 8 · S60-61

quiz.stem: A patient with osteoporosis has significant difficulty swallowing pills. Which administration route among osteoporosis therapies would best fit this patient?

options.B: Daily oral risedronate
options.C: There is no alternative to oral bisphosphonates
options.D: Yearly IV zoledronic acid or a subcutaneous injectable agent

quiz.why: Route of administration and adherence are explicit factors in choosing osteoporosis therapy — IV zoledronic acid or an injectable agent (e.g., denosumab) avoids the swallowing difficulty that limits oral options.
quiz.label: Lecture check 9 · S65-66

quiz.stem: Why is acetaminophen not a reliable first-line choice for an inflammatory joint flare, despite being a good analgesic/antipyretic?

options.B: It has minimal peripheral anti-inflammatory effect
options.C: It is contraindicated in all patients with joint pain
options.D: It is a DMARD and too strong for mild flares

quiz.why: Acetaminophen has minimal peripheral anti-inflammatory effect, unlike NSAIDs — it treats pain and fever, not inflammation itself.
quiz.topic: Putting It All Together: Musculoskeletal Toolkit
quiz.label: Lecture check 10 · S69; S71

quiz.stem: A 70-year-old with CKD and heart failure needs osteoarthritis pain control. Considering systemic risk, which is generally the safest starting point?

options.B: Oral celecoxib
options.C: Acetaminophen or a topical NSAID

quiz.why: Acetaminophen or a topical NSAID avoids the systemic renal/CV risk of oral NSAIDs in a patient with CKD and heart failure.
quiz.topic: Putting It All Together: Musculoskeletal Toolkit
quiz.label: Lecture check 11 · S69; S71

quiz.stem: Which pairing correctly matches a drug with its primary mechanism?

options.B: Colchicine — xanthine oxidase inhibition
options.C: Baclofen — calcium channel blockade in skeletal muscle

quiz.why: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase. Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase; colchicine disrupts microtubules; baclofen is a GABA-B agonist.
quiz.topic: Putting It All Together: Musculoskeletal Toolkit
quiz.label: Lecture check 12 · S69; S71

quiz.stem: A patient on a biologic DMARD develops a fever. What is the most important immediate concern?

options.A: Infection, given the drug’s immunosuppressive effect
options.B: A drug allergy only
options.C: Osteonecrosis of the jaw

quiz.why: Immunosuppression is the shared major risk across all DMARDs — a fever must be treated as a possible infection until proven otherwise.
quiz.topic: Putting It All Together: Musculoskeletal Toolkit
quiz.label: Lecture check 13 · S70; S71

quiz.stem: Which statement about gout pharmacology is correct?

options.B: Acute flares should always be treated with urate-lowering therapy first
options.C: Probenecid lowers uric acid by inhibiting renal tubular reabsorption of urate
options.D: Febuxostat and probenecid are both xanthine oxidase inhibitors

quiz.why: Probenecid is a uricosuric agent that inhibits renal tubular reabsorption of uric acid, increasing its excretion. Colchicine does not lower uric acid; febuxostat (not probenecid) is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor; and urate-lowering therapy is deferred during an acute flare.
quiz.topic: Putting It All Together: Musculoskeletal Toolkit
quiz.label: Lecture check 14 · S70; S71

quiz.stem: A patient with glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis risk should be counseled that the risk is primarily related to which mechanism?

options.A: Increased osteoclast-mediated resorption and decreased bone formation
options.B: Increased osteoblast activity
options.C: Excess vitamin D

quiz.why: Glucocorticoids increase osteoclast-mediated bone resorption and suppress osteoblast-driven bone formation — shifting the remodeling balance toward bone loss.
quiz.topic: Putting It All Together: Musculoskeletal Toolkit
quiz.label: Lecture check 15 · S70; S71

quiz.stem: How does colchicine relieve an acute gout flare?

options.A: It disrupts microtubules, reducing neutrophil migration
options.B: It blocks phospholipase A₂ upstream of COX
options.C: It converts uric acid to allantoin in the joint
options.D: It blocks URAT1, increasing uric acid excretion
options.E: It inhibits xanthine oxidase, lowering uric acid

quiz.why: Colchicine binds tubulin and blocks microtubule polymerization, reducing neutrophil migration and NLRP3 activation (S10; S11; SG U2-M).

whys.A: Colchicine binds tubulin and blocks microtubule polymerization, reducing neutrophil migration and NLRP3 activation (S10; S11; SG U2-M).
whys.E: That is allopurinol/febuxostat; colchicine doesn’t lower uric acid (S71).

quiz.label: Q1 · Mechanism · Gout: Acute Flares & Urate-Lowering Therapy

quiz.stem: A patient on colchicine for a gout flare is prescribed clarithromycin for pneumonia. What is the concern?

options.A: Clarithromycin speeds colchicine clearance, so the flare returns
options.B: Clarithromycin triggers HLA-B*58:01 hypersensitivity
options.C: CYP3A4/P-gp inhibition raises colchicine to toxic levels
options.D: The pair raises uric acid and worsens the flare
options.E: The two together cause hemolysis in G6PD deficiency

whys.A: It is an inhibitor; levels rise (S11).
whys.C: CYP3A4 and P-gp inhibitors such as clarithromycin, cyclosporine, and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors raise colchicine toxicity (S11).
whys.D: The taught interaction is colchicine toxicity (S11).
whys.E: Hemolysis in G6PD deficiency is the uricase warning (S15).

quiz.label: Q2 · Clinical vignette · Gout: Acute Flares & Urate-Lowering Therapy

quiz.stem: A patient of Han Chinese descent with recurrent gout is about to start allopurinol. Which pre-treatment step does the lecture tie to Lecture 1’s pharmacogenomics?

options.A: G6PD testing for hemolysis risk on the drug
options.B: HLA-B*58:01 testing for severe hypersensitivity risk
options.C: TPMT testing for bone marrow toxicity risk
options.D: CYP2D6 genotyping for poor metabolizer status
options.E: Baseline joint aspiration for urate crystals

quiz.topic: Putting It All Together: Musculoskeletal Toolkit

quiz.stem: Based on Figure 1, why do PPIs achieve more complete acid suppression than H2 receptor antagonists?

options.A: PPIs block the final common pathway (the proton pump itself), so they work regardless of which upstream signal is driving acid secretion
options.B: PPIs block only the gastrin pathway, which is the strongest stimulus
options.C: H2RAs block the proton pump directly, while PPIs act upstream
options.D: There is no mechanistic difference between the two classes

quiz.why: H2RAs block only one of three inputs to the parietal cell (histamine), so gastrin and acetylcholine can still drive acid secretion. PPIs irreversibly inhibit the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase proton pump — the single convergence point for all three signals — producing more complete and longer-lasting acid suppression.
quiz.label: Lecture check 1 · S9-10

quiz.stem: A patient taking clopidogrel after a cardiac stent is started on omeprazole for GERD. What is the primary concern with this combination?

options.A: Omeprazole may reduce CYP2C19-mediated activation of clopidogrel, blunting its antiplatelet effect
options.B: Omeprazole increases clopidogrel absorption, raising bleeding risk
options.C: There is no clinically relevant interaction between these two drugs
options.D: Omeprazole should never be combined with any cardiac medication

quiz.why: Clopidogrel is a prodrug that requires CYP2C19 activation. Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, which can reduce clopidogrel’s active metabolite and blunt its antiplatelet effect — a clinically important interaction, especially soon after stent placement.

options.B: Is there any possibility of pregnancy?
options.C: Does the patient have a penicillin allergy?
options.D: Is the patient on a PPI already?

quiz.why: Misoprostol is a potent uterotonic and is contraindicated in pregnancy due to abortifacient risk — pregnancy status must be ruled out (and reliable contraception confirmed) before starting therapy.
quiz.label: Lecture check 3 · S26-27

quiz.stem: A patient with motion sickness needs prophylaxis before a cruise. Based on Figure 9, which drug class targets the pathway most relevant to this cause of nausea?

options.A: H1 / M1 antagonists (e.g., meclizine, scopolamine) — targeting the vestibular system
options.B: 5-HT3 antagonists (e.g., ondansetron) — targeting gut/chemo input
options.C: NK1 antagonists (e.g., aprepitant) — targeting the CTZ
options.D: D2 antagonists (e.g., metoclopramide) — targeting the CTZ

quiz.why: Motion sickness is driven primarily by vestibular system input, which signals through histamine (H1) and muscarinic (M1) receptors — exactly the pathway meclizine and scopolamine block in Figure 9. The other classes target gut/chemo (5-HT3) or CTZ (D2, NK1) inputs, which are not the primary driver here.
