options.C: Tardive dyskinesia (boxed warning)

quiz.why: Metoclopramide carries a boxed warning for tardive dyskinesia with prolonged use or high doses; avoid beyond 12 weeks (S36–S37; SG U3-R8).

whys.A: Acute dystonia occurs early; this is late and long-term (S36).
whys.C: Metoclopramide carries a boxed warning for tardive dyskinesia with prolonged use or high doses; avoid beyond 12 weeks (S36–S37; SG U3-R8).

quiz.label: Q15 · Clinical vignette · Antiemetics

quiz.stem: A patient on citalopram and with a borderline long QT needs an antiemetic after surgery. Why is ondansetron a cautious choice?

options.B: Tardive dyskinesia after one dose
options.C: Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol
options.D: QT prolongation and serotonin syndrome risk

quiz.why: Ondansetron prolongs the QT interval and carries serotonin syndrome risk with serotonergic drugs (S31).

whys.D: Ondansetron prolongs the QT interval and carries serotonin syndrome risk with serotonergic drugs (S31).

quiz.label: Q16 · Clinical vignette · Antiemetics

quiz.stem: A patient with refractory chemotherapy nausea is started on dronabinol. How does it work?

options.A: Activates CB1 receptors in the vomiting center and CTZ
options.B: Blocks substance P at NK1 receptors
options.C: Blocks muscarinic receptors in the vestibular system
options.E: Blocks D2 in the chemoreceptor trigger zone

quiz.why: Dronabinol is a CB1 agonist that reduces neurotransmitter release and stimulates appetite — distinct from 5-HT3, D2, NK1, H1/M1 (S38–S39; SG U3-M).

whys.A: Dronabinol is a CB1 agonist that reduces neurotransmitter release and stimulates appetite — distinct from 5-HT3, D2, NK1, H1/M1 (S38–S39; SG U3-M).

quiz.label: Q17 · Mechanism · Antiemetics

quiz.stem: Why are meclizine and scopolamine the classes that fit motion sickness?

options.A: They activate CB1 receptors in the cortex
options.B: They block D2 receptors in the CTZ
options.C: They block 5-HT3 on gut vagal afferents
options.D: They block NK1 receptors in the CTZ
options.E: They block H1/M1 input from the vestibular system

quiz.why: Motion sickness is vestibular; H1/M1 antagonists block histamine/acetylcholine from the vestibular system (S30; S33 notes; SG U3-R7).

whys.E: Motion sickness is vestibular; H1/M1 antagonists block histamine/acetylcholine from the vestibular system (S30; S33 notes; SG U3-R7).

quiz.label: Q18 · Mechanism · Antiemetics

quiz.stem: Based on Figure 2, a hospitalized patient needs constipation relief within a few hours. Which class is the most appropriate choice?

options.B: Stool softener
options.C: Osmotic or stimulant
options.D: None of these act quickly enough

quiz.why: Figure 2 shows osmotic agents (~2 hours) and stimulant agents (~8 hours) acting far faster than bulk-forming agents or stool softeners (~2–2.5 days) — appropriate choices when relief is needed within hours rather than days.
quiz.label: Lecture check 1 · S7-8

quiz.stem: Why is a subtherapeutic dose of atropine included in the diphenoxylate/atropine combination product?

options.A: To treat the underlying cause of diarrhea
options.B: To discourage intentional overdose/misuse of the opioid component
options.C: To increase the antidiarrheal effect of diphenoxylate

quiz.why: At therapeutic doses, the atropine dose is too low to produce significant anticholinergic effects, but at supratherapeutic (misuse) doses, unpleasant anticholinergic effects (tachycardia, dry mouth, flushing) emerge — an intentional deterrent against abuse of the opioid agonist diphenoxylate.
quiz.label: Lecture check 2 · S12-13

quiz.stem: In Figure 7, which biologic agent acts by a mechanism that is gut-selective rather than systemically immunosuppressive in the same way as the others?

options.B: Adalimumab
options.C: Vedolizumab

quiz.why: Vedolizumab blocks α4β7 integrin, which is relatively selective for gut-homing leukocyte trafficking — giving it a more gut-selective safety profile compared with TNF-α inhibitors or JAK inhibitors, which act more broadly on systemic immune signaling.
quiz.label: Lecture check 3 · S22-23

quiz.stem: A patient with Crohn disease has been in remission on azathioprine for maintenance but now has an acute flare. What is the most appropriate immediate addition to therapy?

options.B: Add a short course of corticosteroids to induce remission
options.C: Switch directly to a stimulant laxative
options.D: Discontinue all therapy until symptoms resolve on their own

quiz.why: Immunomodulators like azathioprine have a slow onset and are not effective for acute flares. Corticosteroids provide faster induction of remission during a flare, while the immunomodulator continues for long-term maintenance.
quiz.label: Lecture check 4 · S26-27

quiz.stem: Based on Figure 10, a patient stable on warfarin starts taking a St. John’s Wort supplement for mood. What is the expected effect on anticoagulation?

options.A: Decreased anticoagulant effect, due to increased warfarin metabolism via CYP3A4 induction
options.B: Increased anticoagulant effect, due to CYP3A4 inhibition
options.C: No effect, since herbal supplements do not interact with prescription drugs
options.D: Increased vitamin K levels directly counteracting warfarin

quiz.why: St. John’s Wort is a well-known CYP3A4 inducer, which increases warfarin metabolism and lowers its anticoagulant effect (a pharmacokinetic interaction) — a distinct mechanism from dietary vitamin K, which opposes warfarin pharmacodynamically by supporting clotting factor synthesis.
quiz.label: Lecture check 5 · S36-37

quiz.stem: A patient on long-term omeprazole therapy is found to have megaloblastic anemia and neurologic symptoms. Which deficiency is most likely, and why?

options.A: Vitamin B12 deficiency, due to reduced acid-dependent absorption
options.B: Vitamin C deficiency, due to increased renal excretion
options.C: Vitamin K deficiency, due to reduced dietary intake
options.D: Vitamin A deficiency, due to fat malabsorption

quiz.why: Long-term PPI use reduces gastric acid, which is needed to release B12 from dietary protein for absorption. This is one of the well-documented long-term PPI adverse effects covered in Session 1 and explains the megaloblastic anemia and neurologic symptoms here.
quiz.label: Lecture check 6 · S42-43

quiz.stem: A patient with well-controlled GERD on a PPI for three years asks whether they should keep taking it indefinitely. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Periodically reassess the need for continued therapy, given long-term risks such as B12 deficiency, hypomagnesemia, fracture, and C. difficile risk
options.B: PPIs have no long-term risks, so continuing indefinitely is always fine
options.C: PPIs should never be used for more than one week
options.D: Switch immediately to an antacid with no further discussion

quiz.why: Long-term PPI use carries real, well-documented risks. Best practice is not indefinite, unexamined continuation — it is periodic reassessment of ongoing need, attempting dose reduction or discontinuation when clinically appropriate, while still treating confirmed indications adequately.
quiz.label: Lecture check 7 · S46-47

quiz.stem: Why do PPIs provide more complete acid suppression than H2 receptor antagonists?

options.A: They block only the gastrin pathway
options.B: They block the final common pathway (the proton pump) regardless of upstream signal
options.C: They neutralize acid directly, like antacids

quiz.why: PPIs block the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase proton pump itself — the final common pathway for gastrin, histamine, and acetylcholine signals — unlike H2RAs, which block only the histamine input.
quiz.topic: Putting It All Together: GI & Nutrition Toolkit
quiz.label: Lecture check 8 · S50; S52

quiz.stem: A patient recently exposed to a macrolide antibiotic needs H. pylori eradication. Which regimen best avoids the concern this history raises?

options.B: Bismuth quadruple therapy
options.C: Antacids alone

quiz.why: Recent macrolide exposure raises concern for clarithromycin resistance, favoring bismuth quadruple therapy over standard clarithromycin-based triple therapy.
quiz.topic: Putting It All Together: GI & Nutrition Toolkit
quiz.label: Lecture check 9 · S50; S52

quiz.stem: Which pairing correctly matches an antiemetic with its receptor target?

options.B: Aprepitant — NK1 receptor
options.C: Meclizine — 5-HT3 receptor

quiz.why: Aprepitant blocks the NK1 receptor. Ondansetron blocks 5-HT3; meclizine blocks H1/M1; metoclopramide blocks D2.
quiz.topic: Putting It All Together: GI & Nutrition Toolkit
quiz.label: Lecture check 10 · S50; S52

quiz.stem: A patient with suspected C. difficile infection asks for something to stop their diarrhea. What is the main concern with giving loperamide here?

options.B: Slowing transit can worsen toxin-mediated colonic injury
options.C: Loperamide treats the underlying infection
options.D: There is no concern in this scenario

quiz.why: Antimotility agents can worsen outcomes in infectious/inflammatory diarrhea like C. difficile by delaying clearance of toxin and slowing transit, raising risk of complications such as toxic megacolon.
quiz.topic: Putting It All Together: GI & Nutrition Toolkit
quiz.label: Lecture check 11 · S51; S52

quiz.stem: Which IBD agent is most gut-selective in its mechanism, rather than broadly systemically immunosuppressive?

options.B: Vedolizumab
options.C: Tofacitinib

quiz.why: Vedolizumab blocks α4β7 integrin-mediated leukocyte gut-homing, giving it a more gut-selective mechanism than TNF-α inhibitors, JAK inhibitors, or thiopurine immunomodulators.
quiz.topic: Putting It All Together: GI & Nutrition Toolkit
quiz.label: Lecture check 12 · S51; S52

quiz.stem: A warfarin patient’s INR drops after starting St. John’s Wort. What mechanism explains this?

options.B: CYP3A4 inhibition, decreasing warfarin metabolism
options.C: Direct vitamin K supplementation

quiz.why: St. John’s Wort is a CYP3A4 inducer, increasing warfarin metabolism and lowering its anticoagulant effect (and INR) — a pharmacokinetic drug-herb interaction.

quiz.label: Lecture check 13 · S51; S52

quiz.stem: Rank the laxative classes by onset, fastest first.

options.B: Secretagogue, then bulk-forming, then osmotic
options.C: All laxative classes act within the same hour
options.E: Stool softener, then bulk-forming, then stimulant

quiz.why: Osmotic and stimulant act within hours; bulk-forming and stool softeners take about 2–2.5 days (S6; SG U3-R9).

whys.D: Osmotic and stimulant act within hours; bulk-forming and stool softeners take about 2–2.5 days (S6; SG U3-R9).

options.B: Linaclotide

options.B: Stimulant senna at bedtime

quiz.stem: A Crohn patient on azathioprine develops gout and is started on allopurinol. What must happen?

quiz.label: Q4 · Clinical vignette · Inflammatory Bowel Disease

quiz.stem: Why is budesonide associated with fewer systemic steroid effects than prednisone?

options.A: It is a 5-ASA prodrug cleaved in the colon
options.B: High first-pass metabolism limits systemic exposure
options.C: It is taken once monthly by injection
options.D: It has no glucocorticoid activity at all
options.E: It blocks α4β7 integrin in the gut

quiz.why: Budesonide has high first-pass metabolism — less systemic exposure than prednisone (S18).

whys.B: Budesonide has high first-pass metabolism — less systemic exposure than prednisone (S18).

quiz.stem: Before starting infliximab for Crohn disease, which steps are required?

options.A: TB, hepatitis B/C screening; vaccines first
options.B: TPMT and NUDT15 genotyping only, nothing else
options.C: G6PD activity testing before the infusion
options.D: A baseline DEXA scan of the spine only
options.E: Nothing until an infection actually appears

whys.A: Screen for tuberculosis and hepatitis B/C, and update vaccines (especially live) before starting biologics (S24).

quiz.stem: Why are fat-soluble vitamins more prone to toxicity than water-soluble vitamins?

quiz.stem: A severely malnourished patient is about to start feeding. Which plan prevents refeeding syndrome?

quiz.stem: A woman taking levothyroxine with her calcium and iron each morning has a high TSH. Best advice?

options.A: Separate them by at least 4 hours
options.B: Stop calcium permanently

quiz.stem: Why is PTU, rather than methimazole, preferred in the management of thyroid storm?

quiz.label: Lecture check 1 · S33; S35

quiz.stem: A patient on chronic glucocorticoid therapy abruptly stops the medication and develops hypotension and weakness. What is the underlying mechanism?

options.A: Direct adrenal gland destruction by the drug
options.B: HPA-axis suppression leaving endogenous cortisol production unable to resume quickly
options.C: An allergic reaction to the glucocorticoid

options.C: Mild seasonal allergies
options.D: A family history of type 2 diabetes

quiz.label: Lecture check 3 · S33; S35

quiz.stem: Why do sulfonylureas carry a higher hypoglycemia risk than DPP-4 inhibitors?

options.A: Sulfonylureas force K-ATP channel closure and insulin release independent of glucose level, unlike the glucose-dependent incretin pathway
options.B: DPP-4 inhibitors have no effect on insulin secretion
options.C: Sulfonylureas work only in type 1 diabetes
options.D: There is no difference in hypoglycemia risk between these classes

quiz.why: Sulfonylureas bind the K-ATP channel directly and force closure regardless of glucose level (Figure 15), while incretin-based agents amplify insulin release only when glucose is already elevated — explaining the difference in hypoglycemia risk.

quiz.stem: A patient with hypoparathyroidism after thyroid surgery needs pharmacologic treatment. Which combination is the mainstay of therapy?

options.C: Bisphosphonate plus denosumab

quiz.label: Lecture check 5 · S34; S35

quiz.stem: A patient taking an SGLT2 inhibitor develops a genital yeast infection. What is the mechanistic explanation?

options.B: Increased urinary glucose excretion promoting fungal overgrowth
options.C: Decreased renal blood flow
options.D: Systemic candidemia from the drug itself

quiz.why: SGLT2 inhibitors block renal glucose reabsorption, increasing urinary glucose concentration and creating a favorable environment for genital fungal overgrowth — a mechanism-based, well-known adverse effect.

quiz.label: Lecture check 6 · S34; S35

quiz.stem: A woman on a combined pill starts rifampin for latent TB. What counseling is needed?

options.B: No change; rifampin has no effect
options.C: Double the pill each day
options.E: Switch rifampin to St. John’s wort

quiz.why: Enzyme inducers (rifampin, some antiepileptics, St. John’s wort) lower contraceptive efficacy (S6).

whys.A: Enzyme inducers (rifampin, some antiepileptics, St. John’s wort) lower contraceptive efficacy (S6).

quiz.label: Q1 · Clinical vignette · Gonadal Hormones & Inhibitors

quiz.stem: Which statement about tamoxifen and raloxifene is correct?

options.B: Raloxifene treats breast cancer
options.C: Both are breast agonists

quiz.why: Tamoxifen is an endometrial agonist (cancer risk); raloxifene blocks the endometrium (S7–S8).

whys.E: Tamoxifen is an endometrial agonist (cancer risk); raloxifene blocks the endometrium (S7–S8).

quiz.label: Q2 · Mechanism · Gonadal Hormones & Inhibitors

quiz.stem: A man on finasteride for BPH has a PSA of 2.0 ng/mL. How should it be interpreted?

options.B: Stop finasteride for a month first
options.C: Double it — about 4.0 — when screening

quiz.why: Finasteride lowers PSA by about half, so double the value (S9).

whys.C: Finasteride lowers PSA by about half, so double the value (S9).

quiz.stem: A patient on insulin and propranolol has a glucose of 45 mg/dL but no tremor or palpitations. Why?

options.A: The meter is reading falsely low
options.B: Hypoglycemia never causes tremor
options.C: Propranolol raises glucose

quiz.why: Beta-blockers can mask hypoglycemia warning symptoms (S13; S67).

whys.B: Tremor is a warning sign masked here (S13).
whys.E: Beta-blockers can mask hypoglycemia warning symptoms (S13; S67).

options.B: Insulin degludec

whys.D: Only regular insulin is given IV (S12 notes).

options.A: 1 mg glucagon IM before any carbs
options.B: 15 g fast carbs, recheck in 15 min
options.C: Wait one hour, then recheck
options.D: Give the next insulin dose early

whys.A: For patients who cannot take oral carbs (S67).

options.B: Add an SGLT2 inhibitor the same day
options.C: Continue without change
options.D: Hold metformin around the contrast study
options.E: Double metformin to cover the stress

whys.D: Hold for contrast dye with reduced kidney function — lactic acidosis risk (S15; S67).

quiz.stem: A patient with a family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma asks about semaglutide for diabetes and weight. Best answer?

options.B: Use it with a DPP-4 inhibitor
options.C: Safe if taken with food
options.D: Safe; it only affects the gut

quiz.why: GLP-1 RAs are contraindicated with personal or family history of MTC or MEN2 (S19).

whys.A: GLP-1 RAs are contraindicated with personal or family history of MTC or MEN2 (S19).

quiz.label: Q8 · Clinical vignette · Non-Insulin Glucose-Lowering Drugs

quiz.stem: Which class most often causes fluid retention and can worsen heart failure?

options.B: DPP-4 inhibitors (sitagliptin)
options.C: SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin)

quiz.why: TZDs: fluid retention/heart failure, weight gain (S14).

whys.D: TZDs: fluid retention/heart failure, weight gain (S14).

quiz.label: Q9 · Mechanism · Non-Insulin Glucose-Lowering Drugs

quiz.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes has NYHA class III heart failure. Which drug is contraindicated?

options.B: Semaglutide
options.C: Pioglitazone

quiz.why: Thiazolidinediones cause fluid retention and are contraindicated in NYHA class III and IV heart failure (p. 799).

whys.C: Thiazolidinediones cause fluid retention and are contraindicated in NYHA class III and IV heart failure (p. 799).

quiz.label: Q10 · Clinical vignette · Non-Insulin Glucose-Lowering Drugs

quiz.stem: What should be monitored after starting cinacalcet?

options.B: Potassium for hyperkalemia
options.C: TSH for hypothyroidism

quiz.why: Cinacalcet lowers PTH and calcium; monitor for hypocalcemia (and QT) (S25–S26).

whys.E: Cinacalcet lowers PTH and calcium; monitor for hypocalcemia (and QT) (S25–S26).

quiz.label: Q11 · Mechanism · Parathyroid Disorders

quiz.stem: Why does a falling GFR change how a renally cleared drug must be dosed?

options.A: Absorption from the gut falls with GFR
options.B: Only the parent drug matters, not metabolites
options.C: The loading dose must always be doubled
options.D: The drug accumulates unless dose or interval is adjusted
options.E: The drug is cleared faster, so doses rise

quiz.why: Reduced GFR causes a renally cleared drug to accumulate if unadjusted; reduce the dose, extend the interval, or both (S5; SG U5-R1).

whys.D: Reduced GFR causes a renally cleared drug to accumulate if unadjusted; reduce the dose, extend the interval, or both (S5; SG U5-R1).

quiz.label: Q1 · Mechanism · Renal Dosing & Diuretic Sites

quiz.stem: An 80-year-old has pneumonia and dehydration. She takes metformin and a DOAC. What is the best dosing habit?

options.A: Stop checking renal function in older adults
options.B: Keep last year’s doses since CrCl is stable
options.C: Re-estimate CrCl now and adjust renally cleared drugs
options.D: Double the loading dose of both drugs
options.E: Adjust only the drugs with toxic metabolites

quiz.why: Acute illness and dehydration can drop GFR quickly; estimate CrCl or eGFR and reassess renally cleared drugs (S8).

whys.C: Acute illness and dehydration can drop GFR quickly; estimate CrCl or eGFR and reassess renally cleared drugs (S8).

quiz.label: Q2 · Clinical vignette · Renal Dosing & Diuretic Sites

quiz.stem: Roughly what share of filtered sodium does each segment reabsorb, from proximal tubule to collecting duct?

options.B: About equal at 25% in every segment

quiz.why: Proximal tubule ~65%, thick ascending limb ~25%, distal tubule 5–8%, collecting duct 2–3% (S7 notes).

whys.D: Proximal tubule ~65%, thick ascending limb ~25%, distal tubule 5–8%, collecting duct 2–3% (S7 notes).

quiz.label: Q3 · Mechanism · Renal Dosing & Diuretic Sites

quiz.stem: Why do loop diuretics increase calcium excretion while thiazides decrease it?

options.A: Loops collapse lumen potential; thiazides aid NCX
options.B: Thiazides act on NKCC2; loops act on NCC
options.C: Loops block calcium channels; thiazides open them
options.E: Loops raise PTH; thiazides suppress PTH

quiz.why: Loops collapse the lumen-positive potential driving paracellular Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ reabsorption; thiazides lower cell Na⁺ so NCX reabsorbs more Ca²⁺ (S11; S13; SG U5-R3).

whys.A: Loops collapse the lumen-positive potential driving paracellular Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ reabsorption; thiazides lower cell Na⁺ so NCX reabsorbs more Ca²⁺ (S11; S13; SG U5-R3).

quiz.label: Q4 · Mechanism · Loop & Thiazide Diuretics

quiz.stem: A patient has recurrent calcium kidney stones and hypertension with normal renal function. Which diuretic fits best?

options.B: Furosemide (loop diuretic)
options.C: Hydrochlorothiazide (thiazide)

quiz.why: Thiazides decrease calcium excretion, useful in recurrent calcium stones; first-line HTN with preserved renal function (S12; S30).

whys.C: Thiazides decrease calcium excretion, useful in recurrent calcium stones; first-line HTN with preserved renal function (S12; S30).
whys.D: Kidney stones are an adverse effect (S36).

quiz.label: Q5 · Clinical vignette · Loop & Thiazide Diuretics

quiz.stem: A patient with heart failure on digoxin starts high-dose furosemide. Which lab change most raises digoxin toxicity risk?

options.B: Metabolic acidosis
options.C: Hypercalcemia

quiz.why: Hypokalemia from loops increases digoxin toxicity (S38).

whys.A: Hypokalemia from loops increases digoxin toxicity (S38).

quiz.label: Q6 · Clinical vignette · Loop & Thiazide Diuretics

quiz.stem: Which adverse effect is most characteristic of loop diuretics given rapidly IV at high doses?

options.B: Ototoxicity
options.C: Hypercalcemia

quiz.why: Ototoxicity, especially with rapid IV administration or high doses; give IV furosemide no faster than 4 mg/min (S10; S27).

whys.B: Ototoxicity, especially with rapid IV administration or high doses; give IV furosemide no faster than 4 mg/min (S10; S27).

quiz.label: Q7 · Mechanism · Loop & Thiazide Diuretics

quiz.stem: An older woman on hydrochlorothiazide is confused, with sodium 122 mEq/L. Which statement fits?

options.A: Thiazide hyponatremia, especially in older adults
options.B: Thiazides raise sodium by blocking ADH
options.C: This is mannitol-type osmotic diuresis
options.D: Loop diuretics cause more hyponatremia than thiazides

quiz.why: Hyponatremia can be significant with thiazides, especially in older adults (S12).

whys.A: Hyponatremia can be significant with thiazides, especially in older adults (S12).

quiz.label: Q8 · Clinical vignette · Loop & Thiazide Diuretics

quiz.stem: A patient with CKD on furosemide 80 mg twice daily has hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg added. Two weeks later he has lost 15 kg, BP is 91/58 and creatinine is 10.8. What happened?

options.B: Thiazide failed, so fluid built up
options.C: Thiazide-induced hypercalcemia

quiz.why: Adding a thiazide to chronic loop therapy can cause dramatic diuresis, hypovolemia and AKI; monitor very closely, ideally inpatient (p. 277; p. 285).

whys.C: Not the cause of AKI here (p. 285).
whys.E: Adding a thiazide to chronic loop therapy can cause dramatic diuresis, hypovolemia and AKI; monitor very closely, ideally inpatient (p. 277; p. 285).

quiz.label: Q9 · Clinical vignette · Loop & Thiazide Diuretics

quiz.stem: Why must saline be given with furosemide to treat hypercalcemia?

options.A: Saline blocks NKCC2 with the loop
options.B: Saline prevents loop ototoxicity in the ear
options.C: Volume loss boosts proximal Ca²⁺ reabsorption

quiz.why: A loop alone causes volume contraction, which enhances proximal Ca²⁺ reabsorption and stops the calcium diuresis; give saline with it (p. 280).

whys.C: A loop alone causes volume contraction, which enhances proximal Ca²⁺ reabsorption and stops the calcium diuresis; give saline with it (p. 280).

quiz.label: Q10 · Mechanism · Loop & Thiazide Diuretics

quiz.stem: Which pairing correctly matches a potassium-sparing diuretic to its mechanism?

options.B: Spironolactone — blocks ENaC directly
options.C: Triamterene — blocks aldosterone receptor

quiz.why: Amiloride and triamterene block ENaC; spironolactone and eplerenone block the mineralocorticoid receptor (S17–S18).

whys.D: Amiloride and triamterene block ENaC; spironolactone and eplerenone block the mineralocorticoid receptor (S17–S18).

quiz.label: Q11 · Mechanism · Potassium-Sparing, CAI & Osmotic Diuretics

quiz.stem: A man needs an aldosterone antagonist for heart failure but developed painful gynecomastia on one before. Which fits?

options.B: Eplerenone (selective blocker)
options.C: Amiloride (ENaC blocker)

quiz.why: Spironolactone has antiandrogen effects (gynecomastia) that eplerenone largely avoids (S17; S33).

whys.B: Spironolactone has antiandrogen effects (gynecomastia) that eplerenone largely avoids (S17; S33).

quiz.label: Q12 · Clinical vignette · Potassium-Sparing, CAI & Osmotic Diuretics

quiz.stem: A hiker plans a rapid ascent to high altitude next week. Which diuretic is used for prophylaxis?

options.B: Hydrochlorothiazide, once daily
options.C: Acetazolamide, from a day before

quiz.why: Acetazolamide is used for altitude sickness prophylaxis, 125–250 mg BID starting a day before ascent (S19; S36).

whys.C: Acetazolamide is used for altitude sickness prophylaxis, 125–250 mg BID starting a day before ascent (S19; S36).

quiz.label: Q13 · Clinical vignette · Potassium-Sparing, CAI & Osmotic Diuretics

quiz.stem: How does mannitol produce diuresis?

options.A: It is filtered but not reabsorbed, holding water in the lumen
options.B: It antagonizes aldosterone at its receptor
options.C: It inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
options.D: It blocks NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb
options.E: It blocks ENaC in the collecting duct

quiz.why: Mannitol is an inert, filtered but poorly reabsorbed solute that holds water in the tubule lumen osmotically (S19–S20).

whys.A: Mannitol is an inert, filtered but poorly reabsorbed solute that holds water in the tubule lumen osmotically (S19–S20).

quiz.label: Q14 · Mechanism · Potassium-Sparing, CAI & Osmotic Diuretics

quiz.stem: A patient with decompensated heart failure and raised intracranial pressure is being considered for mannitol. What is the concern?

options.A: Mannitol is safe because it is inert
options.B: Mannitol expands ECF volume and can worsen heart failure
options.C: Mannitol has no effect on fluid status
options.D: Mannitol causes severe hyperkalemia via ENaC

quiz.why: Mannitol expands extracellular volume; avoid it in heart failure and volume depletion; needs intact renal perfusion (S19–S20; S37).

whys.B: Mannitol expands extracellular volume; avoid it in heart failure and volume depletion; needs intact renal perfusion (S19–S20; S37).

quiz.label: Q15 · Clinical vignette · Potassium-Sparing, CAI & Osmotic Diuretics

quiz.stem: Which acid–base change is a predictable adverse effect of acetazolamide?

options.B: Respiratory alkalosis
options.C: Metabolic alkalosis

quiz.why: Blocking carbonic anhydrase causes bicarbonate diuresis and a mild metabolic acidosis (S19–S20).

whys.E: Blocking carbonic anhydrase causes bicarbonate diuresis and a mild metabolic acidosis (S19–S20).

quiz.label: Q16 · Mechanism · Potassium-Sparing, CAI & Osmotic Diuretics

quiz.stem: A patient with SIADH stays hyponatremic despite fluid restriction at home. Which drug does the textbook use next?

options.B: Mannitol (given orally)
options.C: Hydrochlorothiazide (thiazide)

quiz.why: ADH antagonists are used for SIADH when water restriction fails; tolvaptan is oral, conivaptan IV (p. 276).

whys.D: ADH antagonists are used for SIADH when water restriction fails; tolvaptan is oral, conivaptan IV (p. 276).

quiz.label: Q17 · Clinical vignette · Potassium-Sparing, CAI & Osmotic Diuretics

quiz.stem: Why do loop diuretics increase calcium excretion while thiazide diuretics decrease it?

options.A: Loop diuretics act in the collecting duct; thiazides act in the proximal tubule
options.B: Loop diuretics collapse the lumen-positive potential that drives paracellular calcium reabsorption; thiazides do not
options.C: Thiazides block the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter
options.D: There is no mechanistic difference between the two classes

quiz.why: Loop diuretics block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, collapsing the lumen-positive potential that normally drives paracellular Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ reabsorption, so calcium excretion rises; thiazides act at the distal tubule and, through a separate mechanism, increase distal calcium reabsorption instead.
quiz.topic: Putting It All Together: Renal Toolkit
quiz.label: Lecture check 1 · S33; S35

quiz.stem: A patient's thiazide diuretic stops controlling blood pressure as CKD advances to an eGFR of 22 mL/min. What is the most appropriate change?

options.B: Switch to a loop diuretic
options.C: Add a second thiazide

quiz.why: Thiazide diuretics lose most of their natriuretic efficacy once GFR falls below roughly 30 mL/min. Loop diuretics act upstream at the thick ascending limb and remain effective in advanced CKD.
quiz.topic: Putting It All Together: Renal Toolkit
quiz.label: Lecture check 2 · S33; S35

quiz.stem: A patient starts lisinopril for proteinuric CKD and the serum creatinine rises by 25% within two weeks. What is the most appropriate response?

options.B: Continue therapy with ongoing monitoring, since this rise is expected
options.C: Double the dose

quiz.why: A creatinine rise of up to approximately 30% after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB reflects reduced intraglomerular pressure from efferent arteriolar dilation — an expected hemodynamic effect, not toxicity — so therapy should generally continue with monitoring.
quiz.topic: Putting It All Together: Renal Toolkit
quiz.label: Lecture check 3 · S33; S35

quiz.stem: Why are ACE inhibitors and ARBs preferred first-line therapy for hypertension in proteinuric CKD?

options.A: They preferentially dilate the efferent arteriole, lowering intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria
options.B: They have no renal effects beyond lowering systemic blood pressure
options.C: They are the only antihypertensive class that can be used in CKD
options.D: They increase aldosterone release to protect sodium balance

quiz.why: ACE inhibitors and ARBs preferentially dilate the efferent arteriole, lowering intraglomerular pressure and reducing proteinuria — a structural renoprotective effect beyond systemic blood pressure control, which is why they are preferred in proteinuric CKD specifically.
quiz.topic: Putting It All Together: Renal Toolkit
quiz.label: Lecture check 4 · S34; S35

quiz.stem: A patient on an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic starts a daily OTC NSAID and develops acute kidney injury. What is the mechanism?

options.A: Three independent reductions in glomerular filtration pressure combining additively
options.B: NSAIDs have no renal effects
options.C: The ACE inhibitor directly damages the NSAID
options.D: This combination has no increased risk

quiz.why: This is the "triple whammy": the NSAID constricts the afferent arteriole, the ACE inhibitor dilates the efferent arteriole, and the diuretic causes volume depletion — three independent reductions in glomerular filtration pressure that combine additively to synergistically, precipitating AKI.
quiz.topic: Putting It All Together: Renal Toolkit
quiz.label: Lecture check 5 · S34; S35

quiz.stem: Which drug class is used for BOTH hypertension and angina pectoris via the same underlying mechanism?

options.B: Calcium channel blockers
options.C: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors

quiz.why: Calcium channel blockers treat hypertension via arteriolar dilation (reducing afterload/systemic vascular resistance) and treat angina via the same arteriolar-dilation mechanism (reducing afterload and myocardial oxygen demand) — the clearest example of one drug class, one mechanism, two indications in this unit.
quiz.topic: Putting It All Together: Renal Toolkit
quiz.label: Lecture check 6 · S34; S35

quiz.stem: Why does an ACE inhibitor cause a dry cough?

options.B: It blocks AT1 receptors in the lung
options.C: Angiotensin II rises and irritates airways
options.D: Bradykinin accumulates because ACE also degrades it
options.E: It is an IgE-mediated allergy to the drug

quiz.why: ACE also breaks down bradykinin; blocking it raises bradykinin, causing cough and angioedema (S6).

whys.B: That is an ARB, which spares cough (S7).
whys.D: ACE also breaks down bradykinin; blocking it raises bradykinin, causing cough and angioedema (S6).

quiz.label: Q1 · Mechanism · RAAS Blockers

quiz.stem: A woman of reproductive age with proteinuric CKD needs antihypertensive therapy. What must be addressed first with an ACE inhibitor?

options.B: Bradykinin cough risk only
options.C: Pregnancy risk — fetal renal toxicity

quiz.why: ACE inhibitors (and ARBs) are contraindicated in pregnancy; avoid in women who are or may become pregnant (S5; S7).

whys.C: ACE inhibitors (and ARBs) are contraindicated in pregnancy; avoid in women who are or may become pregnant (S5; S7).

quiz.label: Q2 · Clinical vignette · RAAS Blockers

quiz.stem: Why are ACE inhibitors and ARBs preferred in proteinuric CKD beyond lowering blood pressure?

options.A: They raise GFR by expanding volume
options.B: They increase aldosterone to retain sodium
options.C: They constrict the afferent arteriole
options.E: They are the only class allowed in CKD

quiz.why: Reducing angiotensin II preferentially dilates the efferent arteriole, lowering intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria (S8; SG U5-R8).

whys.D: Reducing angiotensin II preferentially dilates the efferent arteriole, lowering intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria (S8; SG U5-R8).

quiz.label: Q3 · Mechanism · RAAS Blockers

quiz.stem: A patient on metoprolol develops heart block after a second drug is added for blood pressure. Which drug most likely?

options.B: Lisinopril
options.C: Verapamil

quiz.why: Non-dihydropyridines (diltiazem, verapamil) with a beta-blocker risk bradycardia and AV block (S13).

whys.C: Non-dihydropyridines (diltiazem, verapamil) with a beta-blocker risk bradycardia and AV block (S13).

quiz.label: Q4 · Clinical vignette · Other Antihypertensives & Resistant Hypertension

quiz.stem: A pregnant patient needs an oral antihypertensive. Which central agent is the preferred option on the slides?

options.B: Methyldopa
options.C: Losartan

quiz.why: Methyldopa is used in pregnancy (S12; S16; S50).

whys.B: Methyldopa is used in pregnancy (S12; S16; S50).
whys.D: Rebound risk; not the pregnancy agent (S16).

quiz.label: Q5 · Clinical vignette · Other Antihypertensives & Resistant Hypertension

quiz.stem: Why must hydralazine be paired with a beta-blocker and a diuretic?

options.A: To reduce its hepatic first-pass loss
options.B: To prevent bradykinin cough
options.C: To avoid hyperkalemia from RAAS blockade
options.D: To block reflex tachycardia and fluid retention
options.E: To prevent rebound hypertension on stopping

quiz.why: Direct arteriolar dilation triggers reflex tachycardia and fluid retention (S16).

whys.D: Direct arteriolar dilation triggers reflex tachycardia and fluid retention (S16).

quiz.label: Q6 · Mechanism · Other Antihypertensives & Resistant Hypertension

quiz.stem: What happens if clonidine is stopped abruptly?

options.B: Drug-induced lupus
options.C: Bradykinin cough

quiz.why: Abrupt clonidine withdrawal causes rebound hypertension (S16; S49).

whys.E: Abrupt clonidine withdrawal causes rebound hypertension (S16; S49).

quiz.label: Q7 · Mechanism · Other Antihypertensives & Resistant Hypertension

quiz.stem: A man using sildenafil asks for a nitroglycerin prescription for chest pain. What is the key concern?

options.B: Faster nitrate tolerance only
options.C: Life-threatening hypotension

quiz.why: Concurrent PDE5 inhibitors are an absolute contraindication to nitrates — severe hypotension (S19–S20).

whys.C: Concurrent PDE5 inhibitors are an absolute contraindication to nitrates — severe hypotension (S19–S20).

quiz.label: Q8 · Clinical vignette · Nitrates, Angina & the Triple Whammy

quiz.stem: How do nitrates relieve angina?

options.A: They inhibit PDE5 to raise cAMP
options.B: NO raises cGMP, venodilation cuts preload
options.C: They block β1 receptors to slow the heart
options.E: They block ACE to lower angiotensin II

quiz.why: Nitrates release NO → guanylate cyclase → cGMP → venodilation, reducing preload and oxygen demand (S19–S20).

whys.B: Nitrates release NO → guanylate cyclase → cGMP → venodilation, reducing preload and oxygen demand (S19–S20).

quiz.label: Q9 · Mechanism · Nitrates, Angina & the Triple Whammy

quiz.stem: Why does a patient on long-acting isosorbide mononitrate need a nitrate-free interval?

options.B: To clear its toxic metabolite
options.C: To let potassium normalize

quiz.why: Tolerance develops with continuous exposure; a nitrate-free interval (typically overnight) maintains efficacy (S19).

whys.A: Tolerance develops with continuous exposure; a nitrate-free interval (typically overnight) maintains efficacy (S19).

quiz.label: Q10 · Mechanism · Nitrates, Angina & the Triple Whammy

quiz.stem: Which drug class is used for both hypertension and angina via the same mechanism?

options.B: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors
options.C: Calcium channel blockers

quiz.why: CCBs dilate arterioles, lowering afterload — treating both hypertension and angina (S22; SG U5-R10).

whys.C: CCBs dilate arterioles, lowering afterload — treating both hypertension and angina (S22; SG U5-R10).

quiz.label: Q11 · Mechanism · Nitrates, Angina & the Triple Whammy

quiz.stem: A 52-year-old with an intact uterus wants estradiol for hot flashes. What must be added?

options.B: A progestin to protect the endometrium
options.C: Nothing, if the dose is low

quiz.why: Unopposed estrogen with a uterus raises endometrial cancer risk; add a progestin (S6–S7).

whys.B: Unopposed estrogen with a uterus raises endometrial cancer risk; add a progestin (S6–S7).

quiz.label: Q1 · Clinical vignette · Estrogens, Progestins & Contraception

quiz.stem: A 36-year-old smoker with migraine with aura wants contraception. Which choice fits best?

options.B: A combined vaginal ring
options.C: A combined pill at the lowest dose

quiz.why: Estrogen is contraindicated; progestin-only methods avoid estrogen VTE risk and are the correct first choice (S9).

whys.D: Estrogen is contraindicated; progestin-only methods avoid estrogen VTE risk and are the correct first choice (S9).

quiz.label: Q2 · Clinical vignette · Estrogens, Progestins & Contraception

quiz.stem: How do progestins protect the endometrium in combined or hormone therapy?

options.A: They thin cervical mucus to aid clearance
options.B: They lower circulating estrogen levels
options.C: They block aromatase in the endometrium
options.D: They block estrogen receptors in the uterus

quiz.why: Progestins bind progesterone receptors, limiting estrogen-driven proliferation and maturing the endometrium (S6–S7).

whys.D: They act at PR, not ER (S6).
whys.E: Progestins bind progesterone receptors, limiting estrogen-driven proliferation and maturing the endometrium (S6–S7).

quiz.label: Q3 · Mechanism · Estrogens, Progestins & Contraception

quiz.stem: Which adverse effect is specific to depot medroxyprogesterone (DMPA) with prolonged use?

options.B: Hyperkalemia from potassium retention
options.C: Reversible bone mineral density loss

quiz.why: DMPA specifically causes reversible bone density loss with long-term use (boxed warning) (S6; S9; S31).

whys.C: DMPA specifically causes reversible bone density loss with long-term use (boxed warning) (S6; S9; S31).

quiz.label: Q4 · Mechanism · Estrogens, Progestins & Contraception

quiz.stem: A 30-year-old with factor V Leiden asks for contraception. Which feature of combined pills drives her main risk?

options.B: The estrogen component (VTE)

quiz.stem: Which overactive bladder medication is generally preferred in an older adult already taking multiple anticholinergic medications?

options.B: Oxybutynin, for its high potency
options.C: Any antimuscarinic agent, since they are interchangeable
options.D: No pharmacologic therapy should be used in older adults

quiz.why: Because mirabegron works by enhancing beta3-mediated detrusor relaxation rather than blocking muscarinic receptors, it avoids adding to a patient's cumulative anticholinergic burden — a key consideration in older adults, who are more susceptible to anticholinergic-related confusion and cognitive impairment.

quiz.stem: Why is the combination of a nitrate and a PDE5 inhibitor absolutely contraindicated?

options.A: Both drugs independently raise NO/cGMP signaling, and together can cause life-threatening hypotension
options.B: Nitrates block the PDE5 enzyme, making PDE5 inhibitors ineffective
options.C: The combination has no significant interaction and is commonly prescribed together
options.D: PDE5 inhibitors increase nitrate metabolism, reducing anti-anginal efficacy

quiz.why: Nitrates raise NO/cGMP systemically (the mechanism behind their anti-anginal effect), while PDE5 inhibitors prevent cGMP breakdown. Combined, these two independent mechanisms produce profound vasodilation and can precipitate severe, potentially fatal hypotension — the same NO-cGMP pathway shown in Figure 16, now viewed as a drug-interaction risk rather than a therapeutic mechanism.

quiz.stem: Across this unit, what is the common thread linking alpha1 blockers' orthostatic hypotension risk and the nitrate/PDE5-inhibitor contraindication?

options.B: Both are reasons to avoid all genitourinary pharmacology in older adults
options.C: Both are unrelated adverse effects with no shared mechanism
options.D: Both apply only to patients with no cardiovascular disease

quiz.why: Alpha1 blockers act on the same receptor family in the bladder neck/prostate and in blood vessels, and PDE5 inhibitors/nitrates both converge on the same NO-cGMP signaling pathway used in both the corpus cavernosum and the vasculature. Recognizing receptor families as the shared variable — not organ system — is what ties genitourinary and cardiovascular pharmacology together across Units 5 and 6.

quiz.stem: Why is unopposed estrogen avoided in a patient with an intact uterus?

brief.part: L01 · Part 1 · The Language of Pharmacology
hy: PK = what the body does to the drug (ADME); PD = what the drug does to the body (receptors & effect).
ADR = unintended, harmful, at **normal therapeutic doses**; toxicity = dose/exposure **exceeds the therapeutic range**.
Learn, prescribe, and counsel by **generic name** — brand names can hide a shared ingredient → double-dosing.
Pharmacology connects a drug's chemistry to its clinical effect.
traps: "Therapeutic effect" and "pharmacologic effect" are not synonyms — a drug can have pharmacologic effects that are not therapeutic (that is often exactly what an adverse effect is).
ADR vs. toxicity: an ADR happens at normal therapeutic doses; toxicity happens when dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range.
Generic names do NOT vary by manufacturer (one per drug); brand names DO vary — and change between countries.

brief.part: L01 · Part 2 · Drug Development & Regulation
hy: **Efficacy** = ideal trial conditions; **effectiveness** = everyday practice (adherence, comorbidities).
Phase I healthy volunteers → II few hundred patients → III hundreds–thousands (confirm) → IV postmarketing.
Rare adverse effects (1 in 10,000) are often first found in Phase IV.
Risk-benefit is always comparative — ask "compared to what?"
traps: Efficacy vs. effectiveness is a favorite exam distinction: efficacy is the trial result; effectiveness is what happens once real patients with real adherence patterns use the drug.
Phase III — not Phase I, II, or IV — is the large pre-approval trial that confirms efficacy and monitors safety at scale.
Phase III is what most people picture as "the" clinical trial, but regulatory decisions already begin shaping the drug long before that.

brief.part: L01 · Part 3 · Pharmacodynamics: Targets & Receptors
hy: Drug → target → signal transduction → response.
Five target classes: receptors, ion channels, enzymes, transporters, nucleic acids.
Competitive antagonist = curve **shifts right, same Emax**; noncompetitive/irreversible = **lower Emax**.
Inverse agonist lowers baseline activity below normal; an antagonist only blocks.
Pharmacodynamics explains how drugs bind receptors to produce agonism or antagonism.
traps: Classic exam trap: a competitive antagonist shifts the dose-response curve **right** (same Emax, more drug needed); a noncompetitive/irreversible antagonist **lowers the Emax** instead.

A rightward shift with an unchanged plateau is the graphical signature of competitive antagonism — potency falls, but because the antagonism is surmountable, enough agonist can still reach the original Emax.
Inverse agonist ≠ antagonist: only the inverse agonist lowers baseline activity below normal, without any agonist present.
Study-guide distractor: "has no effect on receptor activity whatsoever" matches none of the agonist/antagonist types.

brief.part: L01 · Part 4 · Dose-Response Relationships
hy: **Potency** = dose needed (EC₅₀, lower = more potent); **efficacy** = Emax (ceiling).
Potency and efficacy are independent; efficacy matters more clinically.
**TI = TD₅₀ ÷ ED₅₀**; narrow TI → careful dosing + blood-level monitoring.
Narrow-TI drugs: **warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin**.
traps: A drug can be very potent (tiny dose) but have low efficacy — potency alone never tells you whether a drug "works better."
Same Emax + lower dose needed = MORE POTENT, EQUALLY efficacious — not "more efficacious."
EC₅₀ measures potency — not toxicity and not bioavailability.
A narrow-TI drug is not "safer because it needs a lower dose" — it has a smaller margin and needs closer monitoring.

brief.part: L01 · Part 5 · Pharmacokinetics: ADME — Absorption & Distribution
hy: **F** = fraction of dose reaching systemic circulation unchanged; IV = 100%.
First-pass: oral → GI → portal → liver → systemic; big examples nitroglycerin, propranolol, morphine.
Every route except oral bypasses first-pass (sublingual = direct to systemic veins).
Only **free (unbound)** drug is active; high **Vd** = drug mostly in tissue (e.g., digoxin).
BBB: small, lipophilic, non-ionized drugs cross; P-glycoprotein pumps some back out.
traps: IV = 100% bioavailable with no absorption phase; oral is less than 100%.
Taking an oral drug with food or on an empty stomach does not bypass first-pass metabolism — sublingual does.
A very high Vd does not mean a big anatomic space — it means the drug is mostly in tissue, not plasma.
Only free (unbound) drug is active and can cross membranes — protein-bound drug cannot.

brief.part: L02 · Part 1 · Drug Metabolism & CYP450 Interactions
hy: Phase I (CYP450): oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis. Phase II: conjugation → water-soluble.
**Inhibitor → substrate ↑ → toxicity**; **inducer → substrate ↓ → therapeutic failure**.
Narrow-TI substrate + CYP inhibitor = especially dangerous.
Metabolism can produce toxic metabolites (e.g., NAPQI).
traps: Inhibitor → substrate level UP (toxicity); inducer → substrate level DOWN (therapeutic failure). Don't swap them.
CYP3A4 is a Phase I (CYP450) enzyme — it does not "only affect Phase II metabolism."
Not every drug goes through Phase I first — some go straight to Phase II conjugation.

brief.part: L02 · Part 2 · Drug Excretion & Renal Dosing
hy: Kidney = dominant elimination route; filtration (free drug), secretion (transporters), reabsorption (lipophilic, un-ionized).
**↓ renal function → ↓ clearance → ↑ exposure** → lower dose and/or longer interval, guided by **eGFR/CrCl**.
Renally cleared narrow-TI drugs: many antibiotics, digoxin, lithium.
traps: Only FREE (unbound) drug is filtered at the glomerulus.
Reabsorption REDUCES net elimination — and only lipophilic, un-ionized drug is reabsorbed.
Renal impairment → lower dose and/or longer interval — NOT "no adjustment," a higher dose, or "IV only."

brief.part: L02 · Part 3 · PK Calculations: Half-Life, Steady State & Clearance
hy: **t½** = time for plasma concentration to fall 50%; set by **clearance + Vd**.
Each t½ halves what remains: 50 → 25 → 12.5 → 6.25 → ~3% (~97% eliminated at 5 t½).
**Steady state ≈ 4–5 t½**, regardless of dose; loading dose gets there immediately.
**Clearance** = plasma volume cleared per unit time; total = hepatic + renal.
CKD: clearance ↓ → t½ ↑ → concentration ↑ → adjust dose and/or interval.
traps: After 3 half-lives, 12.5% REMAINS (87.5% eliminated) — read whether the question asks remaining or eliminated.
Time to steady state depends on half-life — not on dose size, bioavailability, or route.
Half-life is not a fixed property — it changes with clearance and Vd (e.g., in renal impairment).
A loading dose does NOT permanently lower the maintenance dose or eliminate monitoring.

brief.part: L02 · Part 4 · Pharmacogenomics
hy: Pharmacogenomics = genetic variation changing drug response (metabolism, transport, target, ADR risk).
**HLA-B*5801 + allopurinol** → severe hypersensitivity risk.
CYP2D6–codeine; CYP2C19–clopidogrel; TPMT–azathioprine.
Genotype is **one input among several**.
traps: HLA-B*5801 before allopurinol = severe hypersensitivity risk — not absorption, not taste, and not irrelevant to drug selection.
Genotype is one input — never the sole basis for therapy.

brief.part: L02 · Part 5 · Putting It All Together: Clinical Decision-Making
hy: Memorize the checklist: indication, contraindications/allergies, renal/hepatic, interactions (CYP450), age/pregnancy, dose/route/monitoring.
**Always check CYP450 interactions before adding a new drug.**
These five ideas are the toolkit for every drug class for the rest of the course, starting with musculoskeletal pharmacology.
traps: The single check most aimed at preventing a toxic, predictable drug-drug interaction is reviewing CYP450 interactions — not brand name, chemical name, or half-life alone.
Weaker home-medication effect + restored by a higher dose = competitive; not restored = irreversible.
Reviewing indication, contraindications, renal/hepatic function, interactions, and monitoring = the clinical decision-making framework — not pharmacogenomic testing or Phase IV surveillance.

brief.part: L03 · Part 1 · Musculoskeletal Pain & the Inflammatory Cascade
hy: Injury → mediators → nociceptor sensitization → pain.
Musculoskeletal pain is driven by inflammatory mediators (prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, cytokines) — NSAIDs and corticosteroids intervene at different points along this cascade.
Corticosteroids = phospholipase A₂ (broad); NSAIDs = COX (prostaglandins).
Prostaglandins drive inflammatory pain, and COX makes them.
traps: Corticosteroids act **upstream** at phospholipase A₂, not at COX — that is why their effect is broader than an NSAID’s.
The lecture’s drugs target nociceptive and inflammatory pain; neuropathic pain is a different unit.

brief.part: L03 · Part 2 · Acetaminophen
hy: Acetaminophen treats pain and fever but is not a reliable anti-inflammatory agent; its overdose toxicity is mediated by NAPQI accumulation.
Overdose: glutathione depleted → NAPQI → hepatocyte injury.
Antidote: N-acetylcysteine (glutathione precursor).
Ask about ALL sources — combination cold/flu/sleep products hide acetaminophen.
Acetaminophen is central, with no real anti-inflammatory effect. Overdose means NAPQI, and the antidote is NAC.

brief.part: L03 · Part 3 · NSAIDs & COX-2 Selective Inhibition
hy: COX-1 = housekeeping (gastric protection, renal blood flow); COX-2 = inflammation.
NSAIDs are effective but carry real GI, renal, and cardiovascular risk; celecoxib trades GI risk for cardiovascular risk (renal risk similar).
NSAID harms: GI, renal, cardiovascular.
Triple whammy: NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic → AKI.
Ketorolac: short-term only; significant GI/renal risk.
COX-1 protects the stomach, platelets and kidney. Nonselective NSAIDs block both isoforms.
Celecoxib cuts GI risk but raises cardiovascular risk, and does not spare the kidney.

brief.part: L03 · Part 4 · Osteoarthritis, Rheumatoid Arthritis & DMARDs
hy: OA = degenerative → pain control; RA = autoimmune → suppress disease activity.
OA ladder: acetaminophen → oral or topical NSAIDs → intra-articular steroids for a single-joint flare.
DMARDs (conventional and biologic — methotrexate, adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, tocilizumab, rituximab, abatacept) modify RA’s disease course rather than only masking symptoms.
Methotrexate: DHFR inhibitor, **weekly**, with folate.
Methotrexate toxicity: liver, marrow, lung; teratogenic.
HCQ = milder RA; sulfasalazine = combinations; leflunomide = if MTX not tolerated.
DMARDs change disease. Methotrexate is weekly, and screen for TB and hepatitis before biologics.
TNF: adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab · IL-6: tocilizumab · B cell: rituximab · T-cell costimulation: abatacept.
Shared risk: immunosuppression → infection.
Before biologics: TB + hepatitis B/C screening, update (live) vaccines.

brief.part: L04 · Part 1 · Gout: Acute Flares & Urate-Lowering Therapy
hy: Acute gout treatment and chronic urate-lowering therapy are different goals, started at different times.
Flare: colchicine, NSAID, or corticosteroid. Prevention: allopurinol/febuxostat (↓ production) or probenecid (↑ excretion).
Colchicine: microtubules; best within 24 h; diarrhea; CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors.
Allopurinol: HLA-B*58:01; febuxostat: boxed CV death warning.
Pegloticase/rasburicase: no G6PD deficiency.

brief.part: L04 · Part 2 · Skeletal Muscle Relaxants
hy: Central (cyclobenzaprine, tizanidine, baclofen) vs. peripheral (dantrolene — muscle; botulinum — junction).
Dantrolene blocks RyR1 SR Ca²⁺ release → malignant hyperthermia.
Baclofen: GABA-B; never stop intrathecal abruptly.
Tizanidine: α2; LFTs; no ciprofloxacin/fluvoxamine.
Cyclobenzaprine: anticholinergic, Beers list, 2–3 weeks.

brief.part: L04 · Part 3 · Bone Pharmacology & Osteoporosis
hy: Bone pharmacology is fundamentally about the balance between osteoblast and osteoclast activity.
PTH: falling calcium → bone resorption, renal reabsorption, vitamin D–mediated gut absorption.
Bisphosphonates first-line; full glass of water, upright 30 minutes.
Anabolic: teriparatide/abaloparatide (2-year limit), romosozumab (boxed CV).
Denosumab = RANKL antibody; stopping → rebound vertebral fractures.
Glucocorticoids: ↑ resorption, ↓ formation → osteoporosis.

brief.part: L04 · Part 4 · Putting It All Together: Musculoskeletal Toolkit
hy: Five takeaways: pain ≠ inflammation; NSAIDs = GI/renal/CV risk; DMARDs change RA; gout = acute vs. chronic; bone = osteoblast vs. osteoclast.
traps: Colchicine treats the flare but **does not lower uric acid**; probenecid is **not** a xanthine oxidase inhibitor.
Baclofen is a GABA-B agonist — not a calcium channel blocker in skeletal muscle (that idea belongs to dantrolene’s RyR1 site).

OA in the CKD + anticoagulant + hypertension patient: oral NSAIDs carry the highest combined risk — CKD (renal/AKI risk), anticoagulant (bleeding risk), hypertension (BP/CV risk); acetaminophen or a topical NSAID is generally safer first-line.

When that patient flares with gout: an oral NSAID is still relatively contraindicated; a short corticosteroid course (oral or intra-articular) is often preferred, colchicine needs renal dose adjustment. Defer allopurinol/febuxostat until the flare resolves.

brief.part: L05 · Part 1 · Acid-Peptic Disease & Gastric Acid Secretion
hy: Acid-peptic disease reflects an imbalance between mucosal defense and aggressive factors (acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs).
H. pylori and NSAIDs cause most PUD.
traps: H2RAs block only the histamine input; gastrin and acetylcholine still drive the pump — PPIs block the final common pathway regardless of which input is active.

brief.part: L05 · Part 2 · Antacids, H2 Blockers & Proton Pump Inhibitors
hy: PPIs block the parietal cell’s final common pathway and are the most potent antisecretory agents, but carry real long-term risks (B12 deficiency, hypomagnesemia, fracture, C. difficile).
Antacids: fast, short, don’t reduce production; separate other drugs by 2 hours.
Cimetidine: CYP inhibitor + gynecomastia; famotidine: renal dosing, minimal CYP.
Omeprazole + clopidogrel: CYP2C19 inhibition blunts activation.

brief.part: L05 · Part 3 · Mucosal Protectants & H. pylori Eradication
hy: H. pylori eradication requires multi-drug regimens (triple or bismuth quadruple therapy), not acid suppression alone.
Misoprostol: PGE1 analog, NSAID-ulcer prevention, never in pregnancy.
Sucralfate needs acid; separate from other drugs by 2 hours.

brief.part: L05 · Part 4 · Antiemetics
hy: Antiemetics are organized by the receptor pathway they block — serotonin (5-HT3), dopamine/neurokinin (CTZ), or histamine/acetylcholine (vestibular) — all converging on the vomiting center.
Metoclopramide: boxed tardive dyskinesia; avoid beyond 12 weeks.
Ondansetron: QT prolongation; give before chemo.

brief.part: L06 · Part 1 · Laxatives & Antidiarrheals
hy: Four laxative buckets: bulk-forming (slowest, safest), osmotic (fast; PEG first-line), stimulant (short-term), secretagogue (IBS-C).
No antimotility agents in C. difficile or bloody/febrile diarrhea.

brief.part: L06 · Part 2 · Inflammatory Bowel Disease
hy: IBD therapy follows a step-wise escalation matched to disease severity — from 5-ASA agents to biologics/small molecules.
Biologic agents share both their targeted mechanisms and their immunosuppression-related safety profile across organ systems (RA in Lecture 2, IBD here).
TPMT/NUDT15 before thiopurines; allopurinol → cut dose by 2/3–3/4.

brief.part: L06 · Part 3 · Nutrition, Vitamins & Dietary Supplements
hy: Nutrition and dietary supplements are not inert — vitamin status, drug-nutrient interactions, and herbal supplements can all meaningfully change drug therapy outcomes.
St. John’s wort induces CYP3A4 → warfarin cleared faster → lower INR.
Long-term PPI or metformin → check B12.
Refeeding: start slowly, check phosphate/potassium/magnesium, thiamine first.

brief.part: L06 · Part 4 · Putting It All Together: GI & Nutrition Toolkit
hy: Five takeaways: pathway targets · PPI risks · IBD step therapy · shared biologic risk · supplements matter.
traps: **Integrated case:** H. pylori + penicillin allergy + macrolide two months ago → bismuth quadruple therapy (allergy rules out amoxicillin triple therapy; macrolide exposure raises clarithromycin-resistance concern).
Her subtherapeutic INR is St. John’s Wort inducing CYP3A4 — stop the supplement (or adjust warfarin) with close INR monitoring.

brief.part: L07 · Part 1 · Pituitary: GH, Prolactin & ADH
hy: Acromegaly: octreotide/lanreotide or pegvisomant (monitor IGF-1); prolactinoma: cabergoline; DI: desmopressin (hyponatremia); SIADH: fluid restriction, then tolvaptan.

brief.part: L07 · Part 2 · Thyroid & Antithyroid Drugs
hy: Levothyroxine: empty stomach, separate calcium/iron/antacids by 4 h, TSH at 6–8 weeks, start low in older/cardiac patients.
PTU for storm and first trimester; methimazole otherwise; fever/sore throat → stop, CBC.

brief.part: L07 · Part 3 · Adrenocorticosteroids & Antagonists
hy: Chronic steroids suppress CRH/ACTH → taper; abrupt stop → adrenal crisis → IV hydrocortisone + fluids.
Addison disease needs a glucocorticoid plus fludrocortisone.

brief.part: L08 · Part 1 · Gonadal Hormones & Inhibitors
hy: No estrogen with prior VTE/stroke, smoker ≥ 35, migraine with aura, estrogen-sensitive cancer, uncontrolled hypertension → progestin-only.
Tamoxifen: endometrial agonist (report bleeding); raloxifene: bone agonist, endometrium blocked; both VTE.

brief.part: L08 · Part 2 · Insulin
hy: Insulin’s main risk is hypoglycemia; beta-blockers mask its warning signs; only regular insulin goes IV.

brief.part: L08 · Part 3 · Non-Insulin Glucose-Lowering Drugs
hy: Metformin first-line (no weight gain, low hypoglycemia); avoid eGFR < 30; hold for contrast; B12.
Older adult with falls → DPP-4 or SGLT2, not a sulfonylurea.

brief.part: L08 · Part 4 · Parathyroid Disorders
hy: High PTH (CKD) → cinacalcet, watch hypocalcemia; low PTH (post-thyroidectomy) → calcitriol + calcium, watch hypercalcemia.

brief.part: L08 · Part 5 · Putting It All Together: Endocrine Toolkit
hy: Five takeaways: shared axis template · know where each drug intervenes · glucose drugs by site · opposite parathyroid strategies · cross-system drugs.
traps: Choosing the most potent glucose-lowering drug instead of the safest for an older adult who falls.

Integrated case — diabetes: a DPP-4 or SGLT2 inhibitor is preferable to a sulfonylurea given the fall history — sulfonylureas force glucose-independent insulin release, raising hypoglycemia-driven fall risk.

Integrated case — thyroid storm: beta-blocker + PTU first, then iodine solution only after PTU (never before — iodine first would supply substrate for new hormone synthesis before synthesis is blocked, worsening the crisis).
Corticosteroids also help in thyroid storm by blunting peripheral conversion and covering relative adrenal insufficiency.

Shared concept: effective endocrine drug selection depends on knowing exactly where in a pathway (or which receptor/site) a drug acts — that position determines both its efficacy and its specific risks.

brief.part: L09 · Part 1 · Renal Dosing & Diuretic Sites
hy: Falling GFR → accumulation → toxicity: cut the maintenance dose, stretch the interval, or both; check CrCl first.
Sodium reabsorbed: proximal ~65%, loop ~25%, distal 5–8%, collecting duct 2–3%.

brief.part: L09 · Part 2 · Loop & Thiazide Diuretics
hy: Loop = NKCC2, thick ascending limb, most potent, ↑ Ca²⁺ excretion, ototoxicity. Thiazide = NCC, DCT, first-line HTN, ↓ Ca²⁺ excretion.
Thiazides fade below GFR ~30 → switch to a loop.

brief.part: L09 · Part 3 · Potassium-Sparing, CAI & Osmotic Diuretics
hy: Potassium-sparing: aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) and ENaC blockers (amiloride, triamterene); hyperkalemia worsens with ACEi/ARB or CKD.
Acetazolamide = glaucoma, altitude sickness, alkalosis; mannitol = ICP/IOP.

brief.part: L10 · Part 1 · RAAS Blockers
hy: ACEi/ARB first-line in proteinuric CKD: efferent dilation lowers intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria.
Creatinine rise up to ~30% is expected; check K⁺ and creatinine in 1–2 weeks; sick-day rules; never in pregnancy.

brief.part: L10 · Part 2 · Other Antihypertensives & Resistant Hypertension
hy: Non-DHP CCB + beta-blocker → bradycardia/AV block; DHP + beta-blocker is fine.
Resistant HTN in CKD: fix the diuretic first (thiazide → loop), then spironolactone with K⁺ monitoring.

brief.part: L10 · Part 3 · Nitrates, Angina & the Triple Whammy
hy: Nitrates: NO → cGMP → venodilation, ↓ preload; nitrate-free interval; never with PDE5 inhibitors.
Triple whammy: NSAID (afferent) + ACEi/ARB (efferent) + diuretic (volume) → AKI; counsel on OTC NSAIDs.

brief.part: L10 · Part 4 · Putting It All Together: Renal Toolkit
hy: Five takeaways: two targetable maps · ACEi/ARB renoprotection · CCB overlap · triple whammy · HTN–CKD cycle.
traps: Reflexively stopping an ACE inhibitor for a ≤30% creatinine rise is the classic trap.
Adding a new drug class when the real problem is a thiazide at low GFR.

brief.part: L11 · Part 1 · Estrogens, Progestins & Contraception
hy: Estrogen = VTE (smoking, age > 35, VTE history); unopposed estrogen = endometrial cancer → always pair with a progestin if the uterus is intact.
Estrogen contraindicated → progestin-only is the right first choice; DMPA = reversible bone loss.

brief.part: L11 · Part 2 · SERMs, Aromatase Inhibitors & Androgens
hy: Tamoxifen: breast antagonist, endometrial agonist → bleeding needs evaluation; raloxifene: endometrium neutral; both VTE.
Aromatase inhibitors: postmenopausal only; bone loss and joint pain.

brief.part: L11 · Part 3 · PCOS & the Reproductive-Metabolic Overlap
hy: PCOS = insulin resistance ↔ hyperandrogenism cycle; metformin (metabolic) + combined contraception (cycles, hirsutism) are usually combined.

brief.part: L12 · Part 1 · Autonomic Control of the Lower Urinary Tract
hy: M3 (detrusor) contracts to void; alpha1 (neck) closes and beta3 (detrusor) relaxes to store.

brief.part: L12 · Part 2 · Overactive Bladder Drugs
hy: OAB in an older adult or anyone on other anticholinergics → mirabegron; oxybutynin has the highest CNS burden.

brief.part: L12 · Part 3 · BPH, Erectile Dysfunction & PDE5 Inhibitors
hy: BPH: alpha1 blocker (days; orthostasis, first dose) + 5-ARI (3–6 months; PSA halved) — often together.
PDE5 inhibitor + any nitrate = absolute contraindication; caution with alpha1 blockers.

brief.part: L12 · Part 4 · Putting It All Together: GU Toolkit
hy: GU receptor families recur in the vasculature: alpha1 blockers lower BP; PDE5 inhibitors and nitrates share cGMP.
traps: Integrated case: a PDE5 inhibitor should not be prescribed while this patient remains on isosorbide mononitrate — both drugs independently raise NO/cGMP signaling; the combination can cause profound, life-threatening hypotension.
This is an absolute contraindication, and any ED treatment decision must involve his cardiologist and consideration of whether his anginal nitrate therapy can be modified first.

Even without the nitrate, tamsulosin and a PDE5 inhibitor both lower blood pressure (alpha1 blockade and NO-cGMP potentiation) — additive orthostatic hypotension warrants spacing doses or close monitoring.
His wife’s new vaginal bleeding on tamoxifen should not be dismissed — tamoxifen’s endometrial agonism raises hyperplasia/cancer risk; she needs prompt gynecologic evaluation.

Match each drug or drug class to its mechanism or site of action — tamoxifen: breast antagonist, bone/endometrium agonist; raloxifene — endometrium neutral; finasteride/dutasteride — 5-alpha-reductase inhibition; oxybutynin — M3 (and M2) antagonism on the detrusor.

Match: mirabegron — beta3 agonism on the detrusor; tamsulosin — uroselective alpha1 antagonism; sildenafil/tadalafil — PDE5 inhibition prolonging cGMP; metformin (PCOS) — insulin sensitization, indirectly lowering ovarian androgens.

summary.text: Pharmacology studies how drugs interact with living systems: **pharmacokinetics** is what the body does to the drug (ADME), and **pharmacodynamics** is what the drug does to the body.
Learn and prescribe by **generic name** — brand names can hide a shared ingredient and cause unintentional double-dosing.
Drugs move from discovery through preclinical testing, **Phase I–III** trials, FDA review, and **Phase IV** postmarketing surveillance — where rare adverse effects are often first found.

Metabolism inactivates drugs, activates prodrugs, or makes active or **toxic metabolites** (e.g., NAPQI); **Phase I** (CYP450 oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) functionalizes and **Phase II** conjugates for excretion.
A **CYP inhibitor raises** a substrate's level (toxicity) and an **inducer lowers** it (therapeutic failure) — always check CYP450 interactions before adding a drug.
The **kidney** is the main elimination route — filtration of free drug, active secretion, reabsorption of lipophilic un-ionized drug — and less renal function means less clearance and more exposure.
Tissue injury releases **prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines** that sensitize nociceptors; **corticosteroids** block phospholipase A₂ upstream, while **NSAIDs** block COX.
summary.src: S6; S9; SG U2-R1; SG U2-R2

summary.text: **Acetaminophen** treats pain and fever but is not a reliable anti-inflammatory; overdose depletes glutathione so **NAPQI** injures the liver, and **N-acetylcysteine** is the antidote.

**COX-1** is the housekeeping enzyme (gastric protection, renal blood flow) and **COX-2** makes inflammatory prostaglandins; **celecoxib** lowers GI risk but raises cardiovascular risk, with similar renal risk.
summary.src: S26; S29; SG U2-R4; SG U2-R5

summary.text: Gout runs **purine → uric acid (xanthine oxidase) → urate crystals → neutrophil flare**; treat the **flare** with colchicine, an NSAID, or a corticosteroid, and **never start urate-lowering therapy during a flare**.

**Allopurinol/febuxostat** cut uric acid production (xanthine oxidase), **probenecid** raises excretion (URAT1), and **pegloticase** breaks uric acid down — watch HLA-B*58:01, febuxostat’s CV boxed warning, and G6PD deficiency.
Muscle relaxants sort by site: **central** (baclofen GABA-B, tizanidine α2, cyclobenzaprine brainstem) vs. **peripheral** (**dantrolene** on RyR1 in muscle; botulinum toxin at the junction).
Acid-peptic disease is a **balance**: acid, pepsin, H. pylori and NSAIDs push against mucus, bicarbonate, prostaglandins and epithelial turnover.
Gastrin, histamine and acetylcholine converge on the **proton pump**: **H2 blockers** cut one input, **PPIs** block the final common pathway, **antacids** neutralize acid already made.
PPIs are the most potent but carry long-term risks — **B12 deficiency, hypomagnesemia, fractures, C. difficile** — and omeprazole blunts **clopidogrel** via CYP2C19.

Laxatives fall into four buckets — **bulk-forming** (slowest, safest), **osmotic** (fast; PEG first-line), **stimulant** (short-term), **secretagogue** (IBS-C) — and osmotic/stimulant act in hours, bulk-forming in days.
**Loperamide** and **diphenoxylate/atropine** slow the gut via mu receptors; never use them in **C. difficile** or bloody/febrile diarrhea, and atropine is there to deter misuse.
IBD therapy **steps up with severity**: 5-ASA → short-term steroids → thiopurines for maintenance (test TPMT/NUDT15; cut dose with allopurinol) → biologics/small molecules.
One **axis** (hypothalamus → pituitary → gland) with **negative feedback**: every exogenous hormone suppresses the levels above it.

**Acromegaly**: octreotide/lanreotide or pegvisomant (monitor IGF-1); **prolactinoma**: cabergoline; **DI**: desmopressin (hyponatremia); **SIADH**: fluid restriction, then tolvaptan (start in hospital).
summary.src: S6; S8; S10; SG U4-R2; SG U4-R3; SG U4-R4

summary.text: **Levothyroxine**: empty stomach, separate calcium/iron/antacids by 4 h, TSH at 6–8 weeks, start low in older/cardiac patients.

**Combined contraception** suppresses GnRH/FSH/LH; no estrogen with prior VTE/stroke, **smoker ≥ 35**, **migraine with aura**, estrogen-sensitive cancer, uncontrolled hypertension → progestin-only. Inducers (rifampin) need backup.
**Tamoxifen** blocks breast but activates endometrium (report bleeding); **raloxifene** activates bone, blocks endometrium; both raise VTE. **Finasteride** lowers DHT and halves PSA.
**Insulin**: rapid (lispro, aspart), short (regular — the only IV insulin), NPH, basal (glargine, detemir, degludec); main risk **hypoglycemia** (rule of 15; beta-blockers mask it).
Falling **GFR** makes renally cleared drugs **accumulate**: check CrCl first, then lower the maintenance dose, extend the interval, or both (loading doses often unchanged).
Each diuretic acts at one segment: **CAI/osmotic** proximal tubule, **loop** thick ascending limb, **thiazide** distal tubule, **K⁺-sparing** collecting duct.
**Loops** (NKCC2, ~25%) are most potent and **raise** urinary calcium; **thiazides** (NCC, ~5–8%) are first-line for hypertension and **lower** it.
The **RAAS**: angiotensinogen → (renin) → angiotensin I → (ACE) → angiotensin II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone; aliskiren, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and aldosterone antagonists each block one step.

**ACE inhibitors/ARBs** are first-line in proteinuric CKD: efferent dilation lowers glomerular pressure; a creatinine rise **up to ~30%** is expected; check K⁺/creatinine in 1–2 weeks; **never in pregnancy**.
summary.src: S5; S8; S10; SG U5-R8; SG U5-R9

summary.text: ACE-inhibitor **cough** is bradykinin, not allergy → switch to an **ARB**; angioedema → stop.
**Estrogens** bind ER-α/β (VTE risk with smoking, age > 35); **unopposed estrogen** with a uterus → endometrial cancer, so add a **progestin**.
summary.src: S5; S6; SG U6-R1; SG U6-R2

summary.text: Estrogen contraindicated (VTE, smoker > 35, migraine with aura) → **progestin-only** is the right first choice; **DMPA** = reversible bone loss.
**SERMs**: tamoxifen blocks breast but stimulates endometrium (new bleeding → evaluate); raloxifene is endometrium-neutral; both raise VTE.
Bladder map: **M3** contracts the detrusor (void); **alpha1** closes the neck and **beta3** relaxes the detrusor (store); somatic nicotinic holds the external sphincter.
**Antimuscarinics** block M3 — dry mouth, constipation, confusion; **oxybutynin** has the highest CNS burden → older adults get **mirabegron** (beta3; may raise BP).
**Alpha1 blockers** relax the outlet in days (orthostasis, first dose, floppy iris); tamsulosin/silodosin are uroselective.
